Coconut cream concentrate | 37.4 min. | 8.4 | 29 | 62.6 | 5.9 |- |} Coconut milk can also sometimes be confused with [[coconut water]]. Coconut water is the clear fluid found within the coconut seed, while coconut milk is the extracted liquid derived from the manual or mechanical crushing of the white inner flesh of mature coconuts.{{cite web|url=https://www.nutrition.org/asn-blog/2010/09/coconut-water/|title=Coconut water|publisher=American Society for Nutrition|date=13 September 2010|author=Henni S|access-date=6 March 2017|archive-date=7 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170307051330/https://www.nutrition.org/asn-blog/2010/09/coconut-water/|url-status=dead}}{{cite book |author=Tetra Pak|title=Coconut Handbook |date=2016 |chapter=Coconut Food Production|publisher=Tetra Pak International S.A. |isbn=978-91-7773-948-7 |url=https://coconuthandbook.tetrapak.com/chapter/coconut-food-production}} Coconut cream should also not be confused with [[creamed coconut]], which is a semi-solid paste made from finely ground coconut pulp, and [[#Cream of coconut|cream of coconut]], which is a processed product made from heavily sweetened coconut cream. ==Traditional preparation== [[File:Râper la pulpe du coco (Tieti, Nord, New Caledonia).jpg|thumb|upright|Coconut being grated]] Coconut milk is traditionally made by grating the white inner flesh of mature coconuts and mixing the shredded coconut pulp with a small amount of hot water in order to suspend the fat present in the grated pulp. The grating process can be carried out manually or by machine. [[Polynesians]] may use special bundles of fibre from [[sea hibiscus]], [[heliconia]] or [[coconut fibre|the coconut itself]] called ''tauaga'' to wring the milk from the meat.See: * {{cite book |last1=Kirch |first1=Patrick Vinton |title=The wet and the dry: irrigation and agricultural intensification in Polynesia |date=1994 |publisher=the University of Chicago press |location=Chicago |isbn=0-226-43749-3 |page=97}} * {{cite book |last1=Koch |first1=Gerd |title=The Material Culture of Tuvalu |date=1984 |publisher=Institute of Pacific Studies, [[University of the South Pacific]] |location=Suva |isbn=9820202051 |pages=78–80 }} * {{cite book |last1=David |first1=Mrs. Edgeworth |author1-link=Cara David |title=Funafuti, Or Three Months on a Coral Island: an Unscientific Account of a Scientific Expedition |date=1899 |publisher=John Murray |location=London |page=207}}{{cite web |title=Tauaga |url=https://www.aucklandmuseum.com/collections-research/collections/record/am_humanhistory-object-32327?c=ecrm%3AE22_Man-Made_Object&prdt=1981-&p=4&ordinal=6 |website=Collections Online|year=2023|publisher=[[Auckland War Memorial Museum]] |access-date=8 December 2024 |language=en}} [[File:The making of coconut milk 137 MKT - Instagram Images - 1080px x 1080px6.jpg|thumb|upright|Grated coconut being pressed through [[cheesecloth]]]] Coconut milk is traditionally divided into two grades: coconut cream (or thick coconut milk) and thin coconut milk. Coconut cream contains around 20% to 50% fat, and (thin) coconut milk contains 5% to 20% fat. Coconut cream is extracted from the first pressings of grated coconut pulp directly through [[cheesecloth]]. Sometimes a small amount of hot water is added, but usually coconut cream is extracted with no added water. Thin coconut milk is produced by subsequent pressings after soaking the squeezed coconut pulp with hot water.{{cite book |last1=Solomon |first1=Charmaine |title=The Complete Asian Cookbook: Indonesia, Malaysia & Singapore |date=2014 |publisher=Hardie Grant Books |isbn=978-1-74358-170-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NrXAAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT7}} [[Gravity separation]] can also be used to derive a top layer of coconut cream and a bottom layer of coconut skim milk. This is achieved by simply allowing the extracted liquid to stand for an hour. Conversely, coconut cream can be diluted into thinner coconut milk by simply adding water.{{cite journal |last1=Birosel |first1=D. M. |last2=Gonzales |first2=Antonia L. |last3=Santos |first3=Milagros P. |title=The nature and properties of the emulsifier system of oil globules in coconut milk and cream |journal=The Philippine Journal of Science |date=1963 |volume=92 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |url=http://philjournalsci.dost.gov.ph/images/pdf_upload/pjs1963/PJS_Vol_92_No1_Mar_1963.pdf}} [[File:തേങ്ങാപ്പാൽ പിഴിയൽ.JPG|thumb|Coconut milk preparation]] Traditionally prepared coconut milk is utilized immediately after being freshly extracted because it spoils easily when exposed to air. It becomes rancid after a few hours at room temperatures {{convert|28|to|30|°C|°F|abbr=on}} due to [[lipid oxidation]] and [[lipolysis]]. Rancid coconut milk gives off a strong unpleasant smell and has a distinctive soapy taste. [[File:Coco3wjf.JPG|thumb|upright|Thick coconut cream derived from the first pressings of the grated coconut]] As coconut cream contains a higher amount of soluble, suspended solids, it works well as a good ingredient for [[dessert]]s and rich and dry [[sauce]]s. Thinner milk contains a lesser amount of soluble solids, and is mainly used in general cooking. The distinction between coconut cream and thin coconut milk is not usually made in [[Western World|western nations]] as fresh coconut milk is uncommon in these countries, and most consumers buy coconut milk or cream in cartons or cans. Coconut milk is also an intermediate step in the traditional [[Coconut oil#Wet process|wet process]] methods of producing [[virgin coconut oil]] by gradual heating, churning, or fermentation. These methods, however, are less efficient than coconut oil production from [[copra]].{{cite book |last1=Kurian |first1=Alice |last2=Peter |first2=K.V. |title=Commercial Crops Technology |date=2007 |publisher=New India Publishing |isbn=978-8189422523 |pages=202–203 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2VFYqwA-Mn4C&pg=PA202}}{{cite book |last1=Grimwood |first1=Brian E. |title=Coconut Palm Products: Their Processing in Developing Countries |date=1975 |publisher=Food & Agriculture Organization |isbn=978-92-5-100853-9 |pages=183–187 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fY5hLeJ-WW4C&pg=PA183}} ===Coconut graters=== [[File:Coconut scrapper in Laclo.jpg|thumb|upright|Traditional coconut grater]] Coconut graters (also called "coconut scrapers"), a necessary tool for traditionally extracting coconut milk, were part of the [[material culture]] of the [[Austronesian peoples]]. From [[Island Southeast Asia]], it was carried along with the sea voyages of the [[Austronesian expansion]] both for colonization and trade, reaching as far as [[Polynesia]] in the east, and [[Madagascar]] and the [[Comoros]] in the west in prehistoric times. The technology also spread to non-Austronesian cultures in coastal [[East Africa]] by proximity.{{cite book|first1=Harriet Joseph|last1=Ottenheimer|editor1-first=Akshay|editor1-last=Sarathi|title =Early Maritime Cultures in East Africa and the Western Indian Ocean: Papers from a conference held at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (African Studies Program) 23–24 October 2015, with additional contributions|chapter =Zilo and Zahula|publisher =Archaeopress Publishing Ltd|year =2018|page=158|isbn = 978-1-78491-713-5}}{{cite book |editor1-last=Diamond |editor1-first=Jared |editor2-last=Robinson |editor2-first=James A. |last1=Kirch |first1=Patrick V. |title=Natural Experiments of History|chapter=Controlled Comparison and Polynesian Cultural Evolution |date=2010 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-07672-3 |page=22 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LdNCb_oHvIQC&pg=PA22}}{{cite journal |last1=Lew |first1=Christopher |title=Tracing the origin of the coconut (''Cocos nucifera'' L.) |journal=Prized Writing 2018–2019 |publisher= University of California, Davis|pages=143–157}} Manual coconut graters remain a standard kitchen equipment in households in the tropical [[Asia-Pacific]] and [[Eastern Africa]], underscoring the importance of coconut milk and coconut oil extraction in the [[Indo-Pacific]].{{cite web |last1=Iddison |first1=Phil |title=Katai: Coconut Scrapers |url=http://www.oxfordsymposium.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/Iddison.pdf |website=Oxford Symposium on Food & Cookery |access-date=18 April 2019 |archive-date=18 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418024949/http://www.oxfordsymposium.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/Iddison.pdf |url-status=dead }} The basic design of coconut graters consists of a low bench or stool with a horizontal serrated disk (made of metal in Asia and Africa, and stone or shell in Oceania) attached on one end. A person sits on the bench and repeatedly scrapes the inner surface of halved coconut shells with both hands over the metal disk. The scrapings are gathered by a container placed below.{{cite book |last1=Kirch |first1=Patrick Vinton |last2=Green |first2=Roger C. |title=Hawaiki, Ancestral Polynesia: An Essay in Historical Anthropology |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-78879-3 |page=152 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WRapfjQ_iTEC&pg=PA152}}{{cite news |last1=Pakkawan |first1=Assawin |title=Traditional coconut graters on show at southern funeral |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/news/general/1360263/traditional-coconut-graters-on-show-at-southern-funeral |website=Bangkok Post |date=14 November 2017 |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite book |last1=Aranas |first1=Jennifer |title=The Filipino-American Kitchen: Traditional Recipes, Contemporary Flavors |date=2012 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-1-4629-0491-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=71TRAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT34}} More modern mechanical coconut graters dating back to the mid-1800s consist of serrated blades with a hand crank. This version is believed to be a [[British Empire|British]] invention.{{cite book |last1=Snodgrass |first1=Mary Ellen |title=Encyclopedia of Kitchen History |date=2004 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-45572-9 |page=233 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SJGNAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA233}} ==Processed coconut milk products== [[File:Coconut milk production.jpg|thumb|upright|Mechanical coconut grinder]] Commercially processed coconut milk products use largely the same processes to extract coconut milk from pulp, though they use more mechanical equipment like deshelling machines, grinders and pulverizers, motorized coconut shredders, and coconut milk extractors. They differ significantly in the bottling or canning process, however. Processed coconut milk products are first filtered through a [[Mesh (scale)|100 mesh]] filters. They are [[pasteurized]] indirectly by [[double boiling]] at around {{convert|70|°C|°F|abbr=on}}, carefully not exceeding {{convert|80|°C|°F|abbr=on}}, the temperature at which coconut milk starts to coagulate. After pasteurization, they are immediately transferred to filling vessels and sealed before being cooled down. They are then packed into bottles, cans, or pouches and [[blast frozen]] for storage and transport.{{cite book|author =Philippine Coconut Authority|title =Coconut Processing Technologies: Coconut Milk|publisher =Department of Agriculture, Republic of the Philippines|series =FPDD Guide No. 2 – Series of 2014|year =2014|url =http://www.pca.da.gov.ph/pdf/techno/coconut_milk.pdf|archive-date =6 November 2020|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20201106130020/http://www.pca.da.gov.ph/pdf/techno/coconut_milk.pdf|url-status =dead}} Manufacturers of canned coconut milk typically combine diluted and comminuted milk with the addition of water as a filler. Depending on the brand and age of the milk itself, a thicker, more paste-like consistency floats to the top of the can (a gravity separation, similar to traditional methods), and is sometimes separated and used in [[recipe]]s that require coconut cream rather than coconut milk. Some brands sold in Western countries undergo [[Homogenization (chemistry)|homogenization]] and contain additional thickening agents and emulsifiers to prevent the milk from separating inside the can. Due to factors like pasteurization and minimal contact with oxygen, processed coconut milk generally has a longer shelf life than traditionally prepared coconut milk. It is also more efficient than traditional methods at extracting the maximum amount of coconut milk from grated coconut. ===Coconut milk powder=== {{main|Coconut milk powder}} Coconut cream can be dehydrated into coconut milk powder which has a far longer shelf life. It is produced by adding [[maltodextrin]] and [[casein]] to coconut cream to improve fluidity and then [[spray drying]] the mixture. The powder is packaged in moisture-proof containers. To use, water is simply added to the coconut milk powder. ===Coconut skim milk=== Coconut skim milk is coconut milk with very low levels of fat (0% to 1.5%). It is a byproduct of coconut cream and coconut oil production and is usually discarded. However, it is increasingly being used as a food ingredient for products which require coconut flavoring without the fats (including coconut powder, coconut honey, and [[coconut jam]]).{{cite journal |journal=CyTA - Journal of Food |date=21 November 2013 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=227–234 |doi=10.1080/19476337.2013.833296|s2cid=95833418 }}{{cite journal |last1=Khuenpet |first1=Krittiya Coconut Milk Production and Its Quality |journal=SHS Web of Conferences |date=6 January 2016 |volume=23 |pages=03002 |doi=10.1051/shsconf/20162303002|doi-access=free }}{{cite book |editor1-last=Mathew |editor1-first=Biju |title=Anchor India 2015 |date=2015 |publisher=Info Kerala |isbn=978-81-921284-9-8 |page=252 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4ktiCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA252}} It can also be used as a base in the production of coconut milk beverages used as milk substitutes, as it does not contain the high levels of fat characteristic of regular coconut milk while still being a good source of soluble proteins.{{cite journal |last1=Tanafranca |first1=Daisy E. |title=Traditional Processed Foods and Their Processing Technologies In The Philippines |journal=Proceedings of the International |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XnrdBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA131}} ===Milk substitutes=== [[File:Coconut Non-Dairy Milk (5082424201).jpg|thumb|upright|A carton of coconut milk beverage, a [[milk substitute]]]] Processed coconut milk can be used as a [[milk substitute|substitute for milk beverages]], usually marketed as "coconut milk beverage". They are sometimes confusingly also simply labeled as "coconut milk", though they are not the same product as coconut milk used for cooking (which is not meant for drinking). Milk substitutes from coconut are basically coconut milk diluted with water or coconut skim milk with additives. They contain less fat and fewer calories than milk, but also less protein. They contain high amounts of [[potassium]] and are good sources of fiber and iron. They are also commonly fortified with [[vitamin D]] and [[calcium]].{{cite book|first1=Meagan|last1=Bridges|editor1-first=Parrish|editor1-last=Carol Rees|title =Practical Gastroenterology|chapter =Moo-ove Over, Cow’s Milk: The Rise of Plant-Based Dairy Alternatives|series =Nutrition Issues in Gastroenterology, Series #171|year =2018|pages=20–27|url =https://med.virginia.edu/ginutrition/wp-content/uploads/sites/199/2014/06/January-18-Milk-Alternatives.pdf}} ===Filled milk=== {{Main|Filled milk}} Coconut milk is also used widely for [[filled milk]] products. It is blended with milk (usually [[skim milk]] or [[powdered milk]]) for its vegetable oils and proteins which act as substitutes for expensive [[butterfat]] in some processed milk products. They include low-fat filled milk, evaporated reconstituted milk, and sweetened condensed milk. ===Cheese and custard production=== Coconut milk can also be used in [[cheese]] and [[custard]] production, substituting at most 50% of [[milk]] without lowering the overall quality of the products. By mixing skim milk with coconut milk, one procedure develops cheeses – including a [[garlic]]-spiced soft cheese called ''queso de ajo'', a [[Gouda cheese]] substitute, and a [[Roquefort cheese|Roquefort]] substitute called "Niyoblue" (a [[portmanteau]] of {{Langx|tl|niyog}}, "coconut", and "blue").{{cite journal |last1=Davide |first1=C.L. |last2=Peralta |first2=C.N. |last3=Sarmago [[calorie|caloric density]] without affecting its [[palatability]].{{cite journal |last1=Escueta |first1=Elias E. |last2=Bourne |first2=Malcolm C. |last3=Hood |first3=Lamartine F. |title=Effect of |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2621.1985.tb12973.x}} ===Cream of coconut=== Cream of coconut is a thick, heavily sweetened, processed coconut milk product resembling [[condensed milk]].{{cite web |title=What is Cream of Coconut and How to Use It |url=http://bakingbites.com/2011/10/what-is-cream-of-coconut/ |website=Baking Bites |date=4 October 2011 |access-date=18 April 2019}} It was originally produced by the Puerto Rican company [[Coco López]] and is used most notably in piña coladas in the United States. It can also be used for other [[cocktail]] drinks and various desserts. It is distinct from coconut cream, and is not interchangeable.{{cite web |title=Cream of coconut |url=https://www.gourmetsleuth.com/ingredients/detail/cream-of-coconut |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140622035816/http://www.gourmetsleuth.com/ingredients/detail/cream-of-coconut |url-status=usurped |archive-date=22 June 2014 |website=Gourmet Sleuth |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web |last1=O'Neil |first1=Darcy |title=Cream of Coconut Recipe |url=https://www.artofdrink.com/ingredient/cream-of-coconut-recipe |website=Art of Drink |date=16 November 2018 |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.bonappetit.com/story/what-is-coconut-cream|last=Wartzman |first=Emma|date=January 31, 2018|title=What Is Coconut Cream Anyway?|work=[[Bon Appétit]]|access-date=July 14, 2019}} ==Cuisine== ===Coconut milk derivatives=== [[File:Lunok or Latik (coconut curds) 2 - Philippines.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Coconut curd]] ''[[latik]]'', a byproduct of traditional coconut oil production from simmered coconut milk]] In the [[Philippines]], coconut milk can also be further processed into [[coconut caramel]] and [[coconut curds]], both known as ''[[latik|latík]]''.{{cite book|author =Edgie Polistico|title =Philippine Food, Cooking, & Dining Dictionary|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =978-621-420-087-0|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=iz8_DwAAQBAJ&q=Arroz+caldo}}{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The coconut caramel ''latík'' made from a reduction of [[muscovado]] sugar and coconut milk has been developed into a commercial product marketed as [[coconut syrup]] (not to be confused with [[coconut sugar]] derived from coconut sap).{{cite book |last1=Thampan |first1=Palakasseril Kumaran |title=Handbook on Coconut Palm |date=1981 |publisher=Oxford & IBH |page=199}} [[File:Yosrisekaya1.jpg|thumb|upright|''Kaya'' [[coconut jam]], made with coconut milk, sugar, and eggs]] A similar product found throughout Southeast Asia is [[coconut jam]]. It is known as ''matamís sa báo'' in the Philippines and uses only coconut milk and sugar.{{cite book |last1=Pradeepkumar |first1=T. |last2=Jyothibhaskar |first2=B. Suma |last3=Satheesan |first3=K.N. |title=Management of Horticultural Crops Part II |date=2008 |publisher=New India Publishing |isbn=978-81-89422-49-3 |pages=572–573 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VHmokNZXbHUC&pg=PA572}} However, the coconut jam versions from [[Indonesia]], [[Malaysia]], and [[Singapore]] (''kaya''); [[Thailand]] (''sangkhaya''); [[Cambodia]] (''sankiah''); and [[Vietnam]] (''banh gan''), add eggs in addition to sugar. The latter versions are sometimes anglicized as "[[coconut custard]]" to distinguish them from the version without egg. Coconut jam and coconut custard have a thicker, jam-like consistency and are used as ingredients or fillings in various traditional desserts.{{cite book |last1=Duruz |first1=Jean |last2=Khoo |first2=Gaik Cheng |title=Eating Together: Food, Space, and Identity in Malaysia and Singapore |date=2014 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4422-2741-5 |page=45 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JojpBQAAQBAJ&q=kaya+coconut&pg=PA45}}{{cite book |last1=Alford |first1=Jeffrey |last2=Duguid |first2=Naomi |title=Hot Sour Salty Sweet: A Culinary Journey Through Southeast Asia |date=2000 |publisher=Artisan Books |isbn=978-1-57965-564-8 |page=302 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cUP30wR8-kUC&pg=PA302}} ===Food=== {{see also|List of dishes using coconut milk}} Coconut milk can be used in both sweet and savory dishes. In many tropical and Asian [[cuisine]]s, it is a traditional ingredient in [[curry|curries]] and other dishes, including desserts. ====Southeast Asia==== In [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesia]], coconut milk is used in various recipes ranging from savoury dishes – such as {{lang|id|[[rendang]]}}, {{lang|id|[[soto (food)|soto]]}},{{cite web |url=http://eatingasia.typepad.com/eatingasia/2009/03/soto-crawl.html |title=A Soto Crawl |publisher=Eating Asia |access-date=5 July 2010}} {{lang|id|[[gulai]]}}, {{lang|id|[[mie celor]]}}, {{lang|id|[[sayur lodeh]]}}, {{lang|id|[[gudeg]]}}, {{lang|id|[[krechek|sambal goreng krechek]]}}, and {{lang|id|[[opor ayam]]}}{{dash}}to sweet [[dessert]]s, such as {{lang|id|[[serabi]]}}, {{lang|id|es [[cendol]]}} and {{lang|id|[[es doger]]}}. [[Soto (food)|Soto]] is ubiquitous in Indonesia and considered one of Indonesia's [[national dish]]es.{{cite web |title=Tourism Ministry declares five dishes national food |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/travel/2018/09/20/tourism-ministry-declares-five-dishes-national-food.html |website=thejakartapost.com |access-date=28 April 2023}} It is also used in [[coconut rice]], a widespread Southeast Asian dish of rice cooked in coconut milk, including the {{lang|zsm|[[nasi lemak]]}} of Malaysia and the {{lang|id|[[nasi uduk]]}} of Indonesia. In [[Malaysian cuisine|Malaysia]], coconut milk is one of the essential ingredients in a lot of the dishes, this includes a few of the popular dishes in the region, such as the ubiquitous {{lang|zsm|[[nasi lemak]]}}{{cite web |last1=Bonny |first1=Tan |title=Nasi Lemak |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_1739_2010-12-13.html |website=Singapore Infopedia |publisher=National Library of Singapore |access-date=10 January 2022}} and {{lang|zsm|[[nasi dagang]]}},{{cite web |url=http://www.jkkn.gov.my/pemetaanbudaya/2016/12/12/5308/ |title= Nasi Dagang Authentic Prawn Laksa |url=https://adamliaw.com/recipe/make-authentic-prawn-laksa/ |website=Adam Liaw |access-date=10 January 2022}} {{lang|zsm|[[gulai]]}}{{cite journal |last1=Raji |first1=Mohd Nazri In the [[Philippines]], diverse dishes cooked in coconut milk are called {{lang|fil|[[ginataan|ginataán]]}}. They can range from savoury dishes to desserts.{{cite book |author=Myke Sarthou |editor=Angelo Comsti |title=The Filipino Family Cookbook: Recipes and Stories From Our Home Kitchen |publisher=Marshall Cavendish International Asia Pte Ltd |year=2014 |page=92 |isbn=978-981-4634-94-6}}{{cite book |editor=IBP |title=Philippines Country Study Guide |publisher=International Business Publications |year=2007 |page=112 |isbn=978-1-4330-3970-6}}{{cite book |author=Linda Civitello |title=Cuisine and Culture: A History of Food and People |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2007 |page=240 |isbn=978-0-471-74172-5}} Coconut milk is widely used to make traditional [[Filipino cuisine|Filipino]] {{lang|fil|[[kakanin|kakanín]]}} (the generic term for rice pastries), including {{lang|fil|[[bibingka]]}} and {{lang|fil|[[Biko (food)|biko]]}}, among others.{{cite book |author=Gene Gonzalez |title=The Little Kakanin Book |publisher=Anvil Publishing, Incorporated |year=2017 |isbn=978-971-27-3192-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BU47DwAAQBAJ }}{{Dead link|date=December 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [[File:Chicken Adobo with Coconut Milk.jpg|thumb|upright|{{lang|fil|[[Philippine adobo|Adobong manók sa gatâ]]}}, a variant of chicken [[Philippine adobo|adobo]] with coconut milk]] In [[Thailand]], coconut milk is used in dishes such as ''[[tom kha kai]]'', ''[[khao tom mat]]'', ''[[mango sticky rice]]'', and ''[[tom yum]]''.{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} ====Latin America and the Caribbean==== In Brazil, coconut milk is mostly used in northeastern cuisine, generally with seafood stews and desserts. In [[Venezuela]], pulp dishes are prepared with coconut milk and shredded fish in a dish called {{lang|es|mojito en coco}}. In [[Colombia]] and [[Panama]], the grated flesh of coconut and coconut milk are used to make sweet {{lang|es|titoté}}, a key ingredient in making {{lang|es|arroz con coco}} (coconut rice). Coconut milk is used to make traditional Venezuelan dishes, such as {{lang|es|majarete}} (a typical Venezuelan dessert), and {{lang|es|arroz con coco}} (the Venezuelan version of coconut rice).{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} ===Drink=== [[File:Cendol in a Glass.JPG|thumb|upright|''[[Cendol]]'', a green jelly drink with iced coconut milk and [[palm sugar]]]] In [[Southeast Asia]], coconut milk is used to make many traditional drinks. ''[[Cendol]]'' is a popular iced drink from this region containing chilled coconut milk and green jellies made of rice flour. Coconut milk is also used in hot drinks such as ''[[bandrek]]'' and ''bajigur'', two popular drinks from Indonesia. Aside from this, coconut milk is also an optional pairing with coffee in various countries of the region notably Vietnam (as {{lang|vi|[[Vietnamese iced coffee#Variations|cà phê dừa]]}}) plus Malaysia and Indonesia (as {{lang|ms|[[kopi (drink)|kopi]] santan}}).{{Cite web |title=Features: A Guide to Vietnamese Coffee |url=https://guide.michelin.com/vn/en/article/features/iconic-dishes-a-guide-to-vietnamese-coffee |access-date=2025-05-31 |website=[[Michelin Guide]] |publisher=[[Michelin]] |language=}} Sweetened coconut milk, and coconut milk diluted with water are two popular coconut beverages in [[southern China]] and [[Taiwan]]. As coconut milk becomes more popular in China, the sweetened coconut milk market is growing rapidly and is likely to reach 22.4 billion yuan (equal to about USD 3.14 billion) by 2026.{{Cite web |last=关晓萌 |title=Beverage firms ready to satisfy consumers eager to toast coconut-based drinks |url=https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202304/05/WS642cbb57a31057c47ebb8638.html |access-date=2026-03-19 |website=www.chinadaily.com.cn}} The jelly-like pulp from the inside of the coconut is often added to coconut water to make a tropical drink. In Brazil, for example, coconut milk is mixed with sugar and ''[[cachaça]]'' to make a cocktail called {{Lang|pt|[[Cocktails with cachaça#Batida (Shaken)|batida de côco]]}}.{{citation |first1=Nilda L. |last1=Rexach |title=The Hispanic Cookbook |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tgckJg8GxKAC |access-date=8 September 2012 |year=1995 |publisher=[[Citadel Press]] |location=New York |language=en, es Nutr.|volume=77|issue=5|pages=1146–1155|date=May 2003|pmid=12716665|doi=10.1093/ajcn/77.5.1146|url=http://www.ajcn.org/content/77/5/1146.full.pdf+html|format=pdf|doi-access=free}}{{cite journal|journal=Nutr Rev|year=2016|volume=74|issue=4|pages=267–280|doi=10.1093/nutrit/nuw002|title=Coconut oil consumption and cardiovascular risk factors in humans|vauthors=Eyres L, Eyres MF, Chisholm A, Brown RC|pmid=26946252|pmc=4892314}} ==Horticulture== In 1943, it was discovered that coconut milk could actively encourage plant growth. Although there are many factors that attribute coconut milk to plant growth, the main cause is the existence of a [[cytokinin]] known as [[zeatin]] found in coconut milk. While the zeatin in coconut milk speeds up plant growth in general, it does not speed up growth in certain plants such as [[radish]]es.{{cite book |title=Cytokinins: Chemistry, Activity, and Function |first1=David W. S. |last1=Mok |first2=Machteld C. |last2=Mok |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yov7iUL7OTAC |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=0-8493-6252-0 |year=1994}}{{rp|8}} However, when 10% coconut milk is added to the substrate on which wheat is grown, substantial improvements have been noted.{{cite book |title=Wheat |first1=Y. P. S. |last1=Bajaj |publisher=Springer |year=1990 |isbn=3-540-51809-6}} ==Commerce== Coconuts are widely produced in tropical climates and exported globally as canned products, most frequently to North America and Europe.{{cite journal |last1=Tinchan |first1=P |last2=Lorjaroenphon |first2=Y |last3=Cadwallader |first3=KR |last4=Chaiseri |first4=S |title=Changes in the profile of volatiles of canned coconut milk during storage |journal=Journal of Food Science |date=2015 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=C49–C54 |doi=10.1111/1750-3841.12730|pmid=25533179 }} In China, coconut milk has become so popular that companies have to import coconuts from neighboring countries to meet the rising domestic demand. This has pushed domestic companies to explore more coconut product categories to capture market attention. A '''cocktail umbrella''' or '''paper [[parasol]]''' is a small [[umbrella]] made from paper, [[paperboard]], and a [[toothpick]]. They are frequently associated with tropical drinks and [[Tiki bars]] and used as a [[cocktail garnish|garnish]] decoration. They are also used in [[dessert]]s or other foods and beverages. The overall form resembles a [[Parasola plicatilis|pleated inkcap]].

==Description==
The umbrella is fashioned out of paper, which can be patterned, with cardboard ribs. The ribs are made from cardboard in order to provide flexibility and to hinge so the umbrella can be pulled shut much like an ordinary umbrella. A small plastic retaining ring is often fashioned against the stem, a toothpick, in order to prevent the umbrella from folding up spontaneously. A sleeve of folded newspaper is located under the collar or base of the cocktail umbrella and is made out of recycled paper from either [[China]], [[India]] or [[Japan]]. As a result, they indicate their country of origin.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.factswt.com/did-you-know-that-all-cocktail-umbrellas-are-made-out-of-recycled-chinese/ |title=Did you know that all cocktail umbrellas are made out of recycled Chinese... |last=Bennet |first=Patrick |date=2014 |publisher=WTF Facts |access-date=21 February 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221161852/https://www.factswt.com/did-you-know-that-all-cocktail-umbrellas-are-made-out-of-recycled-chinese/ |archive-date=21 February 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Origin and history ==
It is not quite certain exactly when the cocktail umbrella came into use. One possible source is [[Donn Beach]], owner of the [[Hollywood, California]]-based restaurant and bar chain Don the Beachcomber. According to cocktail historian [[Dale DeGroff]], Beach started the trend in 1932 after spending much of his time collecting things from the world, most notably from the South Pacific. Beach sold his merchandise, including the cocktail umbrellas, to Victor Bergeron, owner of the [[Emeryville, California]]-based bar chain [[Trader Vic's]]. According to Bergeron's son Joe, Trader Vic's used the paper parasols until their production was halted by [[World War II]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://talesofthecocktail.com/history/myth-and-history-cocktail-umbrella|title=The Myth (and History) of the Cocktail Umbrella|last=McLafferty|first=Clair|date=19 February 2016|website=Tales of the Cocktail|access-date=16 May 2018|archive-date=20 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160820130240/https://talesofthecocktail.com/history/myth-and-history-cocktail-umbrella|url-status=dead}}</ref>

According to Hawaiian-themed author Rick Carroll, Hawaiian bartender [[Harry Yee|Harry K. Yee]] of the Hilton Waikiki was the first to use a paper parasol in a beverage in 1959 during the [[Tiki culture]] craze of the 1950s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.kevdo.com/maitai/harryyee.html|title=The Search for the Ultimate Mai Tai: Harry Yee, King of Tropical Cocktails|last=Crossman|first=Kevin|website=www.kevdo.com|access-date=2018-05-16}}</ref> Yee stated that he initially would use a sugar cane stick as a garnish for his tropical cocktails, but upon seeing how guests would set the sticks in ashtrays and dirty them, switched to [[Vanda (orchid)|Vanda orchids]] in 1955.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Sippin' Safari |date=2017 |publisher=Cocktail Kingdom |location=New York |edition=10 Anniversary expanded}}</ref>
In 1959, Yee switched to the cocktail umbrella for reasons unknown. Some speculate that it's because the bar already stocked the umbrellas as toothpicks or decoration, so they were more readily available.{{cn|date=October 2024}}

Another theory exists that Beach met Yee while vacationing in Hawaii after World War II. It is there that Beach and Yee traded cocktail ideas, recipes, and somewhere along the line, cocktail umbrellas. Afterwards, both of the bartenders began to use the umbrellas in tropical drinks.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.supercall.com/culture/why-serve-drinks-with-umbrellas|title=The Real Reason We Put Paper Umbrellas in Tropical Drinks|last=Mancall-Bitel|first=Nicholas|date=2017-08-31|work=Supercall|access-date=2018-05-16}}</ref>

== Tiki culture craze ==
[[Cocktail]] umbrellas are a [[Great Depression]]-era invention, but they did not take off in popularity until after World War II. According to an [[Eater (website)|Eater]] article published in 2015, many people, during the difficult times faced during the Great Depression, saw the South Pacific as "a place of exotic abandon, where you didn't have to work for a living." Many poor Americans saw tiki culture as an escape from reality.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.eater.com/drinks/2015/8/4/9092437/the-rise-fall-and-resurgence-of-tiki-cocktails|title=How Tiki Cocktails Returned to Rock the Party, Again|work=Eater|access-date=2018-05-22}}</ref> With the rise of the middle class after World War II came families with disposable income. That, combined with Hawaii's statehood and the rise of commercial air travel in the late 1950s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://airandspace.si.edu/exhibitions/america-by-air/online/heyday/heyday11.cfm|title=The Era of Mass Air Travel Begins {{!}} America by Air|website=airandspace.si.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-05-22}}</ref> led to an explosion in the popularity of tiki culture dubbed the "tiki craze". Tiki bars like Trader Vic's and Don the Beachcomber took advantage of the tiki craze, inventing slews of cocktails with a key identifying factor: a cocktail umbrella. The cocktail umbrella became synonymous with tiki cocktails, so much so that the drinks are often called "umbrella drinks".<ref name=":3" />

== Purpose ==
[[File:SantaMartaCarnival2013 24.JPG|thumb|Cocktail umbrella in a pineapple drink.]]
The true purpose of the cocktail umbrella is unknown. Some bartenders say that the cocktail umbrella is only decorative.<ref name=":0" /> Other bartenders have argued that the umbrella provides shade that slows the melting of ice when the drink is served outdoors. However, the temperature outside matters more than direct sunlight when it comes to the melting of ice. The shade from the cocktail umbrella would do nothing to slow this down.<ref name=":1" />  Another hypothesis about the cocktail umbrella's purpose is that its absence can lead to faster evaporation of alcohol due to direct sunlight when the drink is served outdoors. Chemists reject this idea and explain that the presence of a cocktail umbrella has no effect on this.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bonappetit.com/drinks/cocktails/article/cocktail-umbrella-history|title=The Exciting History and Origin of the Cocktail Umbrella|last=Bilow|first=Rochelle|work=Bon Appetit|access-date=2018-05-16|language=en}}</ref> In the past, cocktail umbrellas have served as a gimmick to draw women into bars that were mostly frequented by men. However, this purpose has faded in current times.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.neatorama.com/2012/11/02/Why-Do-They-Put-Umbrellas-in-Your-Drink/|title=Why Do They Put Umbrellas in Your Drink?|work=Neatorama|access-date=2018-05-16|language=en}}</ref>

Currently, the cocktail umbrella has become an important part of the drinks it is found on. It has become a garnish that is essential to the identities of these drinks.<ref name=":2" /> Cocktail garnishes started being used in the 19th century, with non-edible garnishes being introduced after prohibition. Two examples of these non-edible garnishes are cocktail umbrellas and [[swizzle stick]]s. Since their introduction, cocktail umbrellas use as a garnish has become a large part of their purpose.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/cocktail-garnishes-evolution-history-tiki-garnish/|title=PUNCH {{!}} The Gonzo Age of the Cocktail Garnish|last=Punch|website=punchdrink.com|date=8 September 2015 |language=en|access-date=2018-05-19}}</ref> As a garnish, they complete the drink's presentation and identify it as tropical. However, cocktail umbrellas differ from other drink garnishes. Unlike foods commonly used as garnishes, such as cherries, olives, or citrus, cocktail umbrellas do not add to the flavor of the drink and have a purely aesthetic purpose.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.supercall.com/culture/cocktail-and-drink-garnishes|title=Why You Should Never Skip the Garnish On Your Cocktail|last=Mafit|first=Dillon|date=2017-03-07|work=Supercall|access-date=2018-05-18}}</ref>

Alternative uses for cocktail umbrellas also exist. They can be used as toothpicks and may have been used as hat decorations in the past.<ref name=":0" /> It is also possible to use them as hair decorations and [[place card]]s to tell people where to sit at a hosted event.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://everydaypartymag.com/summer-parties/5-uses-cocktail-umbrellas|title=5 Uses for Cocktail Umbrellas - Everyday Party Magazine|date=2015-08-31|work=Everyday Party Magazine|access-date=2018-05-16|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[File:Pina Colada 430 (5076908250).jpg|thumb|Piña Colada with a cocktail umbrella]]
Drinks that commonly use a cocktail umbrella include the [[Blue Hawaii (drink)|Blue Hawaii]], Clipper-Tini, Hawaiian Margarita, Lava Lava, Lava Pi, Mac Nut Martini, [[Mai Tai]], and [[Piña colada|Piña Colada]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.islands.com/9-best-hawaii-drink-recipes/|title=9 Best Hawaii Drink Recipes | Hawaiian Recipes|website=Islands|date=27 June 2008 }}</ref>

Though the most common use for the cocktail umbrella is as a [[Cocktail garnish|garnish]] in drinks there are many other uses people have found. As a decoration piece people have used the umbrellas to make wreaths, table centerpieces, lanterns, and even hair pieces. People have also found ways to turn cocktail umbrellas into art, as is the case with [[Dutch people|Dutch]] trio We Make Carpets. We Make Carpets makes creative carpets out of different everyday objects. For this project, they decided to use 6,000 cocktail umbrellas in their recent creation "Umbrella Carpet 2." This unique use of cocktail umbrellas was displayed at a 2016 design exhibition in the [[Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam|Stedelijk Museum]] in Amsterdam.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/08/23/t-magazine/design/dream-out-loud-stedelijk-museum.html|title=When 6,000 Cocktail Umbrellas Become Art|date=2016-08-23|work=The New York Times|access-date=2018-05-22|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Venues ==
The cocktail umbrellas can be seen used in most cocktail lounges, bars, restaurants, and luaus. The most frequent location to spot the umbrella is restaurants and bars that maintain an "island" theme such as Hawaii.{{cn|date=October 2024}}

Blenheim Ginger Ale: {{Short description|Ginger ale brand}} {{multiple issues| {{more footnotes|date=February 2010}} {{refimprove|date=February 2010}} }} {{Infobox beverage | name = Blenheim Ginger ale | image = Blenheim_Logo.jpg | caption = | type = [[Soft drink]] | proof = | manufacturer = Blenheim Bottling Company | distributor = | origin = {{nowrap|[[United States]]}} | introduced = 1903 | discontinued = | color = Golden | flavor = [[Ginger]] | variants = Old #3 Hot, #5 Not as Hot, #9 Diet | related = | website = http://www.blenheimgingerale.com/ }} '''Blenheim Ginger Ale''' is a [[ginger ale]] bottled by Blenheim Bottlers in [[Hamer, South Carolina|Hamer]], [[Dillon County]], [[South Carolina]], but was originally bottled in [[Blenheim, South Carolina|Blenheim]], [[Marlboro County]], [[South Carolina]]. It has deep roots in the [[Pee Dee]] region of South Carolina, as it was created by a local doctor in the 1890s by mixing [[Jamaica ginger]] and sugar with local mineral waters and dispensed as a tonic for [[Indigestion|dyspepsia]].{{cite news | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1998/02/25/dining/sips-a-southern-ginger-ale-with-sting-in-its-tail.html | title = Sips; A Southern Ginger Ale with a Sting in its Tail | work = New York Times | last1 = Grimes | first1 = William | date = 25 February 1998 | accessdate = February 26, 2016 }} == History == As the story goes, in 1781, Patriot James Spears was attempting to run from the British during the [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]], when his shoe became stuck in the mud of the natural spring; he left it and kept running.{{Cite web | url = http://www.sciway.net/south-carolina/blenheim-ginger-ale.html | title = Hamer, South Carolina - Blenheim Ginger Ale | website = www.sciway.net | access-date = 2016-02-26 }} Upon his return, he recovered his shoe and noticed the amount of water in the depression his shoe left. He tasted the water and noticed its strong mineral content. Word of the natural spring spread quickly and before long, the area became popular among the wealthy plantation owners and by the late 1800s a small town was established. {{Cite web | url = http://www.marlborocounty.sc.gov/History/Blenheim/Pages/default.aspx | title = Town of Blenheim | website = www.marlborocounty.sc.gov | access-date = 2016-02-26 | archive-date = 2016-02-12 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160212195115/http://www.marlborocounty.sc.gov/History/Blenheim/Pages/default.aspx | url-status = dead }}{{Cite web | url = http://www.hmdb.org/marker.asp?marker=50341 | title = Blenheim Mineral Springs Marker | website = www.hmdb.org | access-date = 2016-02-26 }} In the late 1890s, Dr. C. R. May began prescribing the mineral springs' water to his patients complaining of stomach troubles. Because his patients frequently complained about the strong iron-like taste of the water, the doctor decided to make the water more palatable by adding Jamaican ginger and sugar.{{Cite web | url = http://www.blenheimgingerale.com/about-us/blenheim-history/ | title = Blenheim History « Blenheim Ginger Ale | website = www.blenheimgingerale.com | access-date = 2016-02-26 }} The new concoction's popularity took off and Dr. May partnered with A. J. Matheson to open the Blenheim Bottling Company in 1903. Conveniently located next to the mineral springs, the Blenheim Bottling Company plant was constructed in 1920. Producing as little as 18 to 20 cases a day, the company remained a small, humble operation for 90 years.{{Cite web | url = http://antiqology.com/blog/the-blenheim-ginger-ale-story | title = The Blenheim Ginger Ale Story – ANTIQOLOGY – A Unique Blend of Old & New | website = antiqology.com | access-date = 2016-02-26 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131216070027/http://antiqology.com/blog/the-blenheim-ginger-ale-story | archive-date = 2013-12-16 | url-status = dead }} In 1993, Blenheim was bought by Alan Schafer, who also owned the world-famous [[South of the Border (attraction)|South of the Border]] roadside attraction.{{Cite web | url = http://www.sciway.net/sc-photos/dillon-county/blenheims-ginger-ale.html | title = Blenheim's Ginger Ale | website = SC Picture Project | access-date = 2016-02-26 | archive-date = 2016-03-03 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303114748/http://www.sciway.net/sc-photos/dillon-county/blenheims-ginger-ale.html | url-status = dead }} Since the original plant was older, Schafer decided that rather than refurbish the building, he would move the bottling operations to a new plant located next to South of the Border. == Today == Despite a marketing push that began in the late 1990s, Blenheim ginger ale is not widely distributed outside the Carolinas; however in more recent years, the company ships to 44 states and three international distributors.{{Cite web | url = http://www.greenvilleonline.com/story/life/2014/02/19/ginger-its-good-for-what-ails-and-so-much-more/5579239/ | title = Ginger: It's good for what ails and so much more | website = The Greenville News | access-date = 2016-02-26 }}{{Cite web | url = http://www.fayobserver.com/news/business/blenheim-ginger-ale-makes-a-comeback/article_05b4a94e-0a2d-51e5-a9a7-4012b9930aa6.html | title = BLENHEIM GINGER ALE MAKES A COMEBACK | website = Fayetteville Observer | access-date = 2016-02-26 }} The spicy ale has, however, developed a cult following among food and wine aficionados. In February 1998, ''New York Times'' journalist Bill Grimes described the taste this way: "The first swallow brings on a four-sneeze fit. {{for multi|the autobiography by Lawrence Durrell|Bitter Lemons|the publisher|Bitter Lemon Press}}
[[File:Schweppes_Bitter_Lemon.jpg|thumb|right|[[Schweppes]] Bitter Lemon. Vintage bottle shown.]]

'''Bitter lemon''' is a bitter [[lemon]] flavoured  [[soft drink]]. Its signature  taste is a result of inherently bitter lemon [[pith]] being reinforced by the bitter alkaloid [[quinine]]. 

The principal difference between [[tonic water]] and bitter lemon is the lemon juice, pith, and [[Peel (fruit)|peel]]. The juice adds sour, offset by additional sweetener, and the oily peel fragrance. 

The generic bitter lemon drink dates back to 1834.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.schweppes.de/schweppes-classic/original-bitter-lemon |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100523071528/http://www.schweppes.de/schweppes-classic/original-bitter-lemon |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 May 2010 |title=Original Bitter Lemon |publisher=Schweppes.de |access-date=19 September 2011}}</ref>  [[Schweppes]] introduced its brand of bitter lemon in 1957.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.innovation.cadbury.com/allaboutus/ourbrands/Pages/brandhistory.aspx?TabIndex=1 | title=History of our Brands - Beverages | publisher=[[Cadbury]] | access-date=15 August 2011 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316171725/http://www.innovation.cadbury.com/allaboutus/ourbrands/Pages/brandhistory.aspx?TabIndex=1 | archive-date=16 March 2012 }}</ref>

Bitter lemon is consumed both by itself and as a [[Drink mixer|mixer]], and is sold around the world.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=RqUtAAAAIBAJ&sjid=kJ4FAAAAIBAJ&pg=2127,3252078&dq=bitter+lemon&hl=en | title=New Schweppes Bitter Lemon - top-selling mixer from England to Australia - makes its debut in Montreal | publisher=[[The Gazette (Montreal)|The Montreal Gazette]] | date=17 June 1963 | access-date=19 September 2011}}</ref>

A '''cocktail skewer''' or '''cocktail stick''' is a short [[cylinder (geometry)|cylindrical]] stick, made of [[wood]] or sometimes [[metal]], that has a somewhat sharp point on one or both ends.  It is usually used as a [[skewer]] for holding decorations (such as [[cherry|cherries]]) in [[cocktail]]s and also for serving food such as [[amuse-bouche]]s at [[cocktail party|cocktail parties]].

== Injuries ==
Ingestion of cocktail sticks, or fragments of them, has been known to cause injuries in several parts of the [[alimentary canal]].<ref name="umj"/><ref name="bmj"/>

A '''Baby Guinness''' is a [[Mixed drink shooters and drink shots|shooter]], a style of [[cocktail]], or mixed alcoholic beverage, intended to be consumed in one shot. A Baby Guinness does not contain [[Guinness]] stout. Its name is derived from the fact that it is made in such a way as to look like a tiny glass of [[stout]] containing Irish cream and coffee liqueur.

==Preparation==
In a [[shot glass]] a portion of [[coffee liqueur]] is topped by a layer of [[Irish cream]] which is poured over the back of a spoon so that it sits on the coffee liqueur. The ratio of coffee liqueur to Irish cream varies but is generally around 3-to-1. The resulting drink resembles a miniature pint of Guinness stout, with the coffee liqueur serving as the beer and the Irish cream as the head. It is normally served in a [[shot glass]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.bostonherald.com/entertainment/food_dining/food/view/2009_05_27_Baby_Guinness/|title=Baby Guinness|date=May 27, 2009|work=Food and Recipes|publisher=Boston Herald|accessdate=2009-06-24}}</ref>

Some recipes call for the Irish cream to be whipped then spooned on top of the coffee liqueur in order to look more like the head on a pint of Guinness.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.recipezaar.com/Baby-Guinness-243991|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120907083753/http://www.recipezaar.com/Baby-Guinness-243991|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 7, 2012|title=Baby Guinness|date=August 2, 2007|publisher=RecipeZaar|accessdate=2009-06-24}}</ref> Over time, the Baby Guinness became a widely recognized shooter in Irish pubs and beyond, known for its visual resemblance to a miniature Guinness pint.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://metro.co.uk/2025/07/04/baby-guinness-origin-story-reveals-youve-doing-shots-wrong-21162790/ |title=The origin story of Baby Guinness reveals you’ve been doing the shots all wrong |publisher=Metro News |date=2025-07-04 |accessdate=2025-08-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/baby-guinness-shot-cocktail-recipe-history/ |title=The Rise of the Baby Guinness |publisher=PUNCH |date=2025-03-17 |accessdate=2025-08-07}}</ref>

===Variations===
In some places, a Baby Guinness is served with black [[Sambuca]] instead of coffee liqueur<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.drmixology.com/baby_guinness.cfm|title=Baby Guinness|publisher=Dr. Mixology|accessdate=2009-06-24|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505220816/http://www.drmixology.com/baby_guinness.cfm|archivedate=2009-05-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theoxfordretreat.com/menus/Bar.pdf|title=The Oxford Retreat's Bar Menu|publisher=[The Oxford Retreat Pub]|accessdate=2009-06-24}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref> creating a drink similar to a [[Slippery Nipple]].

  | last = Swanson
  | first = Stevenson
  | title = Raise your glass to toast the cocktail: Museums salute 200 years of the mixed drink
  | work = Chicago Tribune
  | publisher = Chicago Tribune
  | date = July 12, 2006

Recipes call for brandy; orange-flavored [[liqueur]], such as [[Curaçao liqueur|curacao]] or [[triple sec]]; and [[bitters]], stirred or shaken with ice, which may or may not be strained out afterward.<ref name="zeldes" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.imbibemagazine.com/Recipe-Chicago-Cocktail |title=Chicago Cocktail |work=Imbibe Magazine |date=April 25, 2009}}</ref> In many versions of the drink, it is topped off with [[champagne (wine)|champagne]]<ref name="Tribune" /><ref name="Drury" /><ref name="savoy">{{cite book
  | last = Craddock
  | first = Harry
  | author-link = Harry Craddock
  | title = The Savoy Cocktail Book
  | year = 1930
  }}
</ref><ref>Stevens, Trey (Feb. 1, 2006). "[http://www.askmen.com/fine_living/drinks_250/271_saturday_night.html Drink & Pickup Line Of The Week] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170916053628/https://www.askmen.com/fine_living/drinks_250/271_saturday_night.html |date=2017-09-16 }}". AskMen.com</ref> or white wine.<ref name="zeldes" /> Some versions call for sugaring the rim of the glass.<ref name="zeldes" /> It can be served on the rocks in a double [[old-fashioned glass]] or, especially in the champagne variation, straight up in a [[champagne coupe]] or [[champagne flute|flute]] or a [[cocktail glass]].

Caribou (drink):
{{Short description|French-Canadian alcoholic beverage}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2024}}
[[File:Carnaval Caribou.jpg|thumb|Caribou]]
{{Canadian cuisine}}
'''Caribou''' is a sweet [[French Canadians|French-Canadian]] alcoholic beverage composed of [[red wine]] and [[Distilled beverage|a spirit]] (usually rye whisky) (mixed 3 parts to 1), and maple syrup or sugar.<ref>{{citation |title=Sacre Blues: An Unsentimental Journey Through Quebec |first=Taras |last=Grescoe |publisher=Macfarlane Walter & Ross |year=2001 |isbn= 978-1-55199-081-1}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=A Warm December in Old Quebec |year=2007 |first=Karen |last=Misuraca |url=http://www.karenmisuraca.com/articles/quebec_xmas.shtml |access-date=16 February 2010 |archive-date=6 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100906073144/http://www.karenmisuraca.com/articles/quebec_xmas.shtml |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=ass>{{citation|title=Quebec's Carnaval is worth freezing your a** off for |first=Julie |last=Ovenell-Carter |date=6 February 2009 |publisher=theseboots.travel |url=http://theseboots.travel/2009/02/06/worth-repeating-quebecs-carnaval-is-worth-freezing-your-a-off-for/ |url-status=usurped |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303133943/http://theseboots.travel/2009/02/06/worth-repeating-quebecs-carnaval-is-worth-freezing-your-a-off-for/ |archivedate=3 March 2012 }}</ref>

Caribou can be made at home but is now available as a premixed beverage by the [[Société des alcools du Québec]]. It can be consumed hot or cold depending on the weather and served with [[citrus]] and [[cinnamon]] in the manner of [[mulled wine]]. [[Cloves]] and [[nutmeg]] are also commonly added to flavour the drink.

The drink has been traditionally served at the [[Quebec Winter Carnival]], where it is carried around by carnival goers in hollow plastic walking canes<ref>{{citation|title=Seven Wonders of Canada: Old Quebec City, Quebec |publisher=CBC.CA |url=http://www.cbc.ca/sevenwonders/wonder_quebec_city.html}}</ref><ref name=ass/> or available at outdoor bars at the event.<ref>{{citation |title=Quebec's Carnival |first=Taras |last=Grescoe |publisher=National Geographic Society |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/traveler/articles/1095quebec.html}}</ref> In recent years, it has also been served in celebration on the [[National Holiday (Quebec)|National holiday of Quebec]]. It is also a staple of the [[Festival du Voyageur]] in [[Winnipeg]], [[Manitoba]],<ref>{{citation |title=Festival du Voyageur official website |url=http://festivalvoyageur.mb.ca/en/festival/fun-food/ |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140302190420/http://festivalvoyageur.mb.ca/en/festival/fun-food/ |archivedate=2 March 2014 }}</ref> where it is sometimes served in glasses made out of ice.

==Origins==
Caribou is supposed to have derived its name from a drink consisting of a mixture of [[caribou]] [[blood]] and whisky which was consumed by hunters and loggers in colonial times to stave off the cold when working.<ref name=ass/><ref>{{citation |first=Sébastien |last=Mieusset |title=Le "Temps des sucres" au Québec |url=http://www.cuisine.tv/cid6799/le-temps-des-sucres-au-quebec.html |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090501072919/http://www.cuisine.tv/cid6799/le-temps-des-sucres-au-quebec.html |archivedate=1 May 2009 }}</ref>

Batini (drink):
{{Notability|date=September 2020}}
A '''Batini''' is a [[vodka]]-based [[cocktail]] that is the official drink of the [[Austin Bat Fest]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Alarcón|first=Claudia|date=September 22, 2006|title=Batini III|url=https://www.austinchronicle.com/food/2006-09-22/404231/|access-date=2021-10-18|website=www.austinchronicle.com|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2019-05-22|title=What to drink at renowned The Driskill Bar in Austin, Texas.|url=https://thirstymag.com/drink-driskill-bar-austin/|access-date=2021-10-18|website=thirsty.|language=en-US}}</ref> The drink was created by bartenders from the Four Seasons Hotel Austin.

== History ==
In August 2004, The Austin Convention and Visitor's Bureau hosted a contest to designate the official drink of Austin.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=16 August 2004|title=Batini named Austin's "official drink"|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/austin/stories/2004/08/16/daily49.html|access-date=2021-10-18|website=www.bizjournals.com}}</ref> Five Austin-area hotels submitted recipes to become the official Batini for the city.<ref name=":0" /> The Four Seasons Austin recipe won the contest and was on the menu at the Lobby Lounge.<ref name=":0" />

In 2006, the Four Seasons won the Batini contest again with their "Batini Black" entrant.<ref name=":1" /> The Batini black was similar to the original, including Tito's Vodka, and Blue Curacao but added in a splash of simple syrup, grapefruit juice, champagne and fresh blackberries.<ref name=":1" />

A Batini contest is an annual event for local bartenders at the Austin Bat Fest.<ref name=":2" />

== Ingredients and preparation ==
The ingredients needed for the Batini are:<ref name=":0" />

* [[Tito's Vodka]] 
* [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]] 
* [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Blue Curacao]]
* [[Sangria]]
* [[Red wine]]
* Cherry garnish

All of the ingredients are shaken together and served with a cherry garnish.<ref name=":0" />

== Variations ==

=== Batini Black ===
Ingredients in a Batini Black are:<ref name=":1" /> 

* [[Tito's Vodka]]
* [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Blue Curacao]]
* Splash of [[simple syrup]]
* [[Grapefruit juice]]
* Fresh blackberries
* Topped with [[champagne]]

Shake together Tito's, Blue Curacao, splash of simple syrup, grapefruit juice, and fresh blackberries. Strain into a cocktail glass and top off with champagne.<ref name=":1" />

Bishop-bowl:
{{Short description|18th to 19th century Denmark punch bowl}}
[[File:Biskopbolle c. 1735.png|thumb|Bishop-bowl manufactured by the Store Kongensgade Factory in Copenhagen, Denmark]]
A '''bishop-bowl''' ({{Langx|da|bispebolle}}) is a [[punch bowl]] shaped in the form of a [[mitre]]. The bishop-bowl was popular in [[Denmark]], [[Schleswig-Holstein]], and [[Norway]] in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries where it was used to serve an [[alcoholic drink]] known as ''biskop'' ({{Literal translation|bishop}}).<ref name="Fleming">{{Cite book|last=Fleming|first=John|author-link=John Fleming (art historian)|title=The Penguin Dictionary of Decorative Arts|last2=Honour|first2=Hugh|author-link2=Hugh Honour|publisher=[[Allen Lane]]|year=1977|isbn=0713909412|location=London|pages=93}}</ref>

The bowls were primarily produced in [[faience]] and were first manufactured in large quantities by the [[Store Kongensgade Faience Manufactury]] in [[Copenhagen]]. Bishop-bowls were later also manufactured in Schleswig-Holstein and Norway and were produced in [[porcelain]] as well as faience.<ref>{{Cite web|title=bispebolle|url=https://naob.no/ordbok/bispebolle|access-date=2025-10-02|website=[[Det Norske Akademis ordbok]]|language=no}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Bispebolle|url=https://digitaltmuseum.no/0210615054070/bispebolle|access-date=2025-10-02|website=[[Nasjonalmuseet]]|language=no}}</ref>

==History==
The drink biskop is of German origins, where it was known as ''bischof''. Its name refers to the violet colour of a [[Bishop|bishop's]] garments.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=biskop|url=https://ordnet.dk/ods/ordbog?query=biskop|access-date=2025-10-02|website=[[Ordbog over det danske Sprog]]|language=da}}</ref> Biskop was one of several types of hot punch which became popular among the [[Danish nobility]] in the 18th century.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=17 December 2017|title=Lav din egen – biskop|url=https://www.dengamleby.dk/mere-om-den-gamle-by/publikationer/juleinspektorens-blog/lav-din-egen-biskop/|access-date=2025-10-02|website=[[Den Gamle By]]|language=da}}</ref> The popularity of the punch led to the manufacture of special punch bowls shaped in the form of a bishop's hat or later as the figure of a bishop.<ref name=":1" />

The first bishop-bowls in Denmark were produced at the Store Kongensgade factory, Denmark's first faience manufacturer, that was founded in 1722.<ref name="DSD">{{cite web|title=Store Kongensgade Fajancefabrik|url=http://denstoredanske.dk/Kunst_og_kultur/Kunsth%C3%A5ndv%C3%A6rk_og_design/Keramik_%28porcel%C3%A6n%2C_fajance%2C_stent%C3%B8j%2C_lert%C3%B8j%29/Store_Kongensgade_Fajancefabrik|url-status=dead|access-date=27 March 2018|website=[[Den Store Danske]]|language=da|archive-date=28 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180328103710/http://denstoredanske.dk/Kunst_og_kultur/Kunsth%C3%A5ndv%C3%A6rk_og_design/Keramik_(porcel%C3%A6n,_fajance,_stent%C3%B8j,_lert%C3%B8j)/Store_Kongensgade_Fajancefabrik}}</ref> The bishop-bowls were the most recognizable items produced by the Store Kongensgade factory. They were typically decorated in blue, though a small number were also produced in [[manganese violet]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Jakobsen|first=Kristian|title=Store Kongensgade Fajancefabrik|url=https://lex.dk/Store_Kongensgade_Fajancefabrik|access-date=2 October 2025|website=Danmarks Nationalleksikon|publisher=[[Den Store Danske]]|language=da}}</ref> The bowls grew to popularity in Denmark in the early 1700s and soon spread to [[Norway]], where they were produced by the Herrebøe Fajansefabrikk from the mid-1700s.<ref>{{Citation|last=Linder|first=Mats|title=bispebolle|date=2025-02-24|work=[[Store norske leksikon]]|url=https://snl.no/bispebolle|access-date=2025-10-02|language=no}}.</ref>

==The drink==
[[File:Frederiksborg - pinch bowl.jpg|thumb|Bishop-bowl from Store Kongensgade with an inscription dedicated to [[Christian VI of Denmark|Christian VI]] which reads "Vivat, Vivat, Vivat, Kong Christian den Siete". The bowl's decorations also include a depiction of a group drinking around a table. ]] 
The basic ingredients of biskop [[Punch (drink)|punch]] are [[red wine]], [[sugar]], and spices which vary by recipe. Most recipes call for [[bitter orange]], [[orange zest]], or [[orange juice]], though others may call for [[cinnamon]] or [[ginger]].<ref>{{Citation|title=bisp – drikk|date=2024-11-26|work=[[Store norske leksikon]]|url=https://snl.no/bisp_-_drikk|access-date=2025-10-02|language=no}}.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Kirkebæk-Johansson|first=Laura|last2=Schnoor|first2=Christopher|date=2017-09-28|title=Nu som vin-anmelder: Lars Mikkelsen skamroser lækker drik fra 1700-tallet|url=https://www.dr.dk/historie/danmarkshistorien/nu-som-vin-anmelder-lars-mikkelsen-skamroser-laekker-drik-fra-1700-tallet|access-date=2025-10-02|website=[[DR (broadcaster)|DR]]|language=da-DK}}</ref> Recipes from the second half of the 19th century frequently mention that [[rum]] can be added to improve drink's taste and [[shelf life]].<ref name=":1" />

A recipe for biskop from Beate Augustine Friedel's cookbook, ''Nye og fuldstændige Confectyr-bog eller grundig Underviisning til selv at forfærdige alle muelige Slags Conditorievare'', was originally published in German, and was translated into Danish in 1795. It calls for three liters of red wine, 1.5 kilos of sugar and the zest and juice of six bitter oranges and 2-3 oranges.<ref name=":1" />

An 1815 recipe by Christopher Jacobsen in the ''Nye Kogebog eller Anviisning til at koge, bage, stege, indsylte, henlægge, indslagte, anrette o.s.v.'' calls for a bottle of red wine, two bitter oranges, and sugar to taste. A later recipe by [[Anne Marie Mangor]], published in her 1876 book, ''Kogebog for smaa Huusholdninger indeholdende Anvisning til forskellige Retters og Kagers Tillavning'', also includes rum. It calls for a bottle of wine, 50 millilitres of rum, 125 grams of sugar, and the zest and juice of two small bitter oranges.<ref name=":1" />

Biskop was often served warm. However, unlike Danish ''[[Mulled wine|gløgg]]'', the drink was also served cold or on ice.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The 1935 ''[[Waldorf-Astoria (1893–1929)|Old Waldorf-Astoria]] Bar Book'' lists a recipe for "bishop" to be served in a [[Pitcher (container)|pitcher]], which calls for sugar, lemon juice, rum, a bottle of red wine, and ice.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Stevens Crockett|first=Albert|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1935-Old-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Book/104|title=The Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book|publisher=A. S. Crockett|year=1935|location=New York|pages=104|language=en}}</ref>

==Legacy==
Early bishop-bowls from Store Kongensgade Faience Manufactury are on display at [[The David Collection]] in Copenhagen<ref>{{cite web|title=European 18th century art: Danish ceramics|url=https://www.davidmus.dk/en/collections/european/danish-ceramics/art|url-status=dead|access-date=27 March 2018|publisher=Davids Samling|archive-date=28 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180328103220/https://www.davidmus.dk/en/collections/european/danish-ceramics/art}}</ref> and at the Museum of National History at [[Frederiksborg Castle]] in [[Hillerød]]. Bishop-bowls from a manufacturer in Schleswig can be seen [[St. Anne's Museum Quarter, Lübeck|St. Anne's Museum]] in [[Lübeck]].

[[Den Gamle By]] has a bishop-bowl shaped in the form of a seated bishop made in [[Kellinghusen]] in Holstein circa 1770. The figure is 34 cm high and the upper half comes off as a lid.<ref name=":1" />

A Danish stamp from 1970 features a drawing of a bishop-bowl. The drawing was created by Claus Achton Friis.<ref name=":1" />

Clam juice:
{{Short description|Broth obtained from clams}}
[[File:Starting lunch with a traditional clam juice shot.jpg|thumb|A [[shot glass]] of clam juice]]
'''Clam juice''' is a [[broth]] derived from steamed [[clam]]s,<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/> which can be consumed on its own or used as an ingredient in various dishes and beverages.

==Preparation==
Clam juice is typically prepared from the liquid obtained from [[Steaming|steamed]] clams.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/> Clam juice may be prepared fresh for consumption,<ref name="OHara Nash 1999"/> or purchased in prepared bottled form.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/><ref name="Broyles 2015"/> Some companies [[Mass production|mass-produce]] prepared clam juice, which is made by steaming fresh clams in water with salt, collecting the extracted liquid known as clam extract or clam liquor, and then filtering it.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/><ref name="Cook's Illustrated"/>

In 1937, William G. Frazier invented a clam opener devised to easily open clams and retain all of the clam juice, which was collected in a bowl.<ref name="USPTO US 2136816 A"/> A patent for the clam opener was issued by the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]] on November 15, 1938.<ref name="USPTO US 2136816 A"/>

==Use in dishes==
[[File:Clam juice being used in preparation of clam chowder.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Bottled clam juice being used in the preparation of [[clam chowder]]]]
Clam juice is sometimes used in the preparation of [[clam chowder]] and other [[chowder]]s.<ref name="Broyles 2015"/> It may be used as an ingredient in various sauces and meat sauces, [[seafood]] dishes, in [[Cooking base|soup bases]], and as a condiment to top foods, similar to the manner that [[fish sauce]] may be used.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/><ref name="Chiarella 2013"/><ref name="Burros 1996"/>

Italian chefs sometimes use clam juice as an ingredient in [[List of seafood dishes|seafood dishes]] and pasta sauces.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/> It is sometimes used during the [[Deglazing (cooking)|deglazing]] process in cooking.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/> It may provide a mineral-like flavor to dishes, and serve as a substrate to assist in combining flavors present in a dish.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/>

==As a beverage==
Some restaurants and bars in the US serve [[shooter (drink)|shots]] of pure clam juice.<ref name="Lybarger 2015"/> For example, the Old Clam House in San Francisco, California serves a shot glass of hot clam juice at the beginning of each meal.<ref name="Lybarger 2015"/> In the early 1900s in the United States, clam juice was purported to be a [[hangover]] remedy.<ref name="Epicurious 2015"/>

[[File:Everleigh Club exterior.jpg|thumb|Exterior of the [[Everleigh Club]], circa 1911]]
The [[Everleigh Club]], a former [[brothel]] in Chicago, Illinois, that was in operation from 1900 to October 1911, would serve iced clam juice and a tablet of aspirin as a starter for breakfast, which began at 2:00 in the afternoon.<ref name="Tait 1997"/><ref name="Washburn"/>

==Beverages with clam juice==
===Soda fountains===
In the United States in the early 1900s, clam juice was used as an ingredient for various beverages at [[soda fountain]]s.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/> Beverages prepared with clam juice included hot clam juice, hot clam soda, hot ginger clam broth, hot celery punch, hot clam cream, clam night cap, tomato clam broth and others.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/><ref name="Fountain 1915 p. 92"/><ref name="Fox"/><ref name="Lillard & Company 1920"/>

During this time, a recipe for hot clam juice used one-half to one-ounce of clam juice in an eight-ounce glass, the remainder of which was filled with hot water.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/> Accompaniments included soda crackers, celery salt, salt and pepper.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/> The beverage was sometimes prepared with the addition of milk or hot milk.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/> The addition of a small portion of butter would enhance the flavor of hot clam juice.<ref name="D.O. Haynes & Company 1909"/>

===Cocktails===
In contemporary times, clam juice is sometimes used as an ingredient or [[drink mixer]] in [[cocktail]]s, such as the [[Caesar (cocktail)|Caesar]],<ref name="OHara Nash 1999"/><ref name="Post-Gazette 2015"/><ref name="CBC.ca 2013"/> also known as a Bloody Caesar.<ref name="CBC.ca 2009"/>

===Clamato===
{{main article|Clamato}}
[[File:Bloody Caesar.jpg|thumb|A Caesar cocktail prepared with Clamato]]
[[Clamato]] is a [[Mass production|mass-produced]] beverage prepared with [[tomato juice]] concentrate, clam juice and spices.<ref name="Drane 2016"/><ref name="O'Brien 2008"/> It also contains [[high-fructose corn syrup]], monosodium glutamate, salt and [[ascorbic acid]].<ref name="O'Brien 2008"/> Clamato is used as an ingredient in the [[Caesar (cocktail)|Caesar]] cocktail.<ref>{{cite book|author=Paul Harrington|author2=Laura Moorhead|name-list-style=amp |others=Designed and illustrated by Douglas Bowman|title=Cocktail: the drinks bible for the 21st century|date=1998|publisher=Viking|location=New York|isbn=978-0-670-88022-5|pages=68–69}}</ref> The [[michelada]], a [[beer cocktail]], is sometimes prepared using Clamato as an ingredient.<ref name="Gold 2015"/>{{clear left}}

A '''beer mix''' usually refers to an [[Alcoholic drink|alcoholic beverage]] which includes one or more additional ingredients. Typically, the beer mix is 40-70% [[beer]]. Popular mix-ins include [[cola]], lemon, and other fruit juices.{{Citation needed|date=August 2022}}

Today, beer mixes are an established part of German drinking culture and are available in a wide range of flavors and varieties, including [[Non-alcoholic drink|non-alcoholic versions]]. Though marketed primarily towards young adults, they can be enjoyed by consumers of all ages.

== History ==
Beer mixes have been available in Germany since early 20th century. The “[[Radler]]" beer mix, which is still popular today, is seen as the pioneer of the market. The drink originated from the summer of 1922, when a [[Munich]] inn was so busy with cyclists that there was the threat of a beer shortage. In order to stretch the remaining beer supply, [[lemonade]] was added, creating the Radler.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-05-28 |title=Radler bzw. Alsterwasser - Bier und Wir |url=https://www.bierundwir.de/sorten/radler.htm |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20200921090108/https://www.bierundwir.de/sorten/radler.htm |archive-date=2020-09-21 |access-date=2026-02-24 |work=Bier und Wir |language=de-DE}}</ref>  Further variants followed, e.g., cola-beer and wheat beer mixes. Up until 1993, it was only permitted to sell freshly prepared beer mixes due to legal requirements.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |title=Willkommen beim Deutschen Brauer-Bund: Biermischgetränke |url=https://www.brauer-bund.de/bier-ist-genuss/biersorten-im-portraet/biermischgetraenke.html |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20191205221224/https://www.brauer-bund.de/bier-ist-genuss/biersorten-im-portraet/biermischgetraenke.html |archive-date=2019-12-05 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=www.brauer-bund.de |language=de}}</ref>

In 1995, the mid-sized German [[Karlsberg (brewery)|Karlsberg Brewery]] in [[Homburg (Saar)]] was the first brewery to use an amendment to the beer tax law which enabled the production and sale of ready-mixed beer mixes in bottles or tins.<ref name="auto"/><ref>Cf. §1 Beer tax law</ref> "MiXery Beer + Cola + X” was therefore one of the first ready-mixed cola and beer drinks. This innovation was initially met with considerable criticism from the beer industry, but the first competitors appeared on the market in 2001 and the market subsequently saw a continuous increase in sales volume.

Further variants, which differed in the type of beer they contained as base, followed. Schöfferhofer Grapefruit is a pioneer in the wheat beer mixes and was launched on the market in 2007 by the Binding Brauerei Brewery.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Schöfferhofer Weizen-Mix – Presse |url=http://www.schoefferhofer-weizen-mix.de/?page_id=102 |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20160404180809/http://www.schoefferhofer-weizen-mix.de/?page_id=102 |archive-date=2016-04-04 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=www.schoefferhofer-weizen-mix.de |language=de-DE}}</ref>
 
A further variant and innovation in the beer mix market followed in 2014 with the introduction of so-called "MiXery Beer-Cocktails" by the Karlsberg Brewery.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saarländische Wochenblatt Verlagsgesellschaft mbH |title=Regionales |url=http://www.gudd-gess.de/regionales/regionales/article/karlsberg-bringt-mixery-beer-cocktails-auf-den-markt/ |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20160916224725/http://www.gudd-gess.de/regionales/regionales/article/karlsberg-bringt-mixery-beer-cocktails-auf-den-markt/ |archive-date=2016-09-16 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=www.gudd-gess.de |language=de}}</ref> These are available in the varieties [[Caipirinha]], [[Mojito]] and [[Sex on the Beach]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=MiXerybeercocktail productgrouppage {{!}} MiXery |url=http://www.mixery.de/de/mixerybeercocktail |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20161222225417/http://www.mixery.de/de/mixerybeercocktail |archive-date=2016-12-22 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=www.mixery.de |language=de}}</ref>

Alongside the alcoholic beer mix segment which accounts for the majority of the market, the non-alcoholic sector is also increasing; a growing number of alcohol-free beer mix products are also available.{{Citation needed|date=March 2023}}

The current leader of the German alcoholic beer mix market is still the MiXery brand with "MiXery Beer + Cola + X" followed by [[Krombacher]] Radler, Oettinger Radler, Beck’s Green Lemon, Schöfferhofer Grapefruit and MiXery Nastrov Flavour iced blue.<ref name="auto1">Cf. The Nielsen Company, 2015</ref> Krombacher is the non-alcoholic beer mix leader.
