The '''''Cafe Royal Cocktail Book''''' is a collection of [[cocktail]] recipes compiled by William J. Tarling, published by the United Kingdom Bartenders Guild in 1937.<ref name="euvslibrary">{{Cite web |url=http://euvslibrary.com/?p=445 |title=Café Royal Cocktail Book by William J Tarling |publisher=[[Universal Exposition of Wines and Spirits|Exposition Universelle des Vins et Spiriteaux]] |access-date=23 November 2016 |archive-date=22 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122222113/http://euvslibrary.com/?p=445 |url-status=live }}</ref> It contains a number of pioneering recipes, including the [[20th Century (cocktail)|20th Century]] and what may have later become the [[margarita]].

==Content==
The book focuses on cocktails developed in the 1920s and 1930s as well as those already approved, developed and used by members of the Bartender's Guild. It also contains some of the earliest known recipes for a range of cocktails. Fewer than 25 copies were originally published by the guild.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.abebooks.co.uk/books/rarebooks/vintage-cocktail-books/ |title=Vintage Cocktail Books: A Recipe for Collecting |access-date=23 November 2016 |archive-date=23 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161123203004/https://www.abebooks.co.uk/books/rarebooks/vintage-cocktail-books/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Tarling compiled the book to raise funds for the guild's sickness fund and the [[Café Royal]]'s sports club fund whilst he was serving as head bartender at the Cafe Royal.<ref name="distillery209">{{Cite web |url=https://www.distillery209.com/bartenders/william-tarling/ |title=Distillery209 |access-date=23 November 2016 |archive-date=12 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712130508/https://www.distillery209.com/age?r=%2fbartenders%2fwilliam-tarling%2f |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Notable cocktails ==
A number of notable cocktails are detailed in the book, including the first recorded recipe of the [[20th Century (cocktail)|20th Century]],<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lyPSCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT86 |title=Cocktails: The New Classics: 60 Recipes |last=Le Bordays |first=Frederic |year=2015 |publisher=Weldon Owen |isbn=978-1-681-88072-3 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> several references to [[absinthe]]<ref>{{cite book|title=The Dedalus Book of Absinthe|first=Phil|last=Baker|page=178|year=2001|publisher=Dedalus|isbn=978-1-873-98294-5}}</ref> and some of the earliest known recipes for drinks made with [[tequila]] and [[vodka]].<ref name="euvslibrary" /> An early reference to a possible precursor to the [[margarita]] was in the book, where it was called a Picador, which did not require a salt-rimmed glass, but used almost the same 7:4:3 ratio (2:1:1 in the book) of concentrations of tequila, freshly squeezed lime juice (or lemon juice, which is not an official margarita ingredient) and Cointreau [[triple sec]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SV5YryuX3_EC&dq=Cafe+Royal+cocktail+book&pg=PA276|title=Cocktails: Over 2250 Cocktails|first=Simon|last=Difford|page=276|publisher=Diffords Guide|year=2008|isbn=978-0-955-62760-6|access-date=2020-09-29|archive-date=2021-07-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712130509/https://books.google.com/books?id=SV5YryuX3_EC&pg=PA276&dq=Cafe+Royal+cocktail+book|url-status=live}}</ref> The book borrowed heavily from Tarling's previous composition of cocktails, the Approved Cocktails of the UKBG, which contained drinks developed by members of the guild.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.euvs.org/en/collection/book/approved-cocktails |title=Approved Cocktails of the UKBG |access-date=23 November 2016 |archive-date=24 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161124025014/http://www.euvs.org/en/collection/book/approved-cocktails |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Facsimile edition ==
There was only one printing of the original edition of the book, and copies have become difficult to find. In 2008 the UKBG, [[Universal Exposition of Wines and Spirits]], and [[Mixellany Limited]] reproduced a [[facsimile edition]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TpDdLwEACAAJ |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book – Google Books |date=May 2008 |isbn=9781907434136 |access-date=23 November 2016 |archive-date=12 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712130456/https://books.google.com/books?id=TpDdLwEACAAJ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Illustrations ==
The original book was illustrated by Frederick Carter, an Associate of the Royal Society of Etchers, Engravers and Illustrators from [[Bradford]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=Frederic Carter ARE 1883–1967: A Study of his Etchings |last=Clark |first=Richard Grenville |publisher=Apocalypse Press |year=1998}}</ref>

Chatham Artillery punch:
{{Short description|Alcoholic beverage}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2021}}
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Chatham Artillery punch
| image       = File:Chatham Artillery Punch.jpg   
| type        = [[Mixed drink]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|Lemons, sugar, whiskey, brandy, rum, Champagne<ref name="Stern 2014">{{cite web|last=Stern|first=Steven|date=29 April 2014|title=Original Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1013708-original-chatham-artillery-punch|access-date=27 February 2021|website=NYT Cooking}}</ref>}}
| served      = Chilled
| garnish     = Grated nutmeg, cherries
}}

'''Chatham Artillery punch''' is a potent [[Punch (drink)|punch]] containing [[rum]], [[whisky]], [[brandy]], and Champagne.<ref name="McKibben 2016">{{cite web|last=McKibben|first=Beth|date=8 July 2016|title=Chatham Artillery Punch: Maybe the Strongest Drink in American History|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/drink/chatham-artillery-punch-maybe-the-strongest-drink/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=pastemagazine.com}}</ref> It also contains [[lemon]]s and sugar.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> Named after the [[Chatham Artillery|Savannah regiment]], it is well-known in the city of [[Savannah, Georgia]],<ref name="McKibben 2016" /> which is located in [[Chatham County, Georgia|Chatham County]].

== History ==
The original recipe and creator are unknown.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One legend has it that [[George Washington]] was presented the punch when he arrived at [[Chatham Artillery]] in 1792, and he gave the regiment two [[cannon]]s.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016">{{cite web|date=8 June 2016|title=Drink This: Chatham Artillery Punch|url=https://www.atlantamagazine.com/dining-news/drink-chatham-artillery-punch/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Atlanta Magazine}}</ref> 

A more plausible story was reported in an 1885 article for the [[The Augusta Chronicle|''Augusta Chronicle'']].<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> It stated that the punch was created in the 1850s, when the [[Republican Blues]] returned from a drill in [[Macon, Georgia|Macon]] and were welcomed back by Sergeant A. B. Luce and the Chatham Artillery.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The punch was said to have been created by adding a quart of brandy, whiskey, and rum along with Champagne, lemon, and sugar to a horse bucket containing crushed ice.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> According to this story, every man who drank it was [[Alcohol intoxication|inebriated]].<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

In 1870, a group of [[Southern United States|Southern]] journalists held a convention in Savannah and were served the punch on a [[riverboat]] cruise.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> They became inebriated and reported their encounter with the drink, proposing guesses of the actual content.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The punch subsequently received national attention.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> President [[Chester A. Arthur|Chester Arthur]] was said to have been bested by the drink.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

In 1900, Admiral [[George Dewey]], a war hero from the [[Battle of Manila Bay|1898 Battle of Manila Bay]], also became inebriated when he imbibed the punch.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One recipe was later named after him.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

The drink was later revised to become less potent.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Miller 2011">{{cite web|last=Miller|first=Marleigh Riggins|date=11 April 2011|title=Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/04/drink-the-book-chatham-artillery-punch-original-recipe-wondrich.html|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Serious Eats}}</ref> In a recipe from 1907, it was written: "Experience has taught the rising generation to modify the receipt of their forefathers to conform to the weaker constitutions of their progeny."<ref name="Miller 2011"/><ref name="Wondrich 2010">{{cite book|last=Wondrich|first=D.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t6LabYdVTZ8C|title=Punch: The Delights (and Dangers) of the Flowing Bowl|publisher=Penguin Publishing Group|year=2010|isbn=978-1-101-44512-9|page=|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref>

After the end of [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] in the late 1930s, the cocktail grew in popularity again.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> One of the last variations was published after Prohibition by the ''[[The New York Sun|New York Sun]]'' in 1939.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The new recipes were substantially different, and sometimes included [[liquor]]s like [[Scotch whisky|scotch]] and [[gin]] and even excluded Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

Another legend is that during [[Sherman's March to the Sea|Sherman's March]] in the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], the residents of Savannah provided Sherman with so much of the punch that he decided to spare the city.<ref name="Pariseau">{{cite web|last=Pariseau|first=Leslie|title=The Great American Bar Crawl: Nine Bartenders Pick Their Favorite Cocktails|url=https://www.gq.com/story/bar-crawl-bartenders-favorite-cocktails-in-america|access-date=27 February 2021|website=GQ|date=21 June 2012 }}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
Many punch recipes call for Santa Cruz rum, which became more popular after Prohibition.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193">{{cite book|last=Moss|first=R.F.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vELTCwAAQBAJ|title=Southern Spirits: Four Hundred Years of Drinking in the American South, with Recipes|publisher=Ten Speed Press|year=2016|isbn=978-1-60774-867-0|page=193|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> It is more likely that heavy, dark rum is more similar to one used in the original recipe.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> [[Catawba (grape)|Catawba wine]] is difficult to find in modern times, and is substituted with a white wine or Champagne.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> In the [[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil (film)|1997 film adaptation]] of the [[John Berendt]] novel ''[[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil]]'', the punch is referenced as "three parts fruit, seven parts liquor{{snd}} whatever's available on both counts".<ref>{{cite AV media|url=|title=Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil|date=November 21, 1997|people=Eastwood, Clint (director); Hancock, John Lee (screenwriter)|language=English|publisher=Warner Bros. Pictures|trans-title=|location=|time=|access-date=|archive-url=|archive-date=|format=|id=|isbn=|oclc=|quote=|medium=motion picture}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
The drink can be prepared by taking lemon [[Zest (ingredient)|peels]] and [[Muddler|muddling]] them with sugar which will extract oils from the lemon peels.<ref name="Stern 2014"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> This mixture is added to lemon juice and is strained.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The lemon-sugar mixture is then added to a large bowl with crushed ice along with brandy, rum, whiskey, and Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> Although not likely traditional, [[Candied fruit|candied cherries]] (and sometimes the juice from the jar) are often added as well.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46">{{cite book|last1=Fowler|first1=D.L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Y-rCfsqL5cC|title=The Savannah Cookbook|last2=Carrington|first2=J.R.|publisher=Gibbs Smith, publisher|year=2008|isbn=978-1-4236-0224-8|page=46|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> Similarly, gin is sometimes added in modern recipes.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

== Variations ==
One variation is called Champagne punch.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> This is less potent version of the drink, and uses [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao]] or [[Cointreau]], a few shot of [[bitters]], fresh [[Strawberry|strawberries]], lemon, [[Syrup|simple syrup]], brandy, and Champagne.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> It is popular at [[wedding reception]]s and Christmas parties.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

There are similar drinks that exist. One is regent's punch, which is popular along the [[East Coast of the United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> Another is the [[Fish house punch]], which is found in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

Airmail (cocktail):
{{Short description|Rum-based cocktail}}
[[File:Air Mail Cocktail.png|thumb|Airmail Cocktail,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=In the mix|url=https://augustine-bar.de/in-the-mix/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=augustine-bar.de|language=English|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140504212541/http://augustine-bar.de:80/in-the-mix/ |archive-date=2014-05-04 }}</ref> garnished with a postal stamp]]
The '''''Airmail'' or ''Air Mail''''' (also ''Airmail cocktail'') is a classic cocktail based on [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] or [[lemon]] juice, [[honey]], and [[sparkling wine]]. It was probably created during or shortly after the period of [[prohibition]] in the [[United States|United States of America]] or on [[Cuba]], i.e. in the 1920s or 1930s.

Airmail Cocktail is also a brand of [https://www.airmailcocktail.com/ ready-to-drink cocktails] created and produced in Cognac (France) since 2020.

== History ==
As with the slightly older [[Aviation (cocktail)|Aviation cocktail]], to whose recipe there is no similarity, the name is reminiscent of [[aviation]] which developed rapidly at that time. In those years when international telephone connections were still a rarity, [[airmail]] was the fastest means of communication across national borders. Because of [[Prohibition in the United States|prohibition]], Americans were only able to legally drink alcohol abroad until 1933. Cuba, among other countries, benefited from this as a pronounced bar and cocktail culture began developing on the island in the 1920s. Since 1925, flights were available from [[Key West]] to [[Havana]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Pioneering Years: Commercial Aviation 1920 – 1930|url=https://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=centennialofflight.net - U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626001311/http://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|archive-date=2015-06-26}}</ref> and in 1930, a regular [[Airmail|airmail service]] was established to and from the island.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last=Ford|first=Doug|date=31 December 2014|title=A return to Havana: the Airmail Cocktail|url=https://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=cold-glass.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150111001408/http://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|archive-date=11 January 2015}}</ref> Shortly after, the ''Airmail Cocktail'' appeared for the first time in an advertising brochure of the then still Cuba-based rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":8" />

In 1941, the recipe was published in a mixology book.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Campbell Whitfield|first=William|title=Here's How. Mixed Drinks.|publisher=Three Mountaineers Inc.|year=1941|editor-last=Shell|editor-first=Ted (Illustrator)|edition=1|pages=36}}</ref> In his recipe collections, ''Just Cocktails'' (1939) and ''Here's How'' (1941), the author W.C. Whitfield had collected numerous drinks from the years of prohibition and provided them with comments partly in laconic style. As far as the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is concerned, Whitfield commented on it  ‘It ought to make you fly high’.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Meehan|first=Jim|title=The PDT Cocktail Book|last2=Gall|first2=Chris|publisher=Sterling Epicur|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4027-7923-7|location=New York|pages=48; 30}}</ref> The cocktail gained further popularity when the recipe was mentioned in the ''Handbook for Hosts'' in [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] magazine in 1949.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Esquire's Handbook for Hosts.|publisher=Grosset & Dunlap Publishers|year=1949|location=New York}}</ref>

In the following decades, the cocktail wasn't very popular, having been published rarely. In the 2010s, however, the cocktail experienced another boom by being mentioned in the ‘[https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11420025-the-pdt-cocktail-book PDT Cocktail Book]’ (2011) and by the promotion of alcoholic drinks by the brand [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|date=26 July 2019|title=Rum trifft Champagner: Das völlig verdiente Revival des Air Mail Cocktails|url=https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=mixology.eu|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614140819/https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/ |archive-date=2021-06-14 }}</ref>

== Ingredients and similar cocktails ==
The basis for the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is a sour mixture of [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] juice and [[honey]] (or honey syrup), which are first shaken on ice in a [[cocktail shaker]] and then strained into a pre-cooled [[Cocktail glass]]. The mixture is then topped up with sparkling wine. The drink is similar to the [[Canchanchara|Canchánchara]],<ref name=":5" /> which consists of the same ingredients except for the [[sparkling wine]]. ‘Esquire’ magazine calls the ''Airmail Cocktail''  a "combination of the cocktails ''French 75'' and ''Honey Bee''".<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=27 September 2019|title=How to make an Air Mail|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216154029/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|archive-date=16 February 2015}}</ref> The [[French 75 (cocktail)|''French 75'']] is a Champagne-based drink and a classic mixture of Gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup, while the ''Honey Bee'' consists of white rum, honey and lemon juice<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=15 May 2020|title=How to make a Honey Bee|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150215020034/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|archive-date=15 February 2015}}</ref> and therefore is akin to a [[Daiquiri]]. A modern cocktail which shares the ingredients rum, lime juice and champagne with the Airmail Cocktail is the [[Old Cuban]], which was created in 2001.

Most recipes feature a mixture ratio of 3 [[Litre|cl]] rum, 1.5 cl lime juice and 1.5 cl honey syrup,<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> which are then topped up with 3 cl champagne<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|date=6 May 2021|title=Airmail Cocktail|url=https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=imbibemagazine.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927230258/https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/ |archive-date=2020-09-27 }}</ref> and either garnished with a slice of lime on the rim of the glass<ref name=":4" /> or not garnished at all<ref name=":5" /> - as usual for cocktails based on sparkling wine. The magazine ''[[Imbibe Magazine|Imbibe]]'' recommends a dash of [[Angostura bitters|Angostura]] (bitters) and a mint leaf,<ref name=":7" /> while the rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]] recommends a postage stamp as garnish.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Air Mail|url=https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=bacardi.com|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422142859/https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/ |archive-date=2021-04-22 }}</ref>

The Cocktail can be prepared with [[Rum#Grades|dark or white rum]]. Dark rum is best complemented with the addition of a comparatively [[Honey#Acid content and flavor effects|aromatic honey]], while white rum prefers the use of a mild honey like [[Honey#Floral source|Acacia blossom honey]].<ref name=":5" /> Cuban rum is often recommended. Substitution of the lime juice with lemon juice is possible.<ref name=":3" /> The honey syrup used for the cocktail is a mixture of 2 parts honey and 1 part water,<ref name=":4" /> which is easier to incorporate into mixtures and to add to taste than pure honey. In most cases, the cocktail is topped up with [[Champagne#Sweetness|dry champagne]], [[Sparkling wine#Crémant|Crémant]] or [[sparkling wine]] (less so with [[Prosecco]]).<ref name=":7" />

It is usually served [[Bartending terminology#Straight, up, and straight up|straight up]] in a pre-cooled [[Champagne glass#Flute|champagne flute]] or [[Champagne glass#Coupe|coupe]].<ref name=":5" /> Some recipes call for much larger quantities of liquid and proportionally more sparkling wine which therefore suggests serving the cocktail in a [[Collins glass]].<ref name=":6" />

Claret cup (drink):
{{short description|Red wine cocktail popular 19th century}}

[[File:Claret cup recipes from The Gentleman's Table Guide (1873).jpg|thumb|Claret-cup recipes from ''The Gentleman's Table Guide'' (1873)]]

'''Claret cup''' is a type of [[wine cocktail]] that was popular in 19th-century [[western Europe]] and [[North America]]. The basic ingredients of claret cup are chilled [[claret]] or similar [[wine]], [[carbonated water]], [[sugar]], and [[flavorings]] that supply a citrusy or herbal aroma. 

One 1877 recipe called for dissolved [[cane sugar]], a bottle of [[claret]], two thin [[lemon]] slices, one [[cucumber]] peel, a glass of [[sherry]], a spoonful of [[brandy]], a spoonful of [[noyeau]] or [[maraschino]], and grated [[nutmeg]]. Then blend, wait, taste test, and add ice and a bottle of carbonated water.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Payne |first=Arthur Gay |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7UICAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA152 |title=Common-sense Papers on Cookery |date=1877 |publisher=Cassell Petter & Galpin |pages=152–155 |language=en}}</ref> The lighter recipe subtracted the sherry and brandy, doubled the soda water, and added a few drops of [[almond extract]].<ref name=":0" /> A strong cup was suitable for drinking with [[dinner]], a lighter one might consumed after [[sport]], such as [[badminton]] or [[cricket]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Terrington |first=William |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7T8CAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA169 |title=Cooling Cups and Dainty Drinks |date=1869 |publisher=George Routledge and Sons |language=en}}</ref> An 1895 recipe from [[America]] added a little [[Curaçao (liqueur)|curaçao liqueur]] and garnished with [[mentha|mint]] sprigs; the same cookbook suggested that someone wanting to make a "claret cup (English style)" build on the American recipe but add "a few [[strawberries]]" and [[borage]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kappeler |first=George J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-XGRDVd7JOwC&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA51 |title=Modern American Drinks: How to Mix and Serve All Kinds of Cups and Drinks |date=1895 |publisher=Saalfield Publishing Company |pages=50–51 |language=en}}</ref> An 1879 recipe for ''superior'' claret cup suggested a ratio of two bottles of claret to one bottle of [[champagne]], plus three glasses of sherry, one glass of [[noyau]], half a [[Pound (mass)|pound]] crushed ice, with a borage or cucumber-curl garnish.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jewry |first=Mary |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n0ICAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA656 |title=Warne's model cookery and house-keeping book |date=1879 |pages=656 |language=en}}</ref>  

Other recipes used grated [[cinnamon]], [[allspice]], [[Clove|cloves]] and [[cardamom]] instead of nutmeg; some added [[Orange (fruit)|orange]] slices or even [[pineapple]] chunks. Riffs on the basic recipe added a broad range of other flavors including [[Kirschwasser]], [[rhubarb]] wine, [[Viola (plant)|violet]] syrup, or [[ginger beer]] (one at a time, not all together).<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Terrington |first=William |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7T8CAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA169 |title=Cooling Cups and Dainty Drinks |date=1869 |publisher=George Routledge and Sons |pages=164–169 |language=en |chapter=Wine Cups}}</ref> Common garnishes and herbal flavorings included the edible borage flower, [[Aloysia citrodora|lemon verbena]], [[citronella oil]], and sprigs of mint or [[lemon balm]].<ref name=":1" /> 

Variations on the theme included the [[champagne cup]], [[Hock (wine)|hock]] cup,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Roberts |first1=George Edwin |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/011553334 |title=Cups and their customs. |last2=Herndon |first2=James B. |last3=Porter |first3=Henry |last4=Herndon/Vehling Collection |date=1863 |publisher=J. Van Voorst |location=London |pages=45 |language=en-gb}}</ref> [[Chablis wine|Chablis]] cup, [[Burgundy wine|burgundy]] cup,<ref name=":2" /> [[cider]] cup, and [[Moselle wine|Moselle]] cup, each with adjustments to the amount of sugar.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g8IHAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA44 |title=DICKENS'S DICTIONARY OF THE THAMES |date=1856 |language=en}}</ref> There was also a variation called Claret Cup à la Henry VIII (although it is unclear how [[Henry VIII]] is involved in the matter):<ref>{{Cite book |last=Reinhardt |first=Charles Nicholas |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/100170798 |title="Cheerio!" a book of punches and cocktails. How to mix them, and other rare, exquisite and delicate drinks... |date=1930 |publisher=The Elf Publishers, Inc. |edition=Revised |series=Book of punches and cocktails |location=New York |pages=27}}</ref>

{{blockquote|CLARET CUP À LA HENRY VIII
Peel off the rind of a lemon and mix both the juice and rind with powdered sugar. Pour over them a glass of Sherry and a bottle of Claret and sweeten to taste. Add a sprig of verbena and a bottle of soda water with a little grated nutmeg. Strain the mixture and serve with ice.}}

The various "wine cups," as they were called, are best when "fresh and sparkling" and thus it was recommended that they be prepared immediately before the opening of a party.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Harris |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CJcrBgAAQBAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA179 |title=About Ices Jellies & Creams |date=2013-10-28 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-18425-3 |pages=179 |language=en}}</ref> An 1894 British [[etiquette]] guide firmly advised readers on the correct service of claret-cup: "Champagne-cup and claret-cup are, in the country, served on a separate table, or in an adjoining room. Small [[Tumbler (glass)|tumblers]] and [[Champagne glass|champagne-glasses]] should be placed upon the same table...in town, where space is made the most of, these drinks are usually placed on the sideboard. A manservant should be at hand to pour out the cup as required."<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Member of the aristocracy |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/100893767 |title=Waiting at table. A practical guide |date=1894 |publisher=F. Warne & Co. |location=London |pages=85 |language=en-go}}</ref> Claret cup can be served out of [[jug|jugs]],<ref name=":4" /> glass pitchers, or a [[punch bowl]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fougner |first=G. Selmer |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/009179164 |title=Along the wine trail: an anthology of wines and spirits |date=1935 |publisher=The Stratford Company |location=Boston |pages=253}}</ref> One guide to fancy beverages recommends preparing and consuming claret cup in the summer months, "regulating the proportion of ice to the weather."<ref>{{Cite book |last=L. S. F |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008614037 |title=Beverages and sauces of colonial Virginia, 1607-1907 |date=1906 |publisher=The Neale publishing company |location=New York and Washington |pages=12}}</ref>

In wintertime, [[Mulled wine|mulled]] claret cups would be served from pots of claret, heated low and slow with sugar and a [[cinnamon stick]], and served warm.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schultz |first=Christian |title=How to Mix Drinks or The Bon-Vivant's Companion - Containing Clear and Reliable Directions for Mixing all the Beverages used in the United States: Together with the most Popular British, French, German, Italian, Russian and Spanish Recipes, Embracing Punches, Juleps, Cobblers in Endless Variety - To Which is Added a Manual for the Manufacture of Cordials, Liquors, Fancy Syrups |date=2017-08-25 |publisher=Read Books Ltd |isbn=978-1-4733-3924-8 |language=en |chapter=191. Claret Cup, or Mulled Claret |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KKcyDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PP12}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> 

The refreshment of claret cup gets a nod in [[Edward Lear]]'s volume of light verse ''More Nonsense''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lear |first=Edward |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001020033 |title=More nonsense, pictures, rhymes, botany, etc. |date=1872 |publisher=Robert John Bush |location=London}}</ref> Soda water, sugar, ice and "burrage" for preparing a claret cup are referenced in the lyrics of [[Thespis (opera)|''Thespis'']] (1871), the first comic-opera collaboration of [[Gilbert and Sullivan|Gilbert & Sullivan]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bradley |first=Ian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KLsUDAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Claret+cup%22&pg=PA25 |title=The Complete Annotated Gilbert & Sullivan: 20th Anniversary Edition |date=2016-05-03 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-939243-8 |pages=25 |language=en}}</ref> Claret cup is served, to the general satisfaction of the characters, in [[George Bernard Shaw]]'s ''[[You Never Can Tell (play)|You Never Can Tell]]'' (1897).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shaw |first=Bernard |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/009793008 |title=You never can tell: a pleasant play |date=1918 |publisher=Brentano's |location=New York}}</ref>

{{ill|Clericó|lt=''Clericó''|es}}, a popular beverage in South America with a similar formula, is a direct [[Loanword|borrowing]] into [[Spanish language|Spanish]] from the [[English language|English-language]] ''claret cup.''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barabino |first1=Américo |last2=Barabino |first2=Americo |date=May 1950 |title=English Influence on the Common Speech of the River Plate |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/333915 |journal=Hispania |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=163 |doi=10.2307/333915|jstor=333915 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Grenadine:
{{Short description|Fruit syrup with a flavor that is both tart and sweet}} {{Other uses}} {{Use American English|date=October 2019}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2020}} [[File:Grenadinesyrup.jpg|thumb|150px|A glass and bottle of grenadine]] '''Grenadine''' ({{IPAc-en|'|g|r|E|n|@|d|i:|n}}) is a nonalcoholic bar [[syrup]] commonly used as a [[cocktail]] ingredient, distinguished by its sweetness, mild flavor, and red color. Popular in [[mixed drink]]s, grenadine syrup was traditionally made from [[pomegranate]], but today is most prevalently made from commercially produced natural or artificial flavors, as well as substitute fruits (such as [[blackcurrant]], [[Sambucus nigra|elderberry]], [[raspberry]], [[gooseberry]] and their juices).{{cite web |title=Rose's Grenadine Product Facts |url=https://www.kdpproductfacts.com/product/a0e3h000003LK5YAAW/roses-grenadine-2-tbsp-us |website=Keurig - Dr. Pepper |access-date=17 May 2024}} ==Name== Grenadine syrup was originally prepared from [[pomegranate juice]], sugar, and water,''Dictionnaire Universel de Cuisine Pratique : Encyclopédie Illustrée D'Hygiène Alimentaire'', [[Joseph Favre]], Paris, 1905, pp. 1088. with its name deriving from the [[French language|French]] word ''grenade'', for [[pomegranate]] (from the [[Latin]] ''grānātum'', "seeded"). It is not related to the [[Grenadines]] archipelago, which takes its name from [[Grenada]], itself from [[Granada]], [[Spain]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HZW-bdkudYkC&dq=Grenadines+granada+grenada&pg=PT185|title=Fodor's Barbados, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, the Grenadines & Grenada|date=December 28, 2010|publisher=Fodor's Travel|isbn=9780307928030|via=Google Books}}
- {{Cite web|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5845/|title=Grenadines Island Group (Grenada)|publisher=UNESCO World Heritage Centre}} ==Modern and commercial variants== As grenadine is subject to minimal regulation, its basic flavor profile can vary widely from the original pomegranate to combinations of unspecified natural and artificial flavors, to the use of other fruits, such as [[blackcurrant]], [[Sambucus nigra|elderberry]], [[raspberry]], and [[gooseberry]].{{cite web|last1=Food and Drug Administration|date=1980-01-10|url=https://www.fda.gov/ICECI/ComplianceManuals/CompliancePolicyGuidanceManual/ucm074531.htm |title=Sec. 550.400 Grenadine|work=CPG 7110.11|access-date=2009-08-23}}{{dead link|date=May 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} To reduce production costs, manufacturers have widely replaced fruit bases with artificial ingredients. The "Rose's" brand (owned by [[Mott's]]) is by far the most common grenadine sold in the United States,{{cite web|publisher=Cadbury Schweppes|date=2000-09-18|url=http://www.cadburyschweppes.com/EN/MediaCentre/PressReleases/snapple_180900.htm| title=Media Release: Cadbury Schweppes to Acquire Snapple Beverage Group for an Enterprise Value of $1,450 Million|access-date=2008-07-05|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20040612173104/http://www.cadburyschweppes.com/EN/MediaCentre/PressReleases/snapple_180900.htm|archive-date=2004-06-12}} and is formulated from (in order of concentration) [[high fructose corn syrup]], [[water]], [[citric acid]], [[sodium citrate]], [[sodium benzoate]], [[FD&C Red 40|FD&C Red #40]], natural and artificial flavors, and [[Brilliant_Blue_FCF|FD&C Blue #1]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.wegmans.com/webapp/wcs/stores/servlet/ProductDisplay?langId=-1&storeId=10052&catalogId=10002&productId=352053|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101106212136/http://www.wegmans.com/webapp/wcs/stores/servlet/ProductDisplay?langId=-1&storeId=10052&catalogId=10002&productId=352053|title=Wegmans - Rose's Grenadine Ingredients|archive-date=November 6, 2010}} ==Use== [[File:The Official Queen Mary Cocktail.jpg|alt=The Queen Mary cocktail: beer, grenadine and Maraschino cherries|thumb|193x193px|The [[Queen Mary (cocktail)|Queen Mary]] is a [[beer cocktail]] using grenadine and [[Maraschino cherry|Maraschino cherries]]]] Grenadine is commonly used to mix both modern and classic [[Cocktail|cocktails]], including: * [[El Presidente (cocktail)|El Presidente]] – [[rum]], orange [[Curaçao (liqueur)|curaçao]], [[vermouth]], and grenadine * [[Mary Pickford (cocktail)|Mary Pickford]] – white rum, [[pineapple juice]] and grenadine * [[Queen Mary (cocktail)|Queen Mary]] – [[beer]], grenadine and [[Maraschino cherry|maraschino cherries]], drizzled with [[cherry]] syrup * [[Singapore sling]] – a [[gin]]-based [[Sling (drink)|sling]] cocktail * [[Tequila sunrise]] – [[tequila]], [[orange juice]] and grenadine * [[Ward 8 (cocktail)|Ward 8]] – [[Whisky|whiskey]], lemon juice, orange juice and grenadine * [[Zombie (cocktail)|Zombie]] – a rum-based Tiki cocktail * [[Terremoto (drink)|Terremoto]] – a traditional chilean cocktail made with pipeño wine, pineapple ice cream and grenadine Grenadine is also a popular ingredient in such non-alcoholic drinks as the [[Shirley Temple (drink)|Shirley Temple]], [[Roy Rogers (drink)|Roy Rogers]] and the [[Diabolo (drink) |Diabolo]]. ==See also== * [[List of syrups]] ==References== {{reflist}} == External links == * {{commons-inline}} [[Category:Drink mixers]] [[Category:Syrup]]
Ginger ale: {{Short description|Soft drink flavoured with ginger}} {{Distinguish|Ginger beer}} {{Use mdy dates|date=May 2013}} {{use Canadian English|date=October 2022}} {{Infobox beverage | name = Ginger ale | image = Vernors ginger ale.jpg | caption = [[Vernors]] golden ginger ale | type = [[Soft drink]] | proof = | manufacturer = | distributor = | origin = {{nowrap|[[Ireland]] and [[Canada]]}} | introduced = 1851 (golden){{break}}1904 (dry) | region = [[Northern Ireland]] and [[Southern Ontario]], [[Canada]] | discontinued = | colour = Golden | flavour = [[Ginger]] | variants = Golden and dry | related = | website = }} {{Cookbook|Ginger ale}} '''Ginger ale''' is a [[Soft drink|carbonated soft drink]] (not an [[ale]]) flavoured with [[ginger]]. It is consumed on its own or used as a [[drink mixer|mixer]], often with spirit-based drinks. There are two main types of ginger ale. The golden style is credited to the Irish doctor Thomas Joseph Cantrell. The dry style (also called the pale style), a paler drink with a much milder ginger flavour, was created by Canadian [[John J. McLaughlin|John McLaughlin]]. ==History== Ginger ale is transparent, whereas [[ginger beer]], a stronger tasting product, is often cloudy due to the residues of brewing. Thomas Joseph Cantrell, an Irish [[apothecary]] and surgeon, manufactured the first ginger ale in [[Belfast]], Northern Ireland, in the 1850s. He set out to create a [[soft drink]]. This was the older "golden style" [[fermented]] ginger ale, dark coloured, generally sweet to taste, with a strong ginger spice flavour,{{clarify|How is this not a *ginger beer*? What did he do different? Was it filtration to make his product clear? If so, clarify and explain why this is not a "ginger beer" by its definition.|date=July 2021}} which he marketed through local beverage manufacturer Grattan and Company.{{cite news |url=http://letslookagain.com/tag/thomas-joseph-cantrell/|title=THE SPARKLING HISTORY OF CANTRELL & COCHRANE |work=Let's Look Again |date=November 2016 |access-date=October 19, 2018}} Grattan embossed the slogan "The Original Makers of Ginger Ale" on its bottles.{{cite web |url=http://www.fohbc.org/PDF_Files/GingerAle_Previtali.pdf |title=Federation of Historical Bottle Collectors |publisher=FOHBC |access-date=2013-10-03 |archive-date=February 27, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140227135038/http://www.fohbc.org/PDF_Files/GingerAle_Previtali.pdf |url-status=dead }} [[File:Canada Dry Pale Ginger Ale Toronto Star ad 1916.jpg|thumbnail|1916 ''Toronto Star'' ad for [[Canada Dry]] ginger ale]] Dry ginger ale was created by Canadian [[John J. McLaughlin]], a chemist and pharmacist.{{cite news |url=http://www.canadiangeographic.ca/magazine/jf02/canadianfoodfirsts.asp |title=Canadian food firsts |work=Canadian Geographic |date=January–February 2002 |access-date=October 31, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624005710/http://www.canadiangeographic.ca/Magazine/JF02/canadianfoodfirsts.asp |archive-date=June 24, 2013 |df=mdy-all }} Having established a [[soda water]] bottling plant in 1890, McLaughlin began developing flavour extracts to add to the water in 1904. That year, he introduced "Pale Dry" Ginger Ale, the bubbly drink that would be patented in 1907 as [[Canada Dry]] Ginger Ale. A success, Canada Dry products were accepted by appointment to the Vice-Regal Household of the [[Governor General of Canada]]. The dry-style also became popular in the United States during the [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] era, when it was used as a [[Drink mixer|mixer]] for alcoholic beverages.{{cite journal |last1=Tallon |first1=Beverley |title=Canada Dry Ginger Ale |journal=The Beaver |volume=88 |issue=6 |page=10}} ===Ingredients=== Traditional ginger ale is [[Fermentation|fermented]] from a microbial [[fermentation starter|starter]] culture ([[yeast]] or ginger bug), [[sugar]], fresh [[ginger root]], other flavourings and [[water]]. Ginger bug can be derived from ginger beer plant containing ''[[Saccharomyces florentinus]]'' and ''[[Lactobacillus hilgardii]]'' or fresh ginger root containing ''[[Lactobacillus]]'' bacteria and wild yeast. The [[carbonation]] comes from the yeast fermentation as opposed to carbonating the finished product. [[Alcohol (drug)|Ethanol]], as a byproduct of fermentation, will be present in the ginger ale but can be controlled by modifying fermentation time. Commercial ginger ale commonly contains [[carbonated water]], sugar or [[high-fructose corn syrup]], and artificial or natural ginger-flavour. Ginger content is often listed on labels in a general "natural aroma" or "[[natural flavoring|natural flavouring]]" statement, to preserve secrecy of the complex proprietary mix of [[spices]], fruits and other flavours used;{{cn|date=July 2021}} lemon, [[Lime (fruit)|lime]], and [[cane sugar]] are the most common ingredients.{{cn|date=July 2021}} [[Pineapple]] and [[honey]] are also occasionally used.{{cn|date=July 2021}} == Processing == === Fermentation === [[File:Yeast and nutrients.JPG|thumb|upright|Yeast]] Traditional ginger ale is [[fermented]] using [[ginger]], yeast, water, sugar, and possibly other flavourings. A ginger bug – a slurry of ginger and sugar used to propagate the yeast and bacteria found on the ginger skin – may be used in place of commercial yeast.{{cite web |last1=Graham |first1=Colleen |title=Make a Ginger Bug for Healthy Homemade Sodas |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/how-to-start-a-ginger-bug-and-make-natural-ginger-soda-3016495 |website=The Spruce Eats |publisher=Dotdash |access-date=29 July 2020 |ref=003 |archive-date=August 7, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807161936/https://www.thespruceeats.com/how-to-start-a-ginger-bug-and-make-natural-ginger-soda-3016495 |url-status=dead }} === Artificial carbonation=== Rather than ferment their product, most commercial ginger ale bottlers will [[Carbonated water|carbonate]] their soda by chilling the water to a low temperature to allow more [[carbon dioxide]] to be dissolved.{{Cite web|url=http://www.madehow.com/Volume-2/Soft-Drink.html|title=How soft drink is made - production process, making, history, used, product, industry, machine|website=www.madehow.com|language=en|access-date=2018-08-09}} Then, [[PH|alkaline]] compounds such as [[sodium bicarbonate]] may be added to reduce acidity. Lastly, carbon dioxide is added and slightly over-pressurized to facilitate movement into storage and the filling machine. ==Uses== [[File:8 Gläser Ginger Ale.jpg|thumb|Glasses of ginger ale with wedges of limes]] Ginger ale is consumed as a [[soft drink]] and a [[Drink mixer|mixer]] in [[mixed drink|cocktail]]s and [[Punch (drink)|punch]].Noah Rothbaum, and David Wondrich. 2021. “Ginger Ale and Ginger Beer.” ''The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails''. New York, Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|9780199311149}} It is sometimes used by non-drinkers or in the performing arts as a [[non-alcoholic mixed drink|non-alcoholic]] substitute for [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne/sparkling wine]] or [[beer]], since the beverages resemble each other in appearance. Ginger ale is also added to beer to make [[shandy]].{{cn|date=June 2025}} Ginger ale has traditionally been used as a home remedy, particularly for [[indigestion]] and nausea.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XFnZCwAAQBAJ |title=National Geographic Complete Guide to Natural Home Remedies: 1,025 Easy Ways to Live Longer, Feel Better, and Enrich Your Life |last=Geographic |first=National |date=2014 |publisher=National Geographic Books |isbn=9781426212604 |page=28 |language=en}}{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IB5IBAAAQBAJ |title=The Art of Seamanship: Evolving Skills, Exploring Oceans, and Handling Wind, Waves, and Weather |last=Naranjo |first=Ralph |date=2014-09-12 |publisher=McGraw Hill Professional |isbn=9780071791588 |pages=66–67 |language=en}} == Nutrition == Ginger ale is usually acceptable for people on a [[clear liquid diet]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yIjKDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA487|title=deWit's Fundamental Concepts and Skills for Nursing - E-Book|last=Williams|first=Patricia A.|date=2016-12-23|publisher=Elsevier Health Sciences|isbn=9780323483285|pages=487|language=en}} It is generally high in sugar, with commercial varieties containing around 10 g of sugar per 100 ml.{{cn|date=September 2023}} ==Variations== === Ginger ale vs ginger beer === Ginger ale and ginger beer are similar beverages, however, there are clear differences during the process. Ginger beer originated in [[England]] in the 1800s while ginger ale was founded in [[Ireland]] approximately 50 years later before it was modernized in 1907 by John McLaughlin.{{Cite news|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/04/20/ginger-ale-vs-ginger-beer_n_1438420.html|title=The Difference Between Ginger Ale And Ginger Beer|last=Daily|first=Kitchen|date=2012-04-20|work=Huffington Post|access-date=2018-08-09|language=en-US}} Original ginger beer contains 11% alcohol, but modern ginger beer contains less than 0.5% alcohol while modern ginger ale has absolutely no alcohol content.{{Cite news|url=https://www.townandcountrymag.com/leisure/drinks/a15873518/alcoholic-ginger-beer-vs-ginger-ale/|title=What's the Difference Between Ginger Beer and Ginger Ale?|date=2018-02-13|work=Town & Country|access-date=2018-08-09|language=en-US}} Ginger beer is brewed with natural [[ginger]], [[Lemon|lemon juice]], sugar and it is fermented with a ginger beer plant culture (mainly ''[[Lactobacillus]]''). The fermentation of the ''Lactobacillus'' produces a cloudy appearance, stronger-tasting and spicier flavour compared to ginger ale. Other differences between ginger ale and ginger beer are in terms of taste and aroma. Whilst ginger ale is mellow and smells sweet, ginger beer has a spicy whiff and gingery taste.{{Cite web|url=https://advancedmixology.com/blogs/art-of-mixology/ginger-beer-vs-ginger-ale-which-one-should-you-use|title=Ginger Beer vs Ginger Ale: Which One Should You Use?|website=Advanced Mixology|access-date=2019-08-18}} === Other flavours === Dry ginger ale is also sold with a [[mentha|mint]] flavouring added.{{where|date=October 2022}} Some mint ginger ale brands have an artificial green [[food colouring|colour]] added, while others are clear. Canada Dry has introduced a line of ginger ale mixed with green tea and one mixed with lemonade.{{when|date=October 2018}} ==Manufacturers== [[File:Ginger ale bottles.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Boylan Bottling Company|Boylan]] ginger ale]] [[Vernors]], [[Blenheim Ginger Ale|Blenheim]], [[A-Treat Bottling Company|A-Treat]], Bull's Head, [[Chelmsford, Massachusetts#History|Chelmsford]], [[Buffalo Rock]], [[Sussex Golden Ginger Ale|Sussex]] and [[Red Rock (drink)|Red Rock]] are brands of golden ginger ale. [[Canada Dry]], and [[Seagram|Seagram's]], both formerly Canadian companies, and [[Schweppes]], are major brands of dry ginger ale. ===North America=== American brands include [[A.J. Canfield Company|Canfield's]], [[Hansen Natural]], [[Vernors]], [[Buffalo Rock]], [[Boylan Bottling Company]], [[Polar Beverages]], [[Ale-8-One]], [[Blenheim Ginger Ale|Blenheim]], [[Foxon Park]], [[Fitz's]], [[Sprecher Brewery|Sprecher]], [[DeMoulas/Market Basket|Market Basket]]/[[Chelmsford, Massachusetts|Chelmsford]], [[Red Rock Cola|Red Rock]], [[Reed's Ginger Brew]], [[Chek (brand)|Chek]] (River of Dreams), [[Shasta (soft drink)|Shasta]], and in Canada; [[Sussex Golden Ginger Ale]]. Vernors is a flavoured golden ginger ale aged for three years in oak barrels before bottling. It was the first U.S. soft drink, originating in 1866, although it was modelled on imported Irish ginger beers. Jagertee:
{{Short description|Alcoholic beverage}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2025}}
'''Jagertee''' (also '''Jägertee''') is an alcoholic punch historically made by mixing [[stroh|"Inländer-Rum"]] with spiced [[black tea]].<ref name=2tb>{{citation|title= Jagertee recipe (archive version)|url=https://www.austria.info/uk/things-to-do/food-and-drink/favourite-austrian-recipes/jaegertee |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929233311/https://www.austria.info/uk/things-to-do/food-and-drink/favourite-austrian-recipes/jaegertee |archive-date=2018-09-29 }}</ref> It is served warm and is typically consumed during winter in the cold parts of [[Central Europe]].<ref name=ltb>{{citation |title=Little Tea Book |first=Rose Marie |last=Donhauser |publisher=Silverback Books |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-59637-074-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9mS-6xfbS80C}}</ref>

Although Jagertee is easily made at home, ready-made mixtures which already contain [[spice]]s and [[sugar]] are sold in shops. The Austrian rum ''[[Stroh]]'' is often used for making it; this [[brand]] also produces its own ready-made variety.

Jagertee has become a popular ''[[après-ski]]'' drink,<ref name=ltb/> especially among [[tourism|tourists]] in the [[Alps]]. Jagertee carts sell the beverage outside at ski resorts and winter festivals.

==Etymology==

The name ''Jagertee'' (alternatively ''Jagatee'' or ''Jägertee'') is derived from the [[Austro-Bavarian language|Austro-Bavarian]] pronunciation of the standard German ''Jäger'' "hunter" + ''Tee'' "tea". According to [[European Community|EC]] Regulation 110/2008, Annex III, No. 32, it is a [[Protected Geographical Status|Protected Designation of Origin]] reserved for the beverage made in Austria.<ref>{{cite web |title= Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 of the EuPopean Parliament and of the Council of 15 January 2008 on the definition, description, presentation, labelling and the protection of geographical indications of spirit drinks and repealing Council Regulation (EEC) No 1576/89  | work=Official Journal on [[EUR-Lex]] | publisher=EU Publications Office | url=http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=OJ:L:2008:039:0016:0054:EN:PDF | access-date=2009-07-15}}</ref> Therefore, varieties made in Germany are sold under names like ''Hüttentee'' ("hut tea") or ''Förstertee'' ("forester tea"). It has also been sold under the name of ''[[Grog]]'' in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

Some rural establishments also serve ''Wilderertee'' ("[[Poaching|poacher's]] tea"), which is even stronger.

Drinking straw:
