Sour (cocktail):
{{short description|Family of classic mixed drinks}}
{{about|the family of cocktails|the spirit used in cocktails|Sourz}}
{{More citations needed|date=October 2020}}
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Sours
| image       = [[File:Whiskey sour.jpg|frameless]]  
| caption     = A whiskey sour garnished with a wheel of lemon and maraschino cherries. 
| type        = [[Cocktail|Cocktail family]]
| base        = [[Gin]], [[Bourbon whiskey]], [[Brandy]], [[Pisco]], [[Rum]], [[Amaretto]]
}}
A '''sour''' is a traditional family of [[mixed drink]]s. ''Sours'' belong to one of the old families of original cocktails and are described by [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] in his 1862 book ''How to Mix Drinks''.<ref name="Cocktail Chronicles">Paul Clarke. [http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2005/09/25/make-yourself-comfortable/ Make Yourself Comfortable]. September 25, 2005. The Cocktail Chronicles. Retrieved on January 1, 2007.</ref> 

Sours are mixed drinks containing a base liquor, [[Lemon juice|lemon]] or [[lime juice]], and a sweetener ([[simple syrup]] or [[orgeat syrup]]).<ref name="Joy 158-159">{{cite book|author=Regan, Gary |title=The Joy of Mixology, The Consummate Guide to the Bartender's Craft |year=2003 |publisher=Clarkson Potter |isbn=0609608843|pages=158–159}}</ref> [[Egg white|Egg whites]] are also included in some sours.

==Types of sours==

===Gin sour===
The '''gin sour''' is a traditional [[mixed cocktail]] that predates [[Prohibition in the United States]]. It is a simple combination of gin, lemon juice, and sugar. Adding carbonated water to this turns it into a [[gin fizz]].

It was popular during the 1940s, and [[Kevin Starr]] includes it in "an array of drinks (the gin sour, the whiskey sour, the [[Rickey (cocktail)#The gin Rickey|gin Rickey]], the [[Tom Collins]], the [[Pink lady (cocktail)|pink lady]], the [[Old fashioned (cocktail)|old fashioned]]) that now seem period pieces, evocative of another era".{{ref|starr}}

===Pisco sour===
{{main|Pisco sour}}
The classic '''pisco sour''' recipe contains [[pisco]] brandy (usually an un-aged grape brandy from Perú), fresh lime juice, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup, egg white, and [[bitters]].<ref name="LA Speakeasy">Navarro, V. [https://www.laspeakeasy.com/pisco-sour/ Classic Pisco Sour] ''LA Speakeasy''</ref> It is [[Cocktail shaker|shaken]], [[Cocktail strainer|strained]], and served [[Straight up (bartending)|straight]] in a cocktail glass then garnished with the bitters (cinnamon can be used). The addition of egg white creates a foamy head when shaken before serving. While pisco sour is flavoured with key lime by default, pisco is combined with other fruit to create mango sour, maracuya ([[passion fruit]]) sour, lucuma sour and so forth.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://peru.com/estilo-de-vida/gastronomia/maracuya-sour-que-necesitas-y-como-se-prepara-este-exquisito-trago-noticia-213918 |title=Maracuya sour: Qué necesitas y cómo se prepara este exquisito trago |first=Redacción |last=Peru.com |date=December 6, 2013 |website=Perú.com}}</ref> Peru has a National Pisco Sour Day (which lasts a weekend) in mid-February,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://elcomercio.pe/noticias/dia-del-pisco-sour |title=Todas las noticias de Día del Pisco Sour |website=El Comercio}}</ref> and Chile has Pisco Day in mid-May.

===Rum sour===

The basic [[Daiquiri]], sometimes called a Daiquiri sour, is made with rum, lime juice and simple syrup.<ref>{{cite web |title=Daiquiri cocktail |website=Difford's |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail}}</ref> One account of the drink's origin is that the general manager of the Spanish-American Iron Core Company, which operated the "Daiquiri" mine, ran out of gin one night when making gin sour for his guests, and switched to rum. This rum sour became known as the Daiquiri. However, earlier printed recipes for rum sour exist such as one from [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] from 1887.<ref>{{cite book |last=Broom |first=Dave |title=Rum The Manual |date=2016 |publisher=Octopus Books |isbn=9781784720667 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HfwyDQAAQBAJ}}</ref>

===Whiskey sour===

{{main|Whiskey sour}}

The '''whiskey sour''' is a [[mixed drink]] containing [[bourbon whiskey]] or [[rye whiskey]], lemon juice, sugar, and optionally a dash of egg white to make it a Boston Sour. It is shaken and served either straight or over ice. The traditional garnish is half an orange slice and a [[maraschino cherry]]. If floated with claret red wine it's called a [[New York sour]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Difford |first=Simon |title=New York Sour |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3398/new-york-sour-cocktail |access-date=September 29, 2022 |website=Diffords Guide}}</ref>

A notable variant of the whiskey sour is the [[Ward 8 (cocktail)|Ward 8]], which often is based with either bourbon or rye whiskey, both lemon and orange juices, and grenadine syrup as the sweetener. The egg white sometimes employed in other whiskey sours is generally not included in this variation.

===Other sours===
* '''[[Amaretto sour]]''': [[Amaretto]] liqueur, lemon juice and sometimes egg white, bitters or sugar syrup.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amaretto Sour|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/53/amaretto-sour|website=Difford's Guide|access-date=21 March 2018}}</ref>
* '''Brandy sour''' or [[brandy daisy]] (Jerry Thomas, 1887): brandy, clear or orange [[curaçao liqueur|curaçao]], sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''[[Caipirinha]]''': [[Cachaça]], sugar, lime, ice in an [[old fashioned glass]].
* '''[[Brandy sour (Cyprus)|Cypriot brandy sour]]''': [[Cyprus brandy]], lemon cordial and bitters, stirred in a tall glass, and topped with soda or lemonade.
* '''[[b:Bartending/Cocktails/Glossary#M|Midori sour]]''': Honeydew melon liquor, grenadine, lemon juice. Poured properly, it resembles a green [[Tequila sunrise (cocktail)|tequila sunrise]] with visible layers.
* '''Santa Cruz sour''' (Jerry Thomas, 1887): Santa Cruz rum, sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''Tequila sour''': Tequila, lemon juice, lime juice, agave nectar, Bittercube Corazon bitters, egg white.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tequila Sour|url=http://recipe.awesomedrinks.com/recipe/tequila-sour/|website=Awesome Drinks}}</ref>

Elderflower cordial:
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2022}}
{{Short description|Kind of soft drink}}
[[File:Picked Elderflower.jpg|thumb|right|The flower of the [[Sambucus nigra|elder]] used in making Elderflower cordial.]]

'''Elderflower cordial''' is a [[soft drink]] made largely from a [[refined sugar]] and water solution and uses the flowers of the European [[Sambucus nigra|elder]] (''Sambucus nigra'' L.). Historically, the cordial was popular in Northwestern Europe where it has a [[Victorian era|Victorian]] heritage. However, versions of an elderflower cordial recipe can be traced to [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] times. In the 21st century, it is consumed in many countries of Europe where people still make it in the traditional way. In some countries, the drink can be found as an aromatic [[syrup]], sold as a concentrated [[Squash (drink)|squash]] that is mixed with still or [[sparkling water]]. [[Elderflower pressé]] is a premixed form of this.

==Production==
[[File:Elderflowercordial.jpg|thumb|right|Elderflower cordial [[steeping]]]]
[[File:Holunderlimonade und espresso.jpg|thumb|Elderflower lemonade in a café in [[Munich]], Germany]]

In the northern hemisphere, elderflowers are in season from the end of May to the beginning of June<ref name='Schofield'>{{Cite book | year=2005 | title = Nature's playground: activities, crafts and games to encourage children to get outdoors | author1=Fiona Danks | author2=Jo Schofield | publisher=frances lincoln ltd | isbn=978-0-7112-2491-9 | pages=66–67 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-wQsAWtvoiAC&dq=Elderflower+cordial&pg=PA67 | accessdate=2011-03-27}}</ref> or later and grow in most of Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia. They grow in a variety of conditions including both wet and dry fertile soils, though they primarily prefer sunny locations. The elder's [[hermaphrodite]] flowers are borne in large [[corymbs]], 10–25 cm in diameter, where the individual flowers are white with five petals, 5–6 mm in diameter, and pollinated by flies. The cream-coloured flowerheads are honey-scented blossoms that are crisp and somewhat juicy, with a highly aromatic smell and flavour. The leaves are bitter-smelling.<ref name='Schofield' /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sambucus+nigra |title=Sambucus nigra |publisher= |date= |accessdate=2012-07-11}}</ref> 

Elderflower cordial can be made relatively easily at home, though it is also produced and sold commercially. The flowerheads are best collected fresh and new when the tiny buds have just opened and come to bloom before the fragrance is tainted with bitterness.<ref name='Schofield' /> The cordial is made by [[steeping]] the elderflower heads in a concentrated sugar solution so the flavour is infused into the syrup. A source of citric acid and [[lemon juice]] is added to help preserve the cordial and add tartness. The mixture is then covered and left to infuse before being strained to release as much juice as possible. For drinking the cordial is typically diluted with either water or [[sparkling water]] though [[tonic water|tonic]], [[Soda water|soda]] or [[gin]] are also used.<ref name='Schofield' />

Commercial production of elderflower cordial uses a scaled-up version of the process described. Commercially produced cordials are generally sold as a concentrated [[Squash (drink)|squash]] and are usually diluted by one part cordial and ten parts water, thus a 500 ml bottle of cordial would be enough for 5.5 litres diluted. The high concentration of sugar in elderflower cordial gives it a long shelf life. There are many commercial producers of elderflower cordial, and cheaper canned fizzy "elderflower drinks" and "elderflower sodas" often use a synthetic cheap elderflower flavouring to save money and labour, as well as a real elderflower extract.

==Elderflower pressé==
[[File:Elderflower pressé.jpg|thumb|A bottle of the soft drink elderflower pressé.]]
'''Elderflower pressé''' is a [[sweetness|sweetened]], [[carbonation|carbonated]] [[soft drink]]. It is made from elderflower cordial or a synthetic equivalent.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sambucus+nigra |title=Sambucus nigra |publisher= |date= |accessdate=2012-07-11}}</ref><ref name='Schofield'/> Other ingredients will include lemons and sweetener.

Elderflower pressé is therefore similar to [[citron pressé]] and [[lemonade]], and effectively a premixed form of elderflower cordial. Like them, it is used as a [[Mixed drink|mixer]] in [[cocktail]]s.<ref name="Peyton & Byrne cocktail menu">{{cite web|title=Peyton & Byrne cocktail menu|url=http://peytonandbyrne.co.uk/userfiles/Menu/Events-Cocktails-Menus.pdf|publisher=[[Oliver Peyton]]|accessdate=18 January 2016|archive-date=1 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120201004741/http://www.peytonandbyrne.co.uk/userfiles/Menu/Events-Cocktails-Menus.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Olive or Twist">{{cite news|title=Olive or Twist (cocktail menu)|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/05/magazine/potables-olive-or-twist.html?pagewanted=all|work=[[The New York Times]]|date = 5 November 2000|accessdate=18 January 2016|last1 = Hyland|first1 = John}}</ref><ref name="Bottles Up">{{cite news|last1=Schettler|first1=Renee|title=Bottles Up|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/food/2000/08/16/on-the-fridge/8ca749a5-1c0e-46ac-8ed6-60e351e45ee7/|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|accessdate=18 January 2016}}</ref>

Fish house punch:
{{short description|Rum-based cocktail}} {| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:23em; max-width: 40%;" cellspacing="5" | style="text-align: center;" |'''Fish-House Punch'''
''There's a little place just out of town,''
''Where, if you go to lunch,''
''They'll make you forget your mother-in-law''
''With a drink called Fish-House Punch.'' |- | style="text-align: left;" |An early-known print reference to Fish-House Punch is in "The Cook" (1885).[http://www.foodreference.com/html/fish-house-punch.html Food poetry]{{Unreliable source?|date=April 2021}} |} [[File:Fish-house punch.jpg|thumb|Fish House Punch]] '''Fish house punch''' is a strong, [[rum]]-based [[Punch (drink)|punch]] containing [[rum]], [[cognac]], and [[peach brandy]]. The drink is typically served over an ice block in a punch bowl and garnished with lemon slices.{{Citation|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB123758172905298941|title=What America's Oldest Club May Quaff|last=Felten|first=Eric|newspaper=The Wall Street Journal|date=2009-03-20|access-date=2009-03-22|url-access=subscription }} ==History== It is held to have been first concocted in 1732 at [[Philadelphia]]'s fishing club, the [[State in Schuylkill]],[http://slakethirst.com/2005/10/07/fish-house-punch/ History of Fish House Punch] also known as the "fish house".{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}} A 1744 note by the secretary of an embassy of [[Virginia]] Commissioners contains what may be the earliest record of the punch. Meeting local notables at the [[Schuylkill River]] in Philadelphia, he described being served "a Bowl of fine Lemon Punch big enough to have Swimmed half a dozen of young Geese." America's first president, [[George Washington]], indulged in thirteen toasts{{snd}} one for each state{{snd}} during a victory celebration at New York's [[Fraunces Tavern]], and it is said that after he partook of fish house punch at Philadelphia's State in Schuylkill, he couldn't bring himself to make an entry in his diary for the following three days.{{cite book|last=Regan|first=Gary|title=The Joy of Mixology|year=2003|publisher=Clarkson Potter|location=New York|pages=3}} The [[State in Schuylkill]] fish house punch is traditionally made in a large bowl that did double duty as a [[baptismal font]] for citizens' infants. "Its an ample space{{nbsp}}... would indeed admit of total immersion," one citizen noted.{{cite book|last=Wondrich|first=David|title=Imbibe!|year=2007|publisher=Penguin Group|location= New York|pages=87}} The "fish house" is said to have been a gentlemen's club devoted to cigars, whiskey, and the occasional fishing foray upon the [[Chesapeake Bay|Chesapeake]] or upon the [[Restigouche River]] in Canada. Another version states that it was created in 1848 by Shippen Willing of Philadelphia, to celebrate the momentous occasion of women being allowed into the premises of the "fish house" for the first time in order to enliven the annual Christmas party.[http://www.greatpartyrecipes.com/history-of-fish-house-punch.html The "Shocking" History of Fish House Punch] It was supposed to be just "something to please the ladies' palate but get them livelier than is their usual wont." The punch, which contains [[rum]], [[cognac]], and [[peach brandy]], is potent, so it is normally diluted with cold [[lemonade]] or sometimes with cold [[black tea]] and called tea punch, or with [[seltzer water]] as that became available in the 19th century. Some punch bowls may not be large enough to accommodate the large ice block called for, and it can be served in a pitcher over ice cubes. ==See also== {{Portal|Philadelphia}} *[[Ti' punch]], a rum-based mixed drink that is especially popular in French-speaking Caribbean states ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=990DE2DD153BEE33A25757C2A9639C94679ED7CF ''The New York Times'': "How Fishhouse Punch is Made.; Ingredients of the State in Schuylkill's Seductive Concoction." (May 24, 1896)] *[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9907E6D6173AE733A25756C1A9679C946497D6CF ''The New York Times'': "Oldest Dining Club in the World;; The State in Schwylkill, Founded in 1732, Still Holds Its Annual Dinner in Its Castle Near Philadelphia{{snd}} All Cooking Is Done by Members, and Each Must Take His Turn at It." (January 15, 1905)] *[http://www.foodista.com/recipe/782QHPJ8/fish-house-punch ''Fish House Punch on Foodista''] {{DEFAULTSORT:Fish House Punch}} [[Category:Cuisine of Philadelphia]] [[Category:Cocktails with rum]] [[Category:Cocktails with brandy]] [[Category:1732 establishments in the Thirteen Colonies]] [[Category:Historical foods in American cuisine]]

Creamed coconut:
{{Short description|Food product}}
{{Not to be confused with|Coconut cream|Cream of coconut|Coconut oil}}
[[File:Condensed coconut milk.jpg|300px|thumb|Creamed coconut]]
[[File:Saganà_unsalted_creamed_coconut_butterA.jpg|200px|thumbnail|right|[[Filipino cuisine]] [[Spread (food)|spread]]]]
'''Creamed coconut''', also known as '''coconut butter''', is a [[coconut]] product made from the unsweetened [[dehydrated]] fresh pulp of a mature coconut, ground to a semi-solid white creamy paste. It is sold in the form of a hard white block which can be stored at room temperature.<ref>{{harvnb|BBC|2015}} {{harvnb|Cocopro|2013}}</ref> (Coconut butter melts at around 24°C, so in warmer weather it is a liquid paste.) The block is generally packaged in a sealed plastic pouch and some separation of the fat and the coconut flesh can be seen. It may also come in bottles similar to how most [[Nut butter|nut butters]] are packaged.<ref>{{Cite web |title=COCONUT BUTTER - Cocowonder.com.ph |url=https://www.cocowonder.com.ph/index.php/product-lines/coconut-products/coconut-spread-jam-butter/coconut-butter |access-date=2024-07-18 |website=www.cocowonder.com.ph}}</ref> In cookery, it is chopped into pieces or grated before it is added to dishes. By adding warm water it can be made into coconut milk or coconut cream substitutes. Adding water to creamed coconut in the ratio 5:2 gives a coconut cream substitute, 5:1 gives a coconut milk substitute.<ref>{{harvnb|Cocopro|2013}}</ref>

Creamed coconut, or coconut butter can also be made by placing unsweetened shredded coconut into the bowl of a food processor and processing on high speed for 10 to 15 minutes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Jennifer |date=2020-04-30 |title=Homemade Coconut Butter Recipe (SCD, Paleo, Whole30, Vegan) |url=https://thehealthierbite.com/homemade-coconut-butter/ |access-date=2023-09-10 |website=The Healthier Bite |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Creamed coconut is added to Indian, South East Asian and Caribbean recipes to enrich curries and sauces. In the west, it is primarily used in confectionery items, desserts, ice cream, and sauces.  Creamed coconut should not be confused with the related [[coconut cream]], which is a liquid extracted from coconut pulp but does not include the coconut pulp itself.<ref>{{harvnb|BBC|2015}}</ref>

Creamed coconut is particularly high in [[saturated fat]] (61% of total composition), and provides 684 [[calorie]]s in a reference amount of {{convert|100|g}}. Values per 100g:<ref>{{harvnb|USDAARS|2014}}</ref>

:*Water: 2 g
:*Protein: 5 g
:*Carbohydrate: 22 g
:*Fats: 69 g

Death in the Afternoon (cocktail):
{{short description|Cocktail made up of absinthe and Champagne}} {{Infobox drink | name = Death in the Afternoon | image = Death In The Afternoon.jpg | caption = Death in the Afternoon | type = [[Wine cocktail]] | base = [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], [[Absinthe]] | drinkware = [[Champagne flute]] }} '''Death in the Afternoon''', also called the '''Hemingway''' or the '''Hemingway Champagne''',{{cite book|title = Ultimate Bar Book: The Comprehensive Guide to over 1,000 Cocktails|last = Hellmich|first = Mittie|publisher = [[Chronicle Books]]|year = 2006|isbn = 978-0-8118-4351-5|page = 154}}{{cite book |title= Knack Bartending Basics: More Than 400 Classic and Contemporary Cocktails|last= Bourgoin|first= Susan|year= 2009|publisher= Globe Pequot|isbn= 978-1-59921-504-4|page= 132}} is a [[cocktail]] made up of [[absinthe]] and [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], invented by [[Ernest Hemingway]]. The cocktail shares a name with Hemingway's 1932 book ''[[Death in the Afternoon]]'', and the recipe was published in ''So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon'', a 1935 cocktail book with contributions from famous authors.{{cite news |title= Trying to Clear Absinthe's Reputation|author= McGee, Harold|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/03/dining/03curi.html|newspaper= [[The New York Times]]|date= 3 January 2007|access-date=15 July 2011}}{{cite book |title= Diffordsguide Cocktails 7|last= Difford|first= Simon|year= 2008|publisher= Diffordsguide|isbn= 978-0-9556276-0-6|page= 122}} Hemingway's original instructions were:
"Pour one jigger absinthe into a Champagne glass. Add iced Champagne until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness. Drink three to five of these slowly."
It is claimed that the cocktail was invented by Hemingway after he spent time in the [[Rive Gauche|Left Bank]], Paris, and enjoyed the absinthe there. The original printed recipe for the drink claimed that it was invented "by the author and three officers of H.M.S. Danae after having spent seven hours overboard trying to get Capt. Bra Saunders’ fishing boat off a bank where she had gone with us in a N.W. gale."{{Cite web|url=http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|title=Drink Like Hemingway: How to Make a Death in the Afternoon|last=Duffy|website=Be Like Hemingway.|access-date=2016-03-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160405210536/http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|archive-date=2016-04-05|url-status=dead}} Death in the Afternoon is known for both its [[decadence]] and its high [[Alcohol proof|strength]].{{cite news|title= Top 5 Absinthe Cocktails|author= English, Camper|url= http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|publisher= [[Epicurious]]|access-date= 15 July 2011|archive-date= 21 July 2011|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110721142043/http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|url-status= dead}}{{cite news |title= Ernest Hemingway's Death in the Afternoon|url= http://www.esquire.com/drinks/ernest-hemingway-drink-recipe|newspaper= [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|access-date=15 July 2011}} There are a number of alternative ways to produce Death in the Afternoon. The absinthe can be added to the glass after the Champagne, as some brands of absinthe will float on the Champagne for a short time. Other alternatives have arisen because of the difficulty of acquiring absinthe; the absinthe can be replaced with [[Absente]], an alternative to absinthe available where it is illegal, or a strong [[pastis]], such as [[Pernod]]. Variants which use an alternative to absinthe are sometimes given a different name, but are also sometimes still referred to as Death in the Afternoon.{{cite book|title= Night+Day San Francisco|author1= Balmain, Julianne|author2= Chynoweth, Kate|year= 2006|publisher= ASDavis Media Group|isbn= 978-0-9759022-9-5|page= [https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132 132]|url-access= registration|url= https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132}} Some recipes direct the person making the cocktail to use ingredients in addition to the Champagne and absinthe; Valerie Mellema recommends that a [[sugar|sugar cube]] and several dashes of [[bitters]] be added to the glass prior to the main ingredients.{{cite book |title= The Professional Bartender's Handbook: A Recipe for Every Drink Known|last= Mellema|first= Valerie|year= 2007|publisher= Atlantic Publishing Company|isbn= 978-0-910627-95-5|page= 154}} The cocktail is milky in appearance on account of the [[Ouzo effect|spontaneous emulsification]] of the absinthe (or substitute), and bubbly, which it takes from the Champagne. After the first sip, however, it becomes significantly less bubbly. Harold McGee, dining and wine writer for ''[[The New York Times]]'', said that it "seemed a waste of effervescence" (though substituting Pernod for the absinthe). ==See also== {{Portal|Drink}} *[[List of cocktails]] ==References== {{reflist}} {{Wine cocktails}} [[Category:Cocktails with absinthe]] [[Category:Cocktails with Champagne]] [[Category:Ernest Hemingway]]
Goombay Smash:
{{Short description|Rum-based beverage from the Bahamas}}
[[File:Goombay Smash upon arrival (5435890609).jpg|thumb]]
'''Goombay Smash''' is a [[rum]] based beverage in the [[Bahamas]].<ref name=gulls>{{cite book |title=Where the Gulls Are: Fishing with Joe |last=Burroughs |first=Bob |date=2011}}</ref> It is traditionally served in a sling or collins glass. The Goombay Smash was created by Emily Cooper, aka Miss Emily, at the Blue Bee Bar in [[Green Turtle Cay|New Plymouth]]. The original recipe is a secret, but it is believed to have contained [[coconut]] rum, [[dirty rum]], [[apricot]] [[brandy]], and [[pineapple juice]].<ref name=gulls/> Imitators and variations commonly use rum, coconut and pineapple juice.<ref name=gulls/> Apricot [[liqueur]] is sometimes used and dark, amber or spiced rums (dirty rums) are preferred. In place of coconut rum, coconut cream can be used. Other variations include [[Creme de Banane]], [[orange juice]] and [[grenadine]].<ref name=gulls/>

Hennchata:
The '''Hennchata''' is a [[cocktail]] consisting of [[Hennessy]] [[cognac]] and Mexican rice [[horchata]] [[agua fresca]]. It was invented in 2013 by Jorge Sánchez at his Chaco's Mexican restaurant in [[San Jose, California]].

==Recipe==
The Hennchata consists of 4 oz horchata plus a 1.5-oz (50 ml) bottle of Hennessy V.S.<ref name=Fox>[http://latino.foxnews.com/latino/lifestyle/2013/06/09/hennchata-grown-up-horchata-has-alcoholic-kick/ "The 'Hennchata': Grown-Up Horchata Has Alcoholic Kick"], [[Fox News Latino]], June 9, 2013.</ref> Jorge Sánchez, the originator, serves it with a straw in a thick-walled, stemmed [[chavela]] glass with the bottle of cognac inverted in a plastic holder clipped to the rim; the brandy bottle empties itself as the level of horchata falls, making the drink more alcoholic as it is consumed.<ref name=Metro>Dan Pulcrano, [http://activate.metroactive.com/2014/06/the-hennchata-how-hennessy-spiked-horchata-became-drink-sensation/ "Drink of the Year: The Hennchata"], ''[[Metro Silicon Valley]]'', June 11, 2014.</ref>

==Origin==
The drink was created by Jorge Sánchez of [[Gilroy, California|Gilroy]], after he took over Chaco's Mexican restaurant in [[downtown San Jose]].<ref name=Fox/><ref name=Metro/> Since its launch in February 2013, an average of 85 a day have been sold, more than 17,000 in a year, and the restaurant has become the largest seller of Hennessy bottles in [[Northern California]].<ref name=Fox/><ref name=Metro/> [[LVMH]] executives have visited and invited Sanchez to red-carpet events.<ref name=Metro/>

Egg in beer:
{{Short description|English idiom}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2021}}
{{Orphan|date=December 2020}}

'''Egg in beer''' refers to the practice, literally or figuratively, of cracking a raw [[Egg as food|egg]] into a glass of [[beer]]. The term is used [[metaphor]]ically, commonly as "what do you want, egg in your beer?" implying that the listener already has something good but is undeservedly asking for more.<ref name="MelilloMelillo2005">{{cite book|author1=Joseph Melillo|author2=Edward M. Melillo|title=American Slang: Cultural Language Guide to Living in the USA|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gvHzNsQoeH4C&pg=PA106|year=2005|publisher=Mottobene Inc|isbn=978-1-59404-017-7|pages=106–}}</ref>

==Literal==
In England, where the consumption of the egg in beer is centuries old, a mix of beer, raw egg, honey and other herbs could be prescribed to the sick.  [[Posset]], famously consumed in ''[[Macbeth]]'' and ''[[The Merry Wives of Windsor]]'', consists partly in eggs whipped with cream, sugar, and beer or wine.  [[Syllabub]] is made by mixing egg whites cream and wine. The egg also clears out cloudier beers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Hezel |first=Anna |date=6 July 2016 |title=A Brief History of Drinking Raw Eggs, from 'Macbeth' to 'Orange Is the New Black' |url=http://www.extracrispy.com/culture/328/a-brief-history-of-drinking-raw-eggs-from-macbeth-to-orange-is-the-new-black |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170630023034/http://www.extracrispy.com/culture/328/a-brief-history-of-drinking-raw-eggs-from-macbeth-to-orange-is-the-new-black |archive-date=30 June 2017 |website=Extra Crispy}}</ref>

According to the [[Elizabethan era|Elizabethan]] theories, out of the four fundamentals characters (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic), eggs are sanguine and beer is choleric.<ref name=":0" />

In 1915, industry journal ''The Mixer and Server'' noted a [[Seattle]] case where a judge decreed that an egg, once cracked into a glass of beer, qualified as a drink and was not in violation of ordinances against giving free food in bars.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date=1915 |title=Egg in Beer is Considered Drink |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.li53p3&view=1up&seq=911 |journal=The Mixer and Server |volume=XXIV |issue=10 |pages=49 |doi= |access-date= |publisher=Hotel and Restaurant Employee's International Alliance and Bartenders' International League of America.}}</ref>

A 1939 article in ''Printing'' magazine notes that Pennsylvania State Brewers' Association had launched a public-relations campaign to "sell the idea that eggs and beer make a pleasing combination."<ref>{{cite book|title=Printing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShwhAQAAMAAJ|year=1939}}</ref> Other Pennsylvania sources refer to this as a "miner's breakfast".<ref name="Smiles2005">{{cite book|author=Jack Smiles|title="Ee-Yah": The Life and Times of Hughie Jennings, Baseball Hall of Famer|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CL2KTvU6jdoC&pg=PA9|date=10 May 2005|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-8428-7|pages=9–}}</ref><ref name="Noon2011">{{cite book|author=Mark A. Noon|title=Yuengling: A History of America's Oldest Brewery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KfZ3k6iz3NQC&pg=PA33|date=23 November 2011|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-8659-5|pages=33–}}</ref>

Since 1999, Giang Cafe (located in [[Hanoi]], Vietnam) has served an egg beer consisting of beer mixed with whipped egg yolks—a variant on traditional Vietnamese [[egg coffee]].<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=2019-04-10 |title=Hanoi egg beer: the frothy Vietnamese cocktail that's hard to beat |url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/travel-leisure/article/3005381/hanoi-egg-beer-frothy-vietnamese-cocktail-thats-hard-beat |work=South China Morning Post |access-date=2023-09-28}}</ref>

==Metaphorical==
{{wiktionary|egg in one's beer}}
Sources differ as to the origin of the [[colloquialism]], with some stating it dates to [[World War II]]<ref name="Sala2013">{{cite book|author=Jenny La Sala|title=Comes A Soldier's Whisper: A Collection of Wartime Letters with Reflection and Hope for the Future|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lbrMUHXIUlEC&pg=PA93|date=15 February 2013|publisher=Trafford Publishing|isbn=978-1-4669-7687-0|pages=93–}}</ref> while others speculate that it dates to the 19th century.<ref name="Axelrod2011">{{cite book|author=Alan Axelrod|title=The Cheaper the Crook, the Gaudier the Patter: Forgotten Hipster Lines, Tough Guy Talk, and Jive Gems|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hYYkAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT112|date=20 July 2011|publisher=Skyhorse Publishing|isbn=978-1-62873-017-3|pages=112–}}</ref> However, a 1933 article in the ''[[Stevens Indicator]]'', mentioning an employee who had not received a raise, notes: "What do you expect, Carl? Egg in your beer?"<ref>{{cite book|title=Stevens Indicator ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WrUnAQAAMAAJ|year=1933}}</ref>

== Flips ==
Mixing beer, an egg and liquor is called a "flip". According to The Whistler's lead bartender in Chicago, Marina Holter, flips date back to as far as the 1690s. Some assume that the liquor kills the [[salmonella]] risks linked to raw eggs consumption.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-02-21 |title=Beer flips are the beer-and-whole egg cocktail—wait, hear me out |url=https://thetakeout.com/beer-flips-how-to-make-beer-and-whole-egg-cocktail-1832759172 |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=The Takeout |language=en}}</ref> It may also be a revisited version of the classic raw egg+alcohol consumed across ages and cultures (and referred to as "Fallujah omelets" in the series ''[[Orange Is the New Black]]'').<ref name=":0" />

== Products ==
In 2021, for [[Easter]], [[Cadbury]] partnered with [[Goose Island Brewery|Goose Island]] to release a [[Cadbury Creme Egg|Creme Egg]]-flavored beer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cadbury Creme Eggs Now Come in Beer Form |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/news/cadbury-creme-eggs-beer-goose-island |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=Food & Wine |language=en}}</ref>

Diki-diki:
{{Short description|Cocktail made with calvados, Swedish Punsch and grapefruit juice}}
[[File:Diki-Diki Cocktail 2016.jpg|thumb|Diki-diki cocktail]]The '''diki-diki''' is a [[cocktail]] made with [[calvados]], [[punsch|Swedish Punsch]], and [[grapefruit|grapefruit juice]], dating back to the 1920s where it was popular in London's higher-end American bar scene but is now more commonly served as a [[Tiki culture|Tiki drink]]. The original recipe calls for shaking the ingredients with ice in 2:1:1 proportions,<ref name="Vermiere">{{cite book |last1=Vermiere |first1=Robert |title=Cocktails: How to Mix Them |date=1922 |publisher=Herbert Jenkins Ltd. |pages=27 |edition=15th printing}}</ref> although many later variations have modified the ratio to greater emphasize the calvados as the base ingredient (4:1:1).

==Historical origin==
Belgian bartender Robert Vermiere is credited with creating the diki-diki, who listed it in his book ''Cocktails: How to Mix Them'', along with a notation that he introduced the cocktail at London's ''Embassy Club'' in February 1922.<ref name="Vermiere"/> Fellow cocktail book author Harry MacElhone commented that "this is a very popular cocktail in London" in his 1923 drink manual ''Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails''.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1923-Harry-of-Ciro-s-ABC-of-mixing-cocktails-second-impression/28 |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date= 1923 |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |publisher=Christopher & Co |place=London|page=28}}</ref> MacElhone's listing employed the more calvados-oriented version with a 4:1:1 ratio. This was also the proportion used in [[Trader Vic's]] ''Bartender's Guide''<ref name="Bergeron">{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Victor |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1948 |publisher=Garden City Books |page=72 |edition=Reprint}}</ref> and Harry Cradock's ''Savoy Cocktail Book ''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cradock |first1=Harry |title=Savoy Cocktail Book |date=1930 |publisher=Constable & Company |location=London |page=59}}</ref>

==Modern-day usage==
The diki-diki is currently served primarily in [[Tiki bar]]s, and as an example has been on the drink menu at the [[Tiki Ti]].<ref name="Tiki Ti">{{cite web |title=Drinks |url=http://www.tiki-ti.com/pages/alpha.html |publisher=[[Tiki Ti]] |accessdate=22 January 2019}}</ref>

There is some disagreement over whether the diki-diki should be considered as a true [[tiki bar|tiki drink]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Diki Diki |url=https://www.moderntiki.com/diki-diki/ |website=moderntiki.com |accessdate=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://forgottencocktails.com/?p=615 |title=Diki Diki Cocktail |date= 30 November 2015|website=forgottencocktails.com |accessdate=22 January 2019}}</ref> Because of the era it was created in, the diki-diki could not have been considered as an express tiki drink as ''first'' envisioned because the Polynesian inspired tiki craze had not yet started.  However, Vermiere did employ an interesting backstory when he created the cocktail by stating that it was named after the "chief monarch of the Island Ubian (Southern Philippines), who is now 37 years old, weighs 23 pounds, and his height is 32 inches".<ref name="Vermiere"/>  While likely a fictionalisation, there nevertheless was a real life Philippine leader named [[Lapulapu]], who was responsible for the death of [[Ferdinand Magellan]] and for whom a later tiki drink was named.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose |page=61}}</ref> The Lapulapu cocktail<ref>{{cite web |title=Drink Menu (Lapu Lapu) |url=http://www.ventikiloungeandlanai.com/classicdrinks/ |website=ventikiloungeandlanai.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Menus |url=http://www.tiki-ti.com/pages/menus.html |website=tiki-ti.com |accessdate=22 January 2019}}</ref> has been served alongside the diki-diki cocktail<ref>{{cite web |title=Drinks Listed Alphabetically |url=http://www.tiki-ti.com/pages/alpha.html |website=tiki-ti.com |accessdate=24 January 2019}}</ref> at the [[Tiki Ti]]. The Puka-Puka cocktail,<ref>{{cite web |title=Cocktails |url=https://tradervicsatl.com/drink/ |website=tradervicsatl.com |accessdate=22 January 2019}}</ref> named after the [[Puka-Puka|Polynesian atoll]] "discovered" by [[Ferdinand Magellan]] in 1521 is also a tiki drink. As such one may wish to consider the shared folklore of the diki-diki cocktail as an inspiration of sorts for the names of the Lapulapu and Puka-Puka tiki cocktails.

Tiki pioneer Victor Bergeron, who named his first restaurant ''Hinky Dinks'',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose |page=29}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Hinky Dink's |url=https://www.critiki.com/location/hinky-dinks-oakland-548/ |website=critiki.com |accessdate=22 January 2019 |archive-date=2 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190202212559/https://www.critiki.com/location/hinky-dinks-oakland-548/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> included the recipe for the diki-diki cocktail in his bartender's guide.<ref name="Bergeron"/>

Doctor (cocktail):
[[File:Cocktail recipe for Doctor Cocktail(1922).png|thumb]]
The '''doctor cocktail''' is a pre-prohibition era cocktail that traces in drink guides to as far back as 1917, when it appeared in Hugo R. Ensslin's ''Recipes for Mixed Drinks''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ensslin |first1=Hugo |title=Recipes for Mixed Drinks |date=1917 |publisher=Unknown |location=New York |page=15}}</ref>  As originally described the cocktail called simply for [[punsch|Swedish Punsch]] mixed with lime juice.

Like many older cocktails, many variations with the same name have been created over time, and drink guides sometimes listed multiple variations in the same book. The core of the cocktail consists of Swedish punsch and some variation of citrus (lime, lemon, or orange), with later variations skewing away from lime and also adding Jamaican [[rum]].

==Historical variations==
After Ensslin's recipe, the doctor cocktail was also listed in Robert Vermiere's 1922 drink book where it dropped the use of lime, calling for 2 parts Swedish punsch, 1 part orange juice, and 1 part lemon juice (2:1:1 ratio).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vermiere |first1=Robert |title=Cocktails How to Mix Them |date=1922 |publisher=Mayflower Printing |location=Plymouth, England |page=28}}</ref>

[[Harry MacElhone|Harry MacElhone's]] guide ''Harry Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails'' listed the ingredients as equal parts Swedish punsch, orange juice, and lemon juice (1:1:1 ratio),<ref>{{cite book |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date=1923 |publisher=Dean & Sons Ltd |location=London |page=28}}</ref> as did a 1927 Italian version (1:1:1 ratio).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grande |first1=Piero |title=Cocktails |date=1927 |publisher=unknown |location=Roma |page=33 |edition=3rd}}</ref> MacElhone's guide however also carried an illustration for "The Recipe of the famous Dr. Cocktail" which called for 2/3 punsch and 1/3 lime juice, while suggesting that lemons could be substituted if one did not have limes on hand.

In 1936 fellow drink book author Frank Meier listed the cocktail as equal parts punsch and white rum, with a teaspoon each of orange and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Punch and Rum - The Doctor Cocktail |url=https://cold-glass.com/2012/08/15/punch-and-rum-the-doctor-cocktail/ |website=cold-glass.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

[[Trader Vic's]] listed the ingredients as 1.5 oz. Swedish punsch, 3/4 oz. Jamaican rum, 1 tsp. orange juice, and 1 tsp. lemon juice. The guide also noted that equal parts Swedish punsch and rum could also be used, and that the juice of 1/2 a lime could take the place of the orange and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Trader Vic |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Garden City Books |location=Garden City, NY |page=216 |edition=1948 reprint}}</ref>

In 1948 Dave Embury noted that there were "several" versions of the cocktail and was going to list four in his book.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embury |first1=Dave |title=Fineart of Mixing Drinks |date=1948 |publisher=Doubleday Company |location=Garden City, NY |page=227}}</ref> The Doctor Cocktail No.1 listed Ensslin's original punsch and lime recipe. No.2 called for equal parts punsch, gin, and lemon juice. No.3 called for the more now common 2:1:1 ratio of punsch, orange juice, and lemon juice.  No.4 called for 3 parts punsch, 2 parts Jamaican rum, and 1 part lime.

Difford's guide likewise lists four different versions, although not all the same as Embury's.<ref>{{cite web |title=Search results for "doctor" |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/search?force_limit=20&q=doctor |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

==Similar cocktails==
In his 1941 bartender's book, ''"Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion"'', Gaige listed a drink that he called the ''Greta Garbo Bows'', that called for one jigger of Swedish Punsch, 1/2 jigger of orange juice, and a 1/2 jigger of lemon juice. This was essentially Vermier's Doctor cocktail version from 1922. Despite the same ingredients, Gaige makes no mention of the doctor cocktail in his notes but says "shake well, strain into cocktail glass, and God bless Miss Garbo".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gaige |first1=Crosby |title=Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion |date=1941 |publisher=M. Barrows & Company |location=New York |page=171 |edition=First}}</ref> [[Greta Garbo]] was a Swedish-American actress, a potential reason for the renaming of a drink that contained Swedish Punsch.

Another cocktail simply called the ''[[Greta Garbo]]'' calls for equal parts Swedish Punsch, gin, and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Greta Garbo Cocktail |url=https://www.absolutdrinks.com/en/drinks/greta-garbo-cocktail/ |website=absolutdrinks.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref> This is the same drink as the Doctor No.2 from Emburry's 1948 cocktail guide.

== Later "doctor" cocktails ==
Early alcoholic concoctions were often thought of as "medicinal", and even in 1948 cocktail books were pondering such questions as "Why are rye and bourbon whiskies frequently prescribed by doctors and Scotch practically never?"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embury |first1=David |title=The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks |date=1948 |publisher=Doubleday |location=Garden City, NY |page=31}}</ref>

Other "doctor" cocktails include the '''Doctor Johnson''', which was a tropical cocktail by design that called for<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tarling |first1=W. J. |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book |date=1937 |publisher=Pall Mall |location=London |page=DO |edition=Coronation}}</ref> 1/4 gin, 1/2 pineapple syrup, 1/8 passion fruit juice, and 1/8 lemon juice shaken with a dash of grenadine and egg white, making it a potential precursor for later [[Tiki bar|Tiki drinks]]. The author of the particular cocktail guide, W.J. Tarling, did not provide notes as to whom the drink was named after, other than saying it was "invented by Tim Hollings".  However, it is potentially telling that the book also included a recipe for the ''Doctor Johnson Jr'', which contained no liquor. Dr. [[Samuel Johnson]] was a prolific English writer who is attributed with many quotes on the character of man and drinking.<ref>{{cite web |title=Quotes on Drinking |url=https://www.samueljohnson.com/drinking.html |website=www.samueljohnson.com |accessdate=10 February 2019}}</ref> His alcohol problem and ultimate need for abstinence was well documented<ref>{{cite journal|title=SAMUEL JOHNSON'S ALCOHOL PROBLEM|last=Madden|first=J.S|date=1967|citeseerx = 10.1.1.284.4792}}</ref> and he was quoted as saying "I can't drink a little, child, therefore I never touch it".

The '''Doctor Funk''' cocktail has more certainty as to its name and has been described as a Tiki drink precursor. Jeff Berry in ''Beachbum Berry Remixed'' states that, unlike most Tiki drinks that were called Polynesian but "made up" in California that "the ''Doctor Funk'', alone among "Polynesian" drinks, does, in fact, have Polynesian roots".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=109 }}</ref> The drink was named after Dr. Bernard Funk, a German physician who was a doctor for [[Robert Louis Stevenson]] in Samoa.<ref>{{cite web |title=The late Dr. Fong has a funky and famous history |url=http://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2013/02/03/lost-cocktails-of-the-mai-kai-the-late-dr-fong-has-a-funky-and-famous-history/ |website=slammie.com |accessdate=27 February 2019}}</ref> Berry provides evidence that the doctor was also a bartender in his own right and lists the drink as being a mixture of light Puerto Rican rum, lime juice, and pomegranate syrup stirred with a teaspoon of Pernod and club soda.

[[Trader Vic's]] attempt to "improve" the Dr. Funk was called '''Dr. Funk's Son'''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Bartender's Guide, Revised |url=https://archive.org/details/tradervicsbarten00trad |url-access=registration |date=1972 |publisher=[[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] |location=Garden City, NY |page=[https://archive.org/details/tradervicsbarten00trad/page/152 152] |edition=revised}}</ref>

[[Joseph Stephen Crane|Stephen Crane]] called his version of the Dr. Funk the '''Dr. Fong''' at ''The Luau'' and his ''Kon-Tiki'' chain of restaurants.<ref>{{cite web |title=From the Los Angeles Public Library Menu Collection: The Luau, a 1950s Tiki Bar in Beverly Hills |url=https://www.laweekly.com/restaurants/from-the-los-angeles-public-library-menu-collection-the-luau-a-1950s-tiki-bar-in-beverly-hills-2376567 |website=laweekly.com |accessdate=17 February 2019}}</ref> Crane, who tongue in cheek referred to himself as high chief "Stefooma", claimed that a "Dr. Fong Foo" was also the overseer of the food and drinks at his ''The Luau'' restaurant.<ref>{{cite web |title=LA public library data base |url=https://dbase1.lapl.org/images/menus/fullsize/c/rb01454-02.jpg |website=dbase1.lapl.org |accessdate=26 February 2019}}</ref> He additionally listed a ''Doc's Grog'' on his 1956 ''The Luau'' menu, which may have been a reference to Dr. Fong Foo, and was likely a rebranded [[Navy Grog]] (Crane called the [[Test Pilot (cocktail)|Test Pilot]] the ''Jet Pilot'', ''Don's Pearl'' became ''Steve's Pearl'', etc.).

== Relationship to 21st century cocktail enthusiasts==
Although similar in name, there is no formal connection between the Doctor cocktail and the author of the book ''Vintage Spirits & Forgotten Cocktails'', written by Ted Haigh (aka, "Doctor Cocktail").<ref>{{cite web |title=Doctor Cocktail |url=https://forgottencocktails.com/?p=621 |website=forgottencocktails.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

There is also no formal connection between the cocktail and [[Jeff Macpherson]] (aka, "Dr. Tiki", former host of [[Tiki Bar TV]]).<ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Bar TV |url=http://www.canada.com/nationalpost/artslife/story.html?id=aadbdfb5-4d90-424e-b638-4c9232c69cdf&k=56529 |website=canada.com |accessdate=26 February 2019|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120805125939/http://www.canada.com/nationalpost/artslife/story.html?id=aadbdfb5-4d90-424e-b638-4c9232c69cdf&k=56529|archive-date = 2012-08-05}}</ref>

'''Cohasset Punch''' is a [[brand]] of [[rum]]-based drink introduced in 1899. First created by [[Chicago]] bartenders Lewis A. Williams and Thomas C. Newman, Cohasset Punch was long associated with the Ladner Bros. bar on [[Madison Street (Chicago)|Madison Street]] in the [[Chicago Loop]], who produced it until the 1980s.<ref name="Wondrich">{{cite encyclopedia | last=Wondrich | first=David | encyclopedia=[[The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails]] | title=Cohasset Punch | publisher=Oxford University Press | publication-place=New York | date=2022 | pages=186–187 | isbn=978-0-19-931113-2 | editor1-last=Wondrich | editor1-first=David | editor2-last=Rothbaum | editor2-first=Noah}}</ref> Though officially classified as a [[liqueur]], Cohasset Punch can also be considered a bottled [[cocktail]] or [[punch (drink)|punch]], and has been referred to as "the definitive Chicago cocktail".<ref name="WSJ">{{citation | last=Felten | first=Eric | title=Drinking the Chicago Way | newspaper=WSJ | url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB122973257260622987 | date=December 20, 2008 | access-date=May 20, 2024}}</ref> In 2024, bottled Cohasset Punch was relaunched under new ownership.<ref name="History">{{cite web | title=History | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/history | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

==History==
In the late 1890s, Chicago saloon owner and liquor dealer Lewis A. Williams{{efn | Lewis Williams' name is spelled "Louis" on some records, but his death notice<ref name="WilliamsObit">{{cite news |title=Death Notices | work=Chicago Tribune | date=July 9, 1935 | page=21 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-lewis-a-williams-death/148446528/}}</ref> uses "Lewis."}} was invited to spend a few weeks at the [[Cohasset, Massachusetts]] summer estate of long-time family friend,<ref name="Crane">{{cite book | title=Footprints and Echoes | last=Crane | first=William H. | date=1927 | location=New York | publisher=E.P. Dutton & Company | pages=55–56 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=91dAAAAAIAAJ}}</ref> actor [[William H. Crane]].<ref name="Wondrich" /><ref name="Bonforts">{{cite magazine | title=The Origin of Cohasset Punch | author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> | magazine=Bonfort's Wine & Spirit Circular | date=August 10, 1902 | page=305 | volume=58 | issue=7}}</ref> Williams overheard some of Crane's other guests discussing rum [[punch (drink)|punch]], and [[telegraphy|wired]] Tom Newman, his business partner back in Chicago, to request a mixed drink that would "surpass anything ever before imbibed by any living soul."<ref name="Bonforts" /> Within 24 hours, a cask of the new punch was loaded onto a railcar and bound for Cohasset. Upon tasting the new concoction, Crane and his guests declared Newman the "king of blenders." Crane wired Newman his thanks and asked for the name of the new drink, and Newman simply wired back the name, "Cohasset".<ref name="Bonforts" />

Williams & Newman began mixing Cohasset Punch at their saloon,<ref name="advertisement">{{cite news |title=Have You Had a Cohasset Punch | work=Chicago Inter Ocean | date=October 16, 1898 | page=8 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-inter-ocean-williams-newman-ad-for/167459716/}}</ref>{{efn | The Williams & Newman saloon was located at 124 [[Dearborn Street]] (now 10 N. Dearborn after the 1911 street renumbering). Williams & Newman was located across the street from the saloon of James McGarry, the inspiration for the [[Mr. Dooley]] character in columns by humorist [[Finley Peter Dunne]].<ref name="Recollections">{{cite book | title=Recollections of Life & Doings in Chicago: From the Haymarket Riot to the End of World War I | last=Hermann | first=Charles H. | date=1945 | location=Chicago | publisher=Normandie House | pages=140–141 | url=https://libsysdigi.library.uiuc.edu/OCA/Books2008-09/recollectionsofl00herm/recollectionsofl00herm.pdf}}</ref>}} serving the blend over a [[peach]] slice soaked in [[brandy]].<ref name="Fougner">{{cite news | last=Fougner | first=G. Selmer | title=Along the Wine Trail | work=New York Sun | date=November 11, 1938 | page=23}}</ref> By the fall of 1899 they were selling Cohasset Punch in bottles, with modest but nationwide distribution.<ref name="Wondrich" /> From the very beginning, each bottle had an image of [[Cohasset, Massachusetts|Cohasset]]'s famous [[Minot's Ledge Light]]house on the label.<ref name="trademark">{{US trademark|60035924}} Mixed Spiritous Beverages. Williams & Newman, Chicago, Ill. Essential feature—The pictoral representation of a lighthouse scene. Used since January, 1899. (filed January 15, 1900) (published February 19, 1901)</ref>{{efn | Labels from 1899 to early 1981 also included illustrations of a sailboat and steamship on either side of the lighthouse.<ref name="trademark" /> Labels from 1981<ref name="81COLA">{{cite web | title=Cohasset Punch | website=COLA Public Registry | url=https://ttbonline.gov/colasonline/viewColaDetails.do?action=publicDisplaySearchBasic&ttbid=81090152 | date=September 28, 1981 | access-date=May 31, 2024}}</ref> until the end of original production replaced these with an illustration of one [[square rig|square-rigged]] [[tall ship]] to the right of the lighthouse. The modern label depicts [[William H. Crane]]’s [[catboat]] ''Chloe'' to the left of the lighthouse, and Crane’s [[steam yacht]] ''The Senator'' (designed by [[Edward Burgess (yacht designer)|Edward Burgess]] and named for [[The Senator (play)|one of Crane's most successful plays]]).<ref name="FAQ">{{cite web | title=FAQ | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/faq | access-date=May 23, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Senator">{{cite news |title=Com. W.H. Crane's Steam Yacht Senator | work=Boston Globe | date=February 14, 1897 | page=28 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-com-w-h-cranes-stea/103338199/}}</ref>}} In 1902, a leading liquor [[trade magazine|trade journal]] remarked that so high was the demand for Cohasset Punch in its city of origin, that "what the [[mint julep]] is to [[Southern United States|the South]], Cohasset Punch is to Chicago."<ref name="Bonforts" /> A recipe appeared for Cohasset Punch in cocktail guides that included sweet [[vermouth]], New England [[rum]], [[lemon]] juice, and [[orange bitters]],<ref name="Sheridan">{{cite book | title=The Complete Buffet Manual | last=Sheridan | first=J.E. | date=1901 | location=Chicago | publisher=Henneberry | pages=47–48 | url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1901-The-Complete-Buffet-Manual-or-How-to-Mix-Fancy-Drinks-by-J-E-Sheridan/46/}}</ref> but regulars believed that this formula did not quite taste like the original.<ref name="Wondrich" /> Of the drink's smoothness compared to its 60-[[Alcohol proof|proof]] strength, a 1938 letter to the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' wrote that after three or four drinks, "a pleasant mellowness steals over you, your imagination glows, you discover humor you never possessed. Then suddenly you push your chair back to stand up, and lo, your legs are merely attached to your body for appearance's sake!"<ref name="Tribune38">{{cite news |title=A Line O' Type or Two | work=Chicago Tribune | date=August 17, 1938 | page=10 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-cohasset-punch-a-line/148447450/}}</ref>

[[File:Ladner Brothers, Home Of Cohasset Punch, 207 West Madison St., Chicago, Illinois (NBY 416934).jpg|thumb|alt=A postcard image featuring exterior and interior images of a bar, and a glass of Cohasset Punch.|A 1940s postcard for the Ladner Bros. "Home of Cohasset Punch" bar at [[Madison Street (Chicago)|Madison]] and [[Wells Street (Chicago)|Wells]] Streets, Chicago]]
[[File:CohassetPunch-1980s.jpg|thumb|alt=A bottle of Cohasset Punch from the mid-1980s sitting atop a bar.|A bottle of Cohasset Punch from the mid-1980s, on display at Simon's Tavern in [[Edgewater, Chicago#Andersonville|Andersonville]], Chicago]]
After Williams & Newman retired in 1916, they sold the rights to Carl Ladner, who continued to serve the drink at the Ladner Bros. bar as well as bottle it for distribution. The bar reopened after [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]], and a large [[neon sign]] touting "The Home of Cohasset Punch" was hung outside.<ref name="Wondrich" /> During the 1930s and 1940s, bottled Cohasset Punch could be found at many of Chicago's restaurants and nightclubs including [[Chez Paree]] and [[Blackhawk (restaurant)|The Blackhawk]], as well as the "Tip Top Tap" bar cars aboard the [[Milwaukee Road]]'s [[Hiawatha (Milwaukee Road trains)|Hiawatha]] passenger trains.<ref name="ChezParee">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Dinner Wine List | publisher=Chez Paree | date=1941}}</ref><ref name="Blackhawk">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Cocktails | publisher=The Blackhawk | date=1943}}</ref><ref name="TipTopTap">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Tip Top Tap Room | publisher=Milwaukee Road | date=1935}}</ref> Ladner Bros. was demolished in 1986<ref name="SunTimes86">{{cite news | last=Davis | first=Jerry C. | title=Prohibition-era Cohasset Punch to fall for W. Madison skyscraper | work=Chicago Sun-Times | date=March 17, 1986 | page=47 | url=https://chicagosuntimes.newsbank.com/doc/news/0EB36CF74D05F922}}{{subscription required}}</ref> by developer [[Lee Miglin]] to make way for the proposed (but never built) 125-story [[Miglin-Beitler Skyneedle]].<ref name="SunTimes89">{{cite news | last=Davis | first=Jerry C. | title=New skyscraper planned—would tower over Sears | work=Chicago Sun-Times | date=May 23, 1989 | url=https://chicagosuntimes.newsbank.com/doc/news/0EB36E5D94B09125}}{{subscription required}}</ref> Production of Cohasset Punch ceased shortly thereafter.

In 2024, the Cohasset Punch brand was revived by a Chicago-based cocktail history enthusiast using historical accounts of its flavor and ingredients.<ref name="Tribune">{{cite news | last=Hammond | first=David | title=Want to party like it's 1899? One Chicagoan is working to revive Cohasset Punch liqueur | work=Chicago Tribune | date=January 12, 2024 | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2024/01/12/want-to-party-like-its-1899-one-chicagoan-is-working-to-revive-cohasset-punch-liqueur/ | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Forbes">{{cite web | last=Hurt | first=Jeanette | title=Drinks Historian Revives Chicago's Signature Cocktail, Cohasset Punch | website=Forbes | date=April 28, 2024 | url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeanettehurt/2024/04/28/drinks-historian-revives-chicagos-signature-cocktail-cohasset-punch/?sh=1ff6a0eb1642 | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

==Serving==
Historically, Cohasset Punch has been served stirred with ice and strained into a cocktail glass over a peach slice. In the early 20th century, this garnish would have likely been a peach slice preserved in brandy.<ref name="Wondrich" /> In the 1970s and 1980s, Cohasset Punch was increasingly served [[Bartending terminology#On the rocks|on the rocks]] or with [[drink mixer|mixers]].<ref name="SanDiego">{{cite news | last=Riggs | first=Rod | title=Pushing an old punch | work=San Diego Union-Tribune | date=November 24, 1986 | page=E-7 | url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/news/117922C40A3F1B6D}}{{subscription required}}</ref><ref name="TribLetters">{{cite news | author=<!--not stated--> | title=LETTERS: Memories Pack a Punch | work=Chicago Tribune | date=August 31, 2008 | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2008/08/31/letters-2766/ | access-date=May 22, 2024}}</ref> The current manufacturer suggests a number of cocktails that can be made with Cohasset Punch.<ref name="Recipes">{{cite web | title=Recipes | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/recipes | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

Hirezake:
[[File:ひれ酒_-_2335080472.jpg|thumb|250x250px|[[Fugu]] ''hirezake'']]
In [[Japanese cuisine]], '''''hirezake''''' ([[Japanese language|Japanese]]: 鰭酒, "fin sake") is a traditional winter<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 June 2016 |title=「甘酒」は夏の季語、では「ヒレ酒」は？〜お酒にまつわる季語が面白い〜 |url=https://jp.sake-times.com/knowledge/culture/kigo-sake |access-date=19 January 2026 |website=SAKE TIMES |language=ja}}</ref> drink of warmed [[sake]] to which the grilled [[Fin|fins]] of various food fish have been added. Most commonly this is the fin of [[fugu]] (pufferfish), but other fish such as [[Ray (fish)|ray]] or [[Pagrus major|sea bream]] may also be used.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=6 February 2023 |title=ヒレ酒(ひれ酒)に合う日本酒は？なんの魚？作り方やコツを紹介 |url=https://www.e-hakutsuru.com/blogs/column/hirezake?srsltid=AfmBOopehJQBA65Z8jXeSnJFULtR4YRrwTUInss2J3_WOP2lVT6kIbsd |access-date=19 January 2026 |website=白鶴オンラインショップ |language=ja}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=11 November 2021 |title=自宅でひれ酒を楽しむ方法。美味しい作り方やおすすめの日本酒も - KUBOTAYA |url=https://magazine.asahi-shuzo.co.jp/enjoy/88 |access-date=19 January 2026 |website=朝日酒造|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=YukariSakamoto |date=2014-03-10 |title=Hirezake – Japan’s Weirdest Hot Saké Drink? |url=https://foodsaketokyo.com/2014/03/10/hirezake-japans-weirdest-hot-sake-drink/ |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=Food Sake Tokyo |language=en}}</ref>

The fins are first [[Food drying|dried]], [[Grilling|grilled]] over a low flame until golden brown, then placed in a cup. Warm sake is then poured over the fins and the cup covered for several minutes to allow the aroma of the fins to infuse the sake before drinking. A milder version of ''hirezake'' can be prepared by igniting the surface of the sake when the cover is removed to burn off some of the alcohol.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |title=Is This the Deadliest Cocktail in the World? |url=https://www.liquor.com/articles/hirezake-fugu-sake/ |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20230326210645/https://www.liquor.com/articles/hirezake-fugu-sake/ |archive-date=2023-03-26 |access-date=2026-02-04 |work=Liquor.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Support |first=SAKETALK Customer |date=2018-10-14 |title=How to Drink Hirezake |url=https://www.sake-talk.com/drink-hirezake/ |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=SAKETALK |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Introduced''': [[Caribbean]], [[Central America]], northern parts of [[South America]], [[West Africa]] | creator = | course = | type = | served = | main_ingredient = [[Coconut]] | variations = | calories = | other = }} '''Coconut milk''' is a [[plant milk]] extracted from the grated pulp of mature [[coconut]]s.{{cite journal |last1=Tulashie |first1=Samuel Kofi |last2=Amenakpor |first2=Jacking |last3=Atisey |first3=Sandra |last4=Odai |first4=Raphael |last5=Akpari |first5=Ephraim Edem Amoah |title=Production of coconut milk: A sustainable alternative plant-based milk |journal=Case Studies in Chemical and Environmental Engineering |date=2022 |volume=6 |article-number=100206 |id=100206 |doi=10.1016/j.cscee.2022.100206 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2022CSCEE...600206T }} The [[opacity]] and rich taste of the milky-white liquid are due to its high [[coconut oil|oil]] content, most of which is [[saturated fat]]. Coconut milk is a traditional food ingredient used in Southeast Asia, Oceania, South Asia, and East Africa. It is also used for cooking in the Caribbean, Central America, northern parts of South America and West Africa, where [[Coconut#Human dispersal|coconuts were introduced]] during the [[Early modern period|colonial era]]. Coconut milk is differentiated into subtypes based on [[fat]] content. They can be generalized into '''coconut cream''' (or thick coconut milk) with the highest amount of fat; coconut milk (or thin coconut milk) with a maximum of around 20% fat; and coconut skim milk with negligible amounts of fat.{{cite book |author=NIIR Board of Consultants and Engineers|title=The Complete Book on Coconut & Coconut Products (Cultivation and Processing) |date=2006 |publisher=Asia Pacific Business Press Inc. |isbn=978-81-7833-007-5 |page=274 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UvXKAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA274}}{{cite book|title=Coconut Handbook |date=2016 |chapter=8. The Chemistry of Coconut Milk and Cream|publisher=Tetra Pak International S.A. |isbn=978-91-7773-948-7 |chapter-url=https://coconuthandbook.tetrapak.com/chapter/chemistry-coconut-milk-and-cream}} Coconut cream can be dehydrated as [[coconut milk powder]], with a far longer [[shelf life]]. This terminology is not always followed in commercial coconut milk sold in Western countries.{{cite book |last1=Lewis |first1=Susana |last2=Lewis |first2=Charles |title=A Taste of Paradise |date=2012 |publisher=Psy Press |isbn=978-1-938318-00-9 |page=18 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RH4nDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA18}} Coconut milk can also be used to produce [[milk substitute]]s (sometimes differentiated as "coconut milk beverages"); these products are meant for drinking, not cooking. A sweetened, processed, coconut milk product from [[Puerto Rico]] is also known as ''cream of coconut'', but is distinct from coconut cream and is not interchangeable. It is used in many desserts and beverages like the [[piña colada]].{{cite web|url=http://ochef.com/498.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305113910/http://ochef.com/498.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=2016-03-05|title=Coconut milk, cream, and sweetened cream|work=ochef.com}} ==Nutrition== {{Nutritional value |name=Coconut milk, raw (liquid expressed from grated pulp and water) |image= |caption= |serving_size={{nowrap|100 g}} |kJ=962 |carbs=5.5 g |starch= |sugars=3.3 g |lactose= |fibre= 2.2 g |fat=23.8 g |satfat=21.1 g |transfat= |monofat=1.0 g |polyfat=0.26 g |omega3fat= |omega6fat= |protein=2.3 g |water=67.6 g |alcohol= |caffeine= |vitA_ug=0 |vitA_iu= |betacarotene_ug=0 |lutein_ug= |thiamin_mg=0.03 |riboflavin_mg=0 |niacin_mg=0.76 |pantothenic_mg=0.18 |vitB6_mg=0.03 |folate_ug=16 |vitB12_ug= |vitC_mg=2.8 |vitD_ug= |vitD_iu= |vitE_mg=0.15 |vitK_ug=0.1 |calcium_mg=16 |iron_mg=1.6 |magnesium_mg=37 |manganese_mg=0.92 |phosphorus_mg=100 |potassium_mg=263 |sodium_mg=15 |zinc_mg=0.67 |note=[https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/170172/nutrients Full Report from the USDA FoodData Central Database] }} In a 100 milliliter (ml) portion, coconut milk contains 230 [[kilocalories]] and is 68% water, 24% total [[Fat (nutrition)|fat]], 6% [[carbohydrate]]s, and 2% [[Protein (nutrient)|protein]] (table). The fat composition includes 21 grams of saturated fat, half of which is [[lauric acid]] (table). Coconut milk is a rich source (20% or more of the [[Daily Value]], DV) of [[manganese]] (40% DV per 100 g), with no other [[micronutrient]]s in significant content (table for USDA source). ==Definition and terminology== Coconut milk is a relatively stable [[oil-in-water emulsion]] with proteins that act as [[emulsifier]]s and [[thickening agent]]s. It is opaque and milky white in color and ranges in consistency from watery to creamy. Based on fat content, coconut milk is divided into different subtypes generally simplified into "coconut cream", "coconut milk", and "coconut skim milk", from highest to lowest respectively. Coconut milk and coconut cream (also called "thin coconut milk" and "thick coconut milk", respectively) are traditionally differentiated in countries where coconuts are native based on the stages of extraction. They are also differentiated in modern standards set by the [[Asian and Pacific Coconut Community]] (APCC) and the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] of the [[United Nations]] (FAO). However, the terminologies are not always followed in commercial coconut milk (especially in western countries) because these standards are not mandatory. This can cause confusion among consumers.
