'''Vodka Cruiser''' is a line of brightly coloured [[vodka]]-based [[alcoholic beverage]]s primarily sold in [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. Sometimes described as an [[alcopop]], this premixed drink is available in seventeen flavours, including guava, lemon, lime, passion fruit, pineapple, raspberry, and other flavours depending on location. The product originates from New Zealand, and is produced by [[Asahi Breweries|Asahi Beverages]], formerly known as Independent Liquor.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-09-30 |title=Asahi buys Cruisers and Woodstock |url=https://www.smh.com.au/business/asahi-buys-cruisers-and-woodstock-20110930-1l0xj.html |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref>

Vodka Cruisers normally come in 275 ml (9.3 oz) bottles, so each bottle contains slightly less alcohol than a standard shot. In 2022, Asahi Australia launched a range of limited-edition 3.1L "Double Magnum" sized bottles, containing the volume of roughly 11 regular cruisers, which could be won in a giveaway to celebrate the brand's 21st birthday.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-14 |title=Vodka Cruiser releases new 'Double Magnum' bottles - here's how to get one |url=https://7news.com.au/lifestyle/food-wine/vodka-cruiser-releases-limited-edition-double-magnum-bottles-heres-how-to-get-one-c-6050909 |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=7NEWS |language=en}}</ref>

== Varieties ==
In late 2003, Independent Liquor introduced a "Cruiser Black" range, containing a higher alcohol volume than standard varieties. In New Zealand, Vodka Cruisers are also available in a 7% alcohol, premium formulation sold in cardboard packages containing 12 cans of 250 ml each. According to the package labelling, each can has an alcohol content equivalent to 1.6 standard drinks, though the New Zealand definition of a standard drink would place one can at 1.75 standard drinks. In 2023, Asahi introduced a second high ABV range with the Vodka Cruiser Double line, which contains the equivalent of 2 standard drinks per beverage and comes packaged in 375ml cans rather than the standard 275ml bottles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Enerva |first=Kaycee |date=2023-03-06 |title=Vodka Cruiser's new line has twice the alcohol |url=https://insidefmcg.com.au/2023/03/06/vodka-cruisers-new-line-has-twice-the-alcohol/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Inside FMCG |language=en-AU}}</ref>

In 2009, Independent Distillers attempted to expand the Cruiser brand across a larger range of premix alcoholic beverages with the introduction of new female-oriented drinks, including the [[Alcopop|ready-to-drink]] line "Lady Luck", which contained half the sugar of a standard vodka cruiser, a [[Lager|blonde lager]] under the name "Hummingbird", and a cider under the name of "Apparella".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Team |first=The Shout |date=2009-09-09 |title=New Beer, Cider and RTDs from Independent |url=https://theshout.com.au/new-beer-cider-and-rtds-from-independent/ |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Shout |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=McIntyre |first=Paul |date=2009-09-09 |title=Alcopop maker hums a new tune |url=https://www.smh.com.au/business/companies/alcopop-maker-hums-a-new-tune-20090909-fhmt.html |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref> Each of these product lines were available for a short period before being discontinued. 

In 2012, Asahi Beverages announced the reformulation of the Vodka Cruiser product line in Australia, introducing six new core flavours to replace the original lineup while reducing the drink's sugar content.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-10-24 |title=New Cruiser flavours, less sugar |url=https://theshout.com.au/new-cruiser-flavours-less-sugar/ |website=The Shout}}</ref>

In 2022, Asahi released 600ml long neck versions of the Guava and Raspberry Vodka Cruiser flavours for a limited time in Australia, following demand from fans on social media.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jackson |first=Stefanie |date=2022-09-21 |title=Vodka Cruiser Long Necks are officially here for a good time not a long time |url=https://www.delicious.com.au/drinks/news/article/vodka-cruiser-releases-limited-edition-long-neck-bottles/z0b8ze79 |website=delicious.}}</ref>

Whynatte Bomb:
{{Short description|Cocktail mix of Jägermeister and Whynatte Latte}}
{{Orphan|date=March 2021}}

{{Infobox drink

| image       = Classic Whynatte1.jpg

| type        = [[Mixed drink]]

The '''Whynatte Bomb''' is a [[cocktail]] that is mixed by dropping a shot of [[Jägermeister]] into a glass of [[Whynatte Latte]].<ref name="explosive">[ Whynatte Bomb Buzzworthy] [[Rolling Stone]] Magazine, April 2008.</ref>

The terms “depth charge” and  “bomb shot” refer to cocktails that are made by dropping a [[shot glass]] filled with liquor into another drink.

==Commercial preparation==
[[Image:WhynatteB1.jpg|left|thumb|350px|The preparation of multiple Whynatte Bombs.]]

A Whynatte Bomb is usually sold with a can of [[Whynatte Latte]] (8 oz) or a half-can of Whynatte Latte (4 oz) poured into a [[pint glass]] and  separately accompanied by Jägermeister in a [[shot glass]]. The glass of Jägermeister is then dropped into the Whynatte. Alternatively, some drinkers will pour equal amounts of Jägermeister and Whynatte into an oversized shot glass, or pub glass.

==Jäger-trains==
A Jäger-train is a [[culinary theatre|theatric]] method for preparing the drinks when multiple "Bombs" have been ordered.
		
Glasses of the mixer are lined up, and an empty glass is placed at one end. Shot glasses of Jägermeister are then balanced on the lips of the glasses. The first shot glass (which is on the empty-glass end) is pushed over; it falls into the mixer in the next glass and — if the glasses are correctly positioned — it will simultaneously knock over the next shot glass. A [[domino effect]] will be created, causing each shot glass to fall into a glass of the mixer.

The world record for a Jäger-train is 672, set on June 22, 2008, at the Vegalou Ultra Bar in [[Omaha]], [[Nebraska]], made with the original [[Jägerbomb]].

==Effects on the drinker==
The effects of a Whynatte Bomb are held to be different from those of other alcoholic drinks.  This is attributed to the fact that the [[energy drink]] has a [[Stimulant|stimulating]] effect upon the [[central nervous system]], whereas the alcohol has a [[Depressant|depressing]] effect. Consequently, some of the effects of [[Drunkenness|intoxication]] are masked.

'''''Somaek''''' ({{Korean|hangul=소맥}}) is a South Korean [[beer cocktail]] made with ''[[soju]]'' and [[beer]].<ref name="Park">{{Cite news|last=Park|first=Ju-min|title=Measuring beloved Korean drink, from smooth to blackout|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/korea-drinking/measuring-beloved-korean-drink-from-smooth-to-blackout-idUSL3E7H60Z020110608|accessdate=30 December 2017|work=[[Reuters]]|date=8 June 2011}}</ref><ref name="Schaap">{{Cite news|last=Schaap|first=Rosie|title=Soju for the Soul|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/14/magazine/soju-for-the-soul.html|accessdate=30 December 2017|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=11 June 2015}}</ref> The beer used is typically a lager-style.

== Description ==
It is a [[syllabic abbreviation]] of two Korean words, ''[[soju]]'' ({{lang|ko|소주}}) and ''[[Beer in North Korea|Maekju]]'' ({{lang|ko|맥주}}, "beer").<ref name="Lee">{{Cite news|last=Lee|first=Jean H.|title=Pyeongchang and the South Korea ski culture|url=https://edition.cnn.com/travel/article/skiing-south-korea-pyeongchang/index.html|access-date=30 December 2017|work=[[CNN Travel]]|date=9 February 2017}}</ref>

The ratio varies liberally.<ref name="Park" /> There is no consensus, but it is widely suggested that the ideal ratio is three parts soju to seven parts beer.<ref name="Victoria">[https://www.honestfoodtalks.com/soju-bomb-somaek-korean-drinking-games/#best-ratio SOJU BOMB, SOMAEK, OR SOMAEKCOL?]</ref>

Sumatra Kula:
{{Short description|Type of cocktail}}
The '''Sumatra Kula''' (also known as '''Sumatra cooler''') is a vintage [[Tiki bar|tiki cocktail]] invented by [[Donn Beach]] that calls for light rum, equal parts orange, lime and white grapefruit juices, and is sweetened with a diluted honey mix.<ref>{{cite web |title=US Copyright renewal registrations |url=https://onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu/cce/cache/ComPrints-1969JulDec.pdf |website=onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu |access-date=February 18, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=TIKI DRINK NOSTALGIA |url=https://www.amountainofcrushedice.com/?p=7951 |website=amountainofcrushiced.com |date = 15 November 2009|access-date=February 18, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A Malayan Mystery |url=https://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2011/10/05/mai-kai-cocktail-review-a-malayan-mist-ery/ |website=slammie.com |date=5 October 2011 |accessdate=18 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Cocktails - The Sumatra Kula |url=https://putneyfarm.com/2012/04/12/tiki-cocktails-the-sumatra-kula/ |website=putneyfarm.com |date=April 12, 2012 |access-date=February 18, 2019}}</ref>

==History==
The Sumatra Kula cocktail was created by Donn Beach, also known as "the beachcomber" because of his ''Don the Beachcomber'' chain of restaurants, and may have been one of his very first drinks, allegedly gaining notoriety after he served it to a reporter from the ''[[New York Tribune]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Don The Beachcomber |url=http://www.donthebeachcomber.com/pages/about-us |website=donthebeachcomber.com |access-date=16 February 2019}}</ref> A book co-authored by his ex-wife Phoebe Beach claims it was his very first original mixed drink and sold for 25 cents.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beaschcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu|page = xii}}</ref> The drink as appearing on a later cocktail menu from his Hollywood location depicts it as being served in a tall curved glass accompanied by a leafy garnish and selling for 85 cents.<ref>{{cite web |title=Donn the Beacomber menu |url=https://scholarsarchive.jwu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=https://www.google.com/&httpsredir=1&article=1031&context=restaurant_menus |website=scholarsarchive.jwu.edu/ |access-date=18 February 2019}}</ref> The drink was not typically ordered at other types of bars but began gaining attention again during the 21st century resurgence in [[tiki culture]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Frou Frou drinks get their day in the sun |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/the-scene/food-drink/Frou-Frou-Drinks-Get-Their-Day-in-the-Sun.html |website=nbcchicago.com |date=27 July 2009 |accessdate=February 18, 2019}}</ref>

Named in part in reference to [[Sumatra]], some also believe that the word "kula" may be a separate and generic reference to the [[Kula ring|"Kula exchange"]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Sumatra Kula- Don the Beachcomber| date=12 December 2016 |url=https://translate.google.com/translate?hl=en&sl=it&u=http://www.giannizottola.com/2016/12/12/sumatra-kula-ricette-tiki/&prev=search|access-date=February 18, 2019}}</ref> which is a reciprocal exchanging of social gifts.{{cn|date=February 2019}} Beach traveled on the cheap through places where Kula was practiced such as Papua New Guinea,<ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki |url=https://www.americanheritage.com/tiki |website=americanheritage.com |access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> making the claim both plausible and speculative. 
In addition to being an explorer of the south pacific, Beach also traveled heavily both as a [[rum-runner]] and when he served overseas in France and Italy during World War II.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beaschcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu}}</ref>

The cocktail is also sometimes mistakenly referred to as a ''Sumatra cooler'', either an intentional play on words or a misunderstanding between similarly sounding "kula" and "cooler" drinks on Beach's menus (such as the [[Q.B. Cooler]]). Regardless, the Sumatra Kula would not be a typical "cooler" drink, as it does not contain any form of [[Carbonated_water|sparkling water]] or other carbonated beverage.

== Variations ==
Like many tiki drinks, multiple variations existed as popular cocktails whose ingredients were not known were "estimated" and given the same name at competing bars.  At the ''Alila Bar'' in Bali tangerine juice and triple-sec was added.<ref>{{cite web |title=Alila menu |url=https://www.alilahotels.com/documents/alila_ubud/alilaubud_cocktail_menu.pdf |website=alilahotels.com |access-date=February 18, 2019 |archive-date=February 19, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190219015647/https://www.alilahotels.com/documents/alila_ubud/alilaubud_cocktail_menu.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[Tiki Ti]] adds [[fassionola]], a passion fruit syrup sometimes credited to Beach.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sumatra Kula |url=http://www.tikiroom.com/tikicentral/bb/viewtopic.php?topic=12538&forum=10)&7 |website=tikiroom.com |access-date=February 18, 2019}}</ref>

Test pilot (cocktail):
{{short description|Type of cocktail}}
The '''test pilot''' cocktail is a vintage [[Tiki culture|tiki drink]] invented by Donn Beach. Beach was known for changing his recipes over time,<ref>{{cite web |title=Jet Pilot soars over its ancestors |url=http://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2012/02/07/mai-kai-cocktail-review-jet-pilot-soars-over-its-ancestors-with-flying-colors/ |website=slammie.com |date=7 February 2012 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> and multiple versions of the test pilot attributed to both him and others make the cocktail one of his more frequently imitated and varied tiki drinks.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=96 }}</ref> Test pilot recipes call for multiple rums and typically include the use of [[falernum]] syrup and lime juice. The more popular also include Pernod ([[pastis]]/[[absinthe]]) and [[bitters]].

==Test pilot versions==
A recipe from a [[Don the Beachcomber]] drink guide calls for 1 oz of Lemon Hart Demerara 151 proof rum and 3/4 oz each of Jamaican dark rum, Puerto Rican dark rum, lime juice, grape juice, and honey. Two dashes each of bitters and grenadine should also be added, then flash blended with cracked ice and served in a double [[old fashioned glass]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beaschcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu|page=47}}</ref> The date of the recipe's origin and when and where it was served is not mentioned.

Another version that Jeff Berry attributes to Donn Beach from circa 1941 while less strong is still very potent and calls for 1 1/2 oz of Jamaican dark rum, 3/4 oz of Puerto Rican light rum, 3 teaspoons of [[Cointreau]], 1/8 a teaspoon of Pernod, a 1/2 oz of both lime juice and falernum syrup, and a dash of bitters.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=96 }}</ref> The use of Pernod and bitters was employed by Beach as one of his signature combinations, and some cocktail enthusiasts feel it is a pivotal part of the recipe.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2006/08/01/test-pilot/ |website=cocktailchronicles.com |date=August 2006 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Classic Tiki - The Jet Pilot |url=https://cold-glass.com/2016/06/05/classic-tiki-the-jet-pilot/ |website=cold-glass.com |date=5 June 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Tiki Drink Recipe |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/04/test-pilot-tiki-drink-recipe.html |website=seriouseats.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> Several additional cocktail recipe references choose to highlight this version.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Cocktail Recipe |url=https://tuxedono2.com/test-pilot-cocktail-recipe |website=tuxedono2.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://www.myrecipes.com/recipe/test-pilot |website=myrecipes.com |accessdate=19 February 2019 |archive-date=3 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190303201505/https://www.myrecipes.com/recipe/test-pilot |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Recipe |url=https://www.supercall.com/recipe/test-pilot-recipe |website=supercall.com |date=9 August 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://kindredcocktails.com/cocktail/test-pilot |website=kindredcocktails.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

A [[Trader Vic's|Trader Vic]] test pilot version listed in his 1972 revised drink guide switches the lime juice for lemon and jettisons the Pernod and bitters, calling only for 1 3/4 oz dark Jamaican rum, 3/4 oz light Puerto Rican rum, 1/4 oz of Cointreau, 1/4 oz falernum, and 1/4 oz lemon juice.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Trader Vic's Bartenders Guide, Revised |date=1972 |publisher=[[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] |location=Garden City, NY |edition=revised|page=186}}</ref>  ''Difford's Guide'' chose to highlight the Trader Vic's version.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1940/test-pilot |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

==The Jet Pilot==
Some Beachcomber and Trader Vic competitors named their versions as the ''Jet Pilot'', including at [[Joseph Stephen Crane|The Luau]] restaurant and the [[Mai-Kai Restaurant|Mai-Kai]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pilot Tiki Cocktails |url=https://blog.distiller.com/pilot-tiki-cocktails/ |website=blog.distiller.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Classic Tiki - The Jet Pilot |url=https://cold-glass.com/2016/06/05/classic-tiki-the-jet-pilot/ |website=cold-glass.com |date=5 June 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> The Jet Pilot was similar to Beach's 1941 version but was slightly spicier with the addition of stronger rum, grapefruit juice, and cinnamon syrup.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Classics Jet Pilot |url=http://cocktailchem.blogspot.com/2011/12/tiki-classics-jet-pilot.html |website=cocktailchem.blogspot.com |date=6 December 2011 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jet Pilot Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/jet-pilot-cocktail-recipe-760532 |website=thespruceeats.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

==Impact on tiki culture==
Beyond the Jet Pilot, other aviation themed tiki cocktails include the similarly named ''Ace Pilot'', Don Beach's [[Q.B. Cooler]], and Trader Vic's [[PB2Y (cocktail)|PB2Y]] (named after the Navy's [[Consolidated PB2Y Coronado|Coronado plane]]).

A [[tiki bar]] named ''Test Pilot'' operates in [[Santa Barbara, California]], that serves a test pilot cocktail, described as having a flavor profile of "house rum blend, clove, citrus, bitters, [and] absinthe foam".<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=http://www.testpilotcocktails.com/ |website=testpilotcocktails.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

Whistle Belly Vengeance:
{{Short description|17th- and 18th-century British drink}}
'''Whistle Belly Vengeance''' is a drink that was made in 17th- and 18th-century Britain and in [[British North America]]. It was made from [[sour beer]] mixed with [[molasses]] and [[bread crumbs]] or crusts, though one recipe printed in 1982 also states dried [[pumpkin]] could be used. In some parts of North America it was drunk as a breakfast.

== Description ==
The drink is known to have been made in the 17th- and 18th-century British Isles and in British North America as a means of making sour beer more drinkable. It was generally made by mixing quantities of sour beer with molasses and breadcrumbs. Richard Erdoes says they came from [[rye bread|"rye-injun" bread]].<ref name=erdoes>{{cite book |last1=Erdoes |first1=Richard |title=1,000 Remarkable Facts about Booze |date=1981 |publisher=Rutledge |isbn=978-0-8317-0958-7 |page=27 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=anJi1zyj1DYC |language=en}}</ref>  The mixture was boiled together in a large kettle and served hot.<ref name=erdoes/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Steele |first1=Joel Dorman |title=Barnes' Centenary History: One Hundred Years of American Independence |date=1875 |publisher=Barnes |page=127 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gdlAAAAAIAAJ |language=en}}</ref>  A 1960 book by the [[Christian Schmidt Brewing Company]] states that crusts of [[brown bread]] could be used in place of breadcrumbs.<ref name=schmidt>{{cite book |title=Taverns of Yesteryear |date=1960 |publisher=C. Schmidt & Sons |page=19 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IHFNAQAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref>  A 1982 work  by the [[American Flint Glass Workers' Union]] describes a recipe of {{convert|1|USflgal|litre}} of weak and sour beer, {{convert|1|USqt|litre}} of molasses and {{convert|1|USdryqt|litre}} of dry bread crumbs or dried pumpkin.<ref>{{cite book |title=American Flint |date=1982 |publisher=American Flint Glass Workers' Union |page=29 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eJ1ZAAAAYAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

A drink by the same name (or sometimes known as "Whip Belly Vengeance") served in the Caribbean is different. Made from a mixture of rum, gin and molasses, it was formerly drunk by the lower classes in that region.<ref>{{cite book |title=Sales Management |date=1961 |publisher=Dartnell Corporation |page=161 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TnoWAQAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

== Use ==
In the 17th and 18th centuries, some guests arriving late at roadside inns found it was the only drink available.<ref name=schmidt/> In some parts of North America, it was drunk as a form of breakfast.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Watson |first1=John Fanning |title=Annals of Philadelphia, and Pennsylvania, in the Olden Time: Being a Collection of Memoirs, Anecdotes, and Incidents of the City and Its Inhabitants, and of the Earliest Settlements of the Inland Part of Pennsylvania |date=1884 |publisher=E. S. Stuart |page=254 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zkg6AQAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref> The American revolutionary era patriot [[James Otis Jr.]] was fond of the drink. He continued to frequent the Royal Coffee House in [[Boston]] long after it had been taken over by British soldiers, because of his fondness for their Whistle Belly Vengeance, which was mixed with rum.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cahill |first1=Robert |title=New England's Riotous Revolution |date=1987 |publisher=Chandler-Smith |isbn=978-0-916787-12-7 |page=25 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qIZ4AAAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

'''''The Oxford Companion to Spirits & Cocktails''''' ('''''OCSC''''') is a book in the [[Book series|series]] of [[Oxford Companions]] published by [[Oxford University Press]]. The book provides an alphabetically arranged reference to [[Liquor|spirit]]s, [[cocktail]]s and other elements of the bar industry, compiled and edited by David Wondrich and Noah Rothbaum, with contributions by several writers including [[Doug Frost (wine)|Doug Frost]], [[Garrett Oliver]] and [[Audrey Saunders]].<ref name="NYT">{{Cite news|last=Garner|first=Dwight|date=2021-12-13|title=An Encyclopedic New Guide to Cocktails Stirred, Shaken, Rolled, Tossed, Swizzled, Muddled...|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/13/books/oxford-cocktails-spirits-david-wondrich-noah-rothbaum.html|access-date=2023-01-03|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="OCSC">{{cite OCSC}}</ref> Also notably contributing to the book is pioneering bartender [[Dale DeGroff]].<ref name="NYT"/> The work is considered the first reference book on the history and trends of distilled spirits.<ref name="RUSA"/>

The reference work includes about 1,150 entries across 864 pages,<ref name="NYT"/> including 30 [[Book design|preliminaries]].<ref name="WP"/> Over 150 writers contributed, including bartenders, distillers, historians, spirits journalists, brewers, and anthropologists. Wondrich, a prolific cocktail historian, was previously author of ''Imbibe!'' and ''Punch'', and has a Ph.D. in Comparative Literature from [[New York University]]. Wondrich took nine years in leading the writing and compiling of the book, having begun in 2012.<ref name="Epicurious"/><ref name="WP"/> The book is a relatively new part of the ''Oxford Companions'' series, the first book of which was published in 1932. This is due to a larger interest in cocktails and spirits in the 21st century, following ''Oxford Companions'' books [[The Oxford Companion to Wine|on wine]] (published 1994) and [[The Oxford Companion to Beer|on beer]] (published 2011).<ref name="WP"/>

The book's introduction describes why the book was laid out as it is, including a focus on origins, early histories, myths and legends, context and analysis. It stays away from more commonplace facts accessible on Wikipedia.<ref name="Epicurious"/>

During the writing process, the book's entries grew; the writers were initially nervous to find enough material, and then became confident; by 2014 the source material became overwhelming. Eventually their compilation was large enough to force the editors to stop; they also limited their scope in several ways, including by omitting reference to anyone who started their career after 2004, at the start of the [[cocktail renaissance]].<ref name="WP"/>

==Reception==
''[[The New York Times]]'' reviewed the book in 2021, describing its thorough coverage of "nearly every aspect of its subject matter, from absinthe spoons to maceration to the Zombie". The article relayed that some of the book's entries are "tight" and "witty", including entries on bartenders, remote bars, neglected writers and the like. Nevertheless the ''Times'' found some material to be "heavy going", including entries on cryoextraction, water-bath stills and sour mash; a nine-page entry on distillation; and long essays on the world region by region.<ref name="NYT"/>

Aaron Goldfarb, writing for ''[[Epicurious]]'' in 2021, claimed the book "will answer every question you've ever had about cocktails".<ref name="Epicurious">{{Cite web|last=Goldfarb|first=Aaron|date=2021-11-04|title='The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails' Will Answer Every Question You've Ever Had About Cocktails|url=https://www.epicurious.com/shopping/the-oxford-companion-to-spirits-and-cocktails-will-answer-every-question-youve-ever-had-about-cocktails-article|access-date=2023-01-03|website=Epicurious|language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2022, the book won the annual Dartmouth Medal, given by librarians of the [[Reference and User Services Association]] (a division of [[American Library Association]]), to outstanding reference works.<ref name="RUSA">{{Cite web|last=Moore|first=Nina|date=2022-01-23|title=Dartmouth Medal for excellence in reference awarded to The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails|url=https://rusaupdate.org/2022/01/dartmouth-medal-for-excellence-in-reference-awarded-to-the-oxford-companion-to-spirits-and-cocktails/|access-date=2023-01-03|website=RUSA Update|language=en-US}}</ref>

Top-shelf liquor:
{{Short description|Marketing description}}
'''Top-shelf liquor''' (or "premium liquor") is a term used in marketing to describe higher-priced alcoholic beverages, typically stored on the top shelves within bars.<ref name=winenthusiast>{{Cite web |title=What Are Top Shelf Liquors—And Does it Matter {{!}} Wine Enthusiast |url=https://www.wineenthusiast.com/basics/top-shelf-liquor-explained/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=www.wineenthusiast.com|date=April 2022 }}</ref> This contrasts to a "rail" or [[well drink]], which are lower cost beverages typically stored on the lower shelves of the bartender's rack.<ref name="Lai">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QyusKkN-tqgC&q=rail+well+vs+call+vs+top-shelf&pg=PA7 |title=Bartending 101: The Basics of Mixology |publisher=[[St. Martin's Press]] |others=[[Harvard Student Agencies, Inc.]] |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-312-34906-6 |editor1-last=Lai |editor1-first=Anne |edition=4th |pages=7–9 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref><ref name="Kulp">{{cite book |last1=Kulp |first1=Kayleigh |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JWCrqWDA_foC&pg=PA113 |title=Booze for Babes: The Smart Woman's Guide to Drinking Spirits Right |publisher=Hundred Proof Publishing Co. |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-9857731-0-6 |page=113 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref><ref name="Katsigris2012">{{cite book |last1=Katsigris |first1=Costas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mwCACgAAQBAJ&q=well&pg=PA704 |title=The Bar and Beverage Book |last2=Thomas |first2=Chris |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-470-24845-4 |edition=5th |page=704}}</ref><ref name="Feinstein">{{cite book |last1=Feinstein |first1=Andrew H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2WPWUeSITlQC&pg=PA567 |title=Purchasing: Selection and Procurement for the Hospitality Industry |last2=Stefanelli |first2=John M. |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons, Inc.]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-470-31485-2 |page=567 |ref=. |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref> 

== Tiers of beverages ==
[[File:Our_bartender_at_Superior,_New_Orleans_2016.jpg|right|thumb|200x200px|The high shelves behind the bartender at New Orleans' Superior bar display the establishment's expensive, "top shelf" liquor brands.]]
The [[Distilled Spirits Council of the United States|Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS)]] divides all spirit categories into four segments: standard, premium, high-end premium, and super premium, with each of the latter three categories often colloquially described under the umbrella of "top shelf".<ref name="winenthusiast" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Your Guide to Premium Spirits: How and When to Buy |url=https://tastersclub.com/blogs/articles/premium-spirits |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Taster's Club |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Highland |first=Carol |date=2021-11-04 |title=The Difference Between Well, Premium And Top Shelf Liquor {{!}} Luxury Activist |url=https://luxuryactivist.com/lifestyle/the-difference-between-well-premium-and-top-shelf-liquor/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>

The categories of premium and super-premium beverage describe top-shelf liquors which may possess additional special attributes, including, but not limited to: [[brand]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=goat |date=2021-01-20 |title=What makes a premium spirit? |url=https://bbbdrinks.com/what-makes-a-premium-spirit/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=bbb drinks |language=en-GB}}</ref> batch size, rarity, aging, craftsmanship, revenue for the manufacturer,<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Galante |first=Meredith |date=2019-07-23 |title=The Hot Trend for a New Generation of Drinkers: Super-Premium Spirits |url=https://www.dimins.com/blog/2019/07/23/new-drinkers-super-premium-spirits/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Dimensional Insight |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=What Exactly Is a Super Premium Spirit Anyway? |url=https://fortune.com/longform/what-is-a-super-premium-spirit/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref> and marketing budget.<ref name=winenthusiast />

Research by [[GlobalData]] forecasts the market share of the premium/super-premium segment to grow by 13% in 2024, with 40% of global liquor consumers already consuming the category.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Growing Premium Cocktail Craze! |url=https://bartenderspiritsawards.com/en/blog/insights-1/the-growing-premium-cocktail-craze-473.htm |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Bartender Spirits Awards |language=en}}</ref>

== Social reception ==
The trend of certain drinks being labeled "top-shelf" or "premium" and being demanded by consumers based on this status is described as "[[premiumization]]."<ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Diageo: Asia leading the premiumization of spirits? |url=https://run.unl.pt/handle/10362/122743 |date=2021-01-18 |degree=masterThesis |first=Joana Beatriz Gonçalves Dos |last=Reis}}</ref>
Increased demand from consumers based on perceived "premium" status has been measured to be on the rise since 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-10 |title=Alcohol Trends 2023: Key Factors Shaping the Industry this Year |url=https://overproof.com/2022/11/10/alcohol-trends-2023/ |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=Overproof |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plata |first1=Alejandro |last2=Motoki |first2=Kosuke |last3=Spence |first3=Charles |last4=Velasco |first4=Carlos |date=2022-03-01 |title=Trends in alcohol consumption in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic: A cross-country analysis |journal=International Journal of Gastronomy and Food Science |volume=27 |article-number=100397 |doi=10.1016/j.ijgfs.2021.100397 |pmid=35003399 |issn=1878-450X|pmc=8717736 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-21 |title=Consumers are buying more premium alcohol, seltzers |url=https://www.supermarketnews.com/beverage/consumers-are-buying-more-premium-alcohol-seltzers |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=Supermarket News |language=en}}</ref>

Premium labeling, however, is often a topic of debate among consumers and critics. Some use the term premium as a measure of quality, describing liquors made with "natural ingredients and more careful distilling and aging processes"<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hsupublished |first=Jeremy |date=2010-06-24 |title=Is Premium Liquor Really Better than the Cheap Stuff? |url=https://www.livescience.com/32665-is-premium-liquor-really-better-than-the-cheap-stuff.html |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=livescience.com |language=en}}</ref> 

To others industry insiders, the term has been described as "meaningless" with those who purchase premium liquors "really just paying for a mass-produced spirit with an excessively high marketing budget."<ref name="winenthusiast" />

Some scientific studies have indicated that one's decision to purchase alcohol perceived as premium is not tied to quality at all, but rather a driven subconscious pursuit of [[Social status|status]], complex social factors and desire to [[Conformity|conform]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cunningham |first=Nicole |date=2023-12-31 |title=The role of social group influences when intending to purchase premium alcohol |journal=Cogent Business & Management |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |doi=10.1080/23311975.2023.2174093 |issn=2331-1975|doi-access=free |hdl=10419/294265 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A '''sour''' is a traditional family of [[mixed drink]]s. ''Sours'' belong to one of the old families of original cocktails and are described by [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] in his 1862 book ''How to Mix Drinks''.<ref name="Cocktail Chronicles">Paul Clarke. [http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2005/09/25/make-yourself-comfortable/ Make Yourself Comfortable]. September 25, 2005. The Cocktail Chronicles. Retrieved on January 1, 2007.</ref> 

Sours are mixed drinks containing a base liquor, [[Lemon juice|lemon]] or [[lime juice]], and a sweetener ([[simple syrup]] or [[orgeat syrup]]).<ref name="Joy 158-159">{{cite book|author=Regan, Gary |title=The Joy of Mixology, The Consummate Guide to the Bartender's Craft |year=2003 |publisher=Clarkson Potter |isbn=0609608843|pages=158–159}}</ref> [[Egg white|Egg whites]] are also included in some sours.

==Types of sours==

===Gin sour===
The '''gin sour''' is a traditional [[mixed cocktail]] that predates [[Prohibition in the United States]]. It is a simple combination of gin, lemon juice, and sugar. Adding carbonated water to this turns it into a [[gin fizz]].

It was popular during the 1940s, and [[Kevin Starr]] includes it in "an array of drinks (the gin sour, the whiskey sour, the [[Rickey (cocktail)#The gin Rickey|gin Rickey]], the [[Tom Collins]], the [[Pink lady (cocktail)|pink lady]], the [[Old fashioned (cocktail)|old fashioned]]) that now seem period pieces, evocative of another era".{{ref|starr}}

===Pisco sour===
{{main|Pisco sour}}
The classic '''pisco sour''' recipe contains [[pisco]] brandy (usually an un-aged grape brandy from Perú), fresh lime juice, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup, egg white, and [[bitters]].<ref name="LA Speakeasy">Navarro, V. [https://www.laspeakeasy.com/pisco-sour/ Classic Pisco Sour] ''LA Speakeasy''</ref> It is [[Cocktail shaker|shaken]], [[Cocktail strainer|strained]], and served [[Straight up (bartending)|straight]] in a cocktail glass then garnished with the bitters (cinnamon can be used). The addition of egg white creates a foamy head when shaken before serving. While pisco sour is flavoured with key lime by default, pisco is combined with other fruit to create mango sour, maracuya ([[passion fruit]]) sour, lucuma sour and so forth.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://peru.com/estilo-de-vida/gastronomia/maracuya-sour-que-necesitas-y-como-se-prepara-este-exquisito-trago-noticia-213918 |title=Maracuya sour: Qué necesitas y cómo se prepara este exquisito trago |first=Redacción |last=Peru.com |date=December 6, 2013 |website=Perú.com}}</ref> Peru has a National Pisco Sour Day (which lasts a weekend) in mid-February,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://elcomercio.pe/noticias/dia-del-pisco-sour |title=Todas las noticias de Día del Pisco Sour |website=El Comercio}}</ref> and Chile has Pisco Day in mid-May.

===Rum sour===

The basic [[Daiquiri]], sometimes called a Daiquiri sour, is made with rum, lime juice and simple syrup.<ref>{{cite web |title=Daiquiri cocktail |website=Difford's |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail}}</ref> One account of the drink's origin is that the general manager of the Spanish-American Iron Core Company, which operated the "Daiquiri" mine, ran out of gin one night when making gin sour for his guests, and switched to rum. This rum sour became known as the Daiquiri. However, earlier printed recipes for rum sour exist such as one from [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] from 1887.<ref>{{cite book |last=Broom |first=Dave |title=Rum The Manual |date=2016 |publisher=Octopus Books |isbn=9781784720667 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HfwyDQAAQBAJ}}</ref>

===Whiskey sour===

{{main|Whiskey sour}}

The '''whiskey sour''' is a [[mixed drink]] containing [[bourbon whiskey]] or [[rye whiskey]], lemon juice, sugar, and optionally a dash of egg white to make it a Boston Sour. It is shaken and served either straight or over ice. The traditional garnish is half an orange slice and a [[maraschino cherry]]. If floated with claret red wine it's called a [[New York sour]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Difford |first=Simon |title=New York Sour |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3398/new-york-sour-cocktail |access-date=September 29, 2022 |website=Diffords Guide}}</ref>

A notable variant of the whiskey sour is the [[Ward 8 (cocktail)|Ward 8]], which often is based with either bourbon or rye whiskey, both lemon and orange juices, and grenadine syrup as the sweetener. The egg white sometimes employed in other whiskey sours is generally not included in this variation.

===Other sours===
* '''[[Amaretto sour]]''': [[Amaretto]] liqueur, lemon juice and sometimes egg white, bitters or sugar syrup.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amaretto Sour|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/53/amaretto-sour|website=Difford's Guide|access-date=21 March 2018}}</ref>
* '''Brandy sour''' or [[brandy daisy]] (Jerry Thomas, 1887): brandy, clear or orange [[curaçao liqueur|curaçao]], sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''[[Caipirinha]]''': [[Cachaça]], sugar, lime, ice in an [[old fashioned glass]].
* '''[[Brandy sour (Cyprus)|Cypriot brandy sour]]''': [[Cyprus brandy]], lemon cordial and bitters, stirred in a tall glass, and topped with soda or lemonade.
* '''[[b:Bartending/Cocktails/Glossary#M|Midori sour]]''': Honeydew melon liquor, grenadine, lemon juice. Poured properly, it resembles a green [[Tequila sunrise (cocktail)|tequila sunrise]] with visible layers.
* '''Santa Cruz sour''' (Jerry Thomas, 1887): Santa Cruz rum, sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''Tequila sour''': Tequila, lemon juice, lime juice, agave nectar, Bittercube Corazon bitters, egg white.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tequila Sour|url=http://recipe.awesomedrinks.com/recipe/tequila-sour/|website=Awesome Drinks}}</ref>

Wincarnis:
{{Short description|British tonic wine}} '''Wincarnis''' is a brand name of a British [[tonic wine]], popular in [[Jamaica]] and some other former British colonies.{{citation |url=http://edinburghnews.scotsman.com/index.cfm?id=595292004 |title=Scottish tonic that's a hit in the Caribbean |work= Edinburgh News |date=25 May 2004 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20050317043229/http://edinburghnews.scotsman.com/index.cfm?id=595292004 |archivedate=17 March 2005}} The name is derived from "wine ''carnis''", from the Latin meaning "of meat." It is a [[fortified wine]] (17%) now made to a secret recipe of grape juice, malt extracts, herbs and spices, but it no longer contains meat. Wincarnis has a similar taste to sweet [[sherry]]. [[File:The Great Restorative - geograph.org.uk - 532334.jpg|thumb|"Wincarnis: The Great Restorative," advertisement in [[Goodwick]], Wales.]] ==History== Wincarnis was produced before 1881{{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/palmersindextot59unkngoog/palmersindextot59unkngoog_djvu.txt|title=Palmer's index to "The times" newspaper (1884)|year=1790}} by Coleman and Co Ltd in [[Norwich]], England. Devised by William Juby Coleman, it was originally called '''Coleman's Liebig's Extract of Meat and Malt Wine'''.{{cite web | last = Homan | first = Peter | authorlink = | title = Medicated Cheer | publisher = The Pharmaceutical Journal | date = December 2003 | url = http://www.pharmj.com/Editorial/20031220/christmas/cheer.html |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071224144949/http://www.pharmj.com/Editorial/20031220/christmas/cheer.html |archivedate=24 December 2007 | doi = | accessdate = 2007-09-17 }}{{citation |url=https://www.edp24.co.uk/features/what-a-tonic-the-tale-of-how-wincarnis-energised-a-nation-1-5060028 |title=What a tonic! The tale of how Wincarnis energised a nation |date=13 June 2017 | first=Derek |last= James |work=Eastern Daily Press|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170613162718/https://www.edp24.co.uk/features/what-a-tonic-the-tale-of-how-wincarnis-energised-a-nation-1-5060028/ |archive-date=13 June 2017 }} It was advertised as made with [[Port Wine]], [[Liebig's Extract of Meat Company|Liebig's Extract of Meat]] and [[Malt#Malt extract|extract of Malt]], and called "the finest tonic and restorative in the world". The brand was eventually owned by Hedges & Butler (part of [[Bass Brewery|Bass]]), which was acquired in 1998 by Ian Macleod Distillers Ltd of Broxburn, Scotland. Wincarnis is currently made by Broadland Wineries in Norfolk, and sold by Macleod.{{Cite web |title=Wincarnis Original |url=https://www.broadlanddrinks.com/brands/wincarnis/wincarnis-original |access-date=21 April 2023 |website=Broadland Drinks}} ==Markets== Wincarnis is now marketed as an aperitif wine. In Jamaica it is mixed with [[stout]] and [[milk]]. In Singapore, Malaysia and the Gulf, it is taken by new mothers as a tonic. It is well known by older people in the UK who use it as a tonic when not well. Ian MacLeod Distilleries marketing offers the ingredients:
Wincarnis Tonic Wine is a carefully formulated blend of enriched wine and malt extract with a unique infusion of selected therapeutic herbs and spices including [[gentian root]], [[mugwort]], [[angelica root]], [[balm mint]], [[fennel]] seed, [[coriander]] seed, [[peppermint]] leaves, [[cardamom]] seeds and cassia bark ... is a natural tonic incorporating herbs traditionally recognised for their ability to combat common ailments and alleviate their symptoms. It is rich in vitamins, especially energy-giving Vitamin B complex, and can have beneficial effects on the circulation system and blood pressure.[http://www.ianmacleod.com/brands/?id=26 Wincarnis Wines – Ian Macleod Distillers]
